items.title: AWS Network Firewall introduces automated internet firewall mode (Preview)
items.summary: AWS Network Firewall now offers automated internet firewall mode (Preview). In this mode, Network Firewall applies your centrally defined rules to traffic at the internet gateway of each of your virtual private clouds (VPCs). It also performs built-in network address translation (NAT) for outbound-only connections. A subnet that reaches the internet needs only one route, directly to the internet gateway. You no longer need to deploy firewall endpoints and NAT gateways in each VPC and configure the routes between them and the subnets. If you’re new to internet traffic inspection, you can start with AWS managed rule groups for Network Firewall . AWS security experts maintain and update these rule groups to help protect your workloads against changing threats. You can deploy these managed rule groups centrally across your environment. With automated internet firewall mode, you can: Inspect traffic at the internet gateway – Each VPC gets its own firewall for inbound and outbound IPv4 and IPv6 traffic, with built-in NAT for outbound-only IPv4 connections. Manage centrally, inspect in each VPC – You define policies in AWS Network Security Manager or start from an AWS managed template. Each VPC’s traffic passes its own firewall, so each VPC you add brings its own inspection capacity. The same central policy also works for VPCs with overlapping Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) ranges. Extend coverage to new VPCs – You can create a scope that includes all existing and future VPCs, so your policy applies to new VPCs when teams create them. In this post, we explain how automated internet firewall mode works and how it fits your existing architecture. We also walk through the steps to deploy it across your environment. How automated internet firewall mode works In automated internet firewall mode, Network Firewall applies your rules at the internet gateway of each VPC. Before this launch, inspecting a VPC’s internet traffic meant routing each subnet through a firewall endpoint. Resources that needed outbound-only connectivity also went through a NAT gateway. This mode helps simplify that model by moving inspection to each VPC’s internet gateway. Each subnet now has one route to the internet gateway, where the firewall inspects the traffic and performs built-in NAT (Figure 1). Figure 1: Outbound traffic before and after automated internet firewall Each VPC gets its own firewall, not a share of one. When you use VPC endpoint associations to protect multiple VPCs with one firewall, those VPCs share that firewall’s capacity in each Availability Zone. In automated internet firewall mode, each VPC’s firewall supports throughput of up to 100 Gbps in each Availability Zone ( Service quotas ). It also works when VPCs have overlapping CIDR ranges, because their traffic doesn’t meet in a shared inspection network where the addresses would conflict. The firewall inspects inbound and outbound traffic. For outbound-only connectivity, the firewall first inspects the traffic and then performs NAT, so your rules and logs see each workload’s private IP address. Built-in NAT translates outbound IPv4 connections from resources without a public IP address, and IPv6 traffic isn’t translated. If your destinations accept only allowlisted source addresses, an Amazon VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM) policy lets you choose the NAT addresses that automated internet firewall mode uses ( NAT for outbound traffic ). The firewall uses Network Firewall Next Generation firewall policies . You can start from AWSManagedTemplateIGWFirewallBaseline , an AWS managed template that AWS security experts maintain. You can then add AWS managed rule groups and your own rule groups . Automated internet firewall mode only inspects traffic that crosses the internet gateway. For traffic between VPCs and to on-premises networks over AWS Direct Connect or AWS Site-to-Site VPN , we recommend a transit gateway-attached Network Firewall . Subnet connectivity options Before this launch, a public subnet had a direct route to the internet gateway, and its resources used public IP addresses, so they could connect out and accept inbound connections. A private subnet had no direct route, and its resources reached the internet through a NAT gateway. With automated internet firewall mode, a subnet that reaches the internet can route 0.0.0.0/0 directly to the internet gateway, so the route table no longer separates public from private. Instead, each subnet’s connectivity type decides how its resources reach the internet. You set it in the Network Security Manager policy, not on the subnet. Table 1 maps each type to the model you know. Connectivity type Works like What happens Flexible (recommended) A public and a private subnet in one A resource with a public IP address, such as an Elastic IP address, gets bidirectional access, as in a public subnet. A resource without one gets outbound-only access through built-in NAT, similar to a private subnet. Bidirectional A public subnet Resources with a public IP address connect out and accept inbound connections. Resources without one can’t reach the internet. Outbound-only A private IPv4 subnet behind a NAT gateway, or an IPv6 subnet behind an egress-only internet gateway Unsolicited inbound connections are dropped. Resources without a public IP address connect out through built-in NAT, and resources with one keep their own address. Excluded A subnet without a firewall Traffic bypasses the firewall and built-in NAT. The firewall inspects traffic in each type except excluded (Figure 2). Each policy sets one default connectivity type for all subnets in scope. You can override it for specific subnets based on tags or on Amazon Resource Name (ARN) . When a subnet matches more than one override, the first one in the list applies. Figure 2: Flexible, bidirectional, and outbound-only subnets are inspected. Excluded subnets aren’t. Connectivity types also decide which inbound connections reach your resources. The firewall inspects inbound connections to resources with a public IP address in flexible and bidirectional subnets, such as the Network Load Balancer for a non-HTTP service in Figure 3. Figure 3 also shows the outbound path, where instances without a public IP address connect out through the firewall and then built-in NAT. For web applications and APIs, we still recommend AWS WAF on Amazon CloudFront in front of an Application Load Balancer . You can set that load balancer’s subnet to excluded so Network Firewall doesn’t inspect the same request again. Keep in mind that excluded applies in both directions, so any outbound traffic from that subnet also bypasses the firewall. Figure 3: Inbound and outbound traffic showing inbound, outbound, and excluded connections Managing automated internet firewall mode You manage automated internet firewall mode in AWS Network Security Manager. With AWS Organizations , a central security team deploys policies from the Network Security Manager administrator account to the whole organization, to organizational units (OUs), or to specific accounts. Network Security Manager also supports a single-account model, where it applies policies only to that account’s VPCs. You can start from the Network Firewall console or the Network Security Manager console, but the firewall itself is read-only outside Network Security Manager. Network Security Manager uses three components (Figure 4): Policy – Combines rules and templates with the connectivity type, enforcement mode, logging, and priority. Rules are the building blocks. A traffic inspection rule decides how the firewall handles traffic, and a firewall configuration rule sets options such as the enforcement mode or logging. A template is an ordered, reusable group of rules, such as AWSManagedTemplateIGWFirewallBaseline , that you can share across policies. Scope – Selects your organization, OUs , accounts, or VPCs. Deployment – Binds a policy to a scope. Network Security Manager then creates and manages a firewall in each VPC in scope. Figure 4: A deployment binds a policy to a scope, and Network Security Manager creates a firewall in each VPC in scope This model matters most when you manage many VPCs. Because Network Security Manager applies the policy at the internet gateway, the firewall is designed so that VPC owners and subnet owners without the proper privileges can’t bypass inspection by changing routes. Subnets set to excluded and Availability Zones where automated internet firewall mode isn’t supported aren’t inspected. Many organizations want one security baseline everywhere, while some accounts, organizational units, or applications need rules in addition to the baseline. To do this, you create two policies, each deployed to its own scope. The organization policy holds a baseline template, and the Account A policy holds the same baseline template plus Account A’s rules (Figure 5). The template lets you maintain the baseline rules once and reuse them in both policies. Where policies overlap, the policy with the lower priority number applies in full, and the policies don’t merge. In Account A, the Account A policy (priority 100) wins over the organization policy (priority 1000) , so it must include the baseline template. Its enforcement mode, logging, and connectivity type also replace the organization policy’s. To learn more, see How AWS Network Security Manager works . Figure 5: The Account A policy, priority 100, takes priority in Account A. Other accounts get the organization policy, priority 1000. Getting started We recommend starting in monitor mode , especially in VPCs with existing workloads. In monitor mode, the firewall logs what your rules would do but doesn’t drop traffic because of them. After the logs show the results you expect, switch the policy to enforce. In this example, we create a policy in monitor mode in six steps. Start from the AWS Management Console for Network Firewall. On the Firewalls page, open the Internet firewalls tab and choose Create in AWS Network Security Manager . The Quick create and deploy page opens in the Network Security Manager console. Select Network Firewall automated internet firewall as the firewall type. Figure 6: Create a new internet firewall Define protections. Choose Manage templates and add AWSManagedTemplateIGWFirewallBaseline . Under Enforcement mode , select Monitor , and choose destinations for alert logs and flow logs. Figure 7: Define protections and set destinations for logs Enter a name for the policy and check its Policy priority . Where policies overlap, the lower number takes priority. The new policy gets a priority that evaluates after your existing policies of the same firewall type, and you can change it later in the policy editor. Figure 8: Set the policy details Set the scope. For example, you can set the scope for Accounts and OUs to include the entire organization and the scope for VPCs to include all existing and future VPCs. To learn more about scopes, see How AWS Network Security Manager works . Figure 9: Set the scope Choose the Subnet connectivity type . For example, select Flex (recommended) . Figure 10: Choose the subnet connectivity type Review your settings and choose Create and deploy . Cross-account visibility lets Network Security Manager see resources in the accounts in the scope. Figure 11: Review and deploy Network Security Manager then creates a firewall at the internet gateway of each VPC in scope. For the full steps, including the organization baseline with account-specific rules, see Getting started with automated internet firewall . Migrating existing VPCs to automated internet firewall mode When you deploy automated internet firewall mode to an existing VPC, you might not need to change routes on day one. With the flexible type, the firewall inspects existing resources and keeps the addresses they already use (Figure 12): Instance with an Elastic IP address – The firewall inspects its traffic, and the instance keeps its Elastic IP address. Instance behind a NAT gateway – The firewall inspects the traffic after the NAT gateway translates it and doesn’t translate it again. Your rules and logs see the NAT gateway’s private IP address as the source. Instance with no public IP address in a subnet that routes to the internet gateway – The firewall inspects its traffic, and built-in NAT gives it outbound-only access, which it didn’t have before. To keep resources without a public IP address isolated from the internet, set the subnet’s connectivity type to bidirectional instead. Resources with a public IP address then keep bidirectional connectivity, and resources without one can’t reach the internet. Figure 12: Day-one source addresses in an existing VPC with Flexible subnets Later, at your own pace, you can retire each NAT gateway by routing its subnets directly to the internet gateway. Built-in NAT then takes over. The source address changes to one that automated internet firewall mode assigns or one from your IPAM policy pool, so update allow lists that name the NAT gateway’s address first. Your logs then show each workload’s private IP address. If you inspect inbound or outbound internet traffic today with Network Firewall endpoints, automated internet firewall mode can take over that inspection. After you confirm that your new policy covers the same rules, you can remove the endpoints and routes that you use for internet traffic. For each architecture, see Working with existing architectures . Availability and pricing Automated internet firewall mode (Preview) is available in all AWS commercial Regions. For pricing, see AWS Network Firewall pricing . During the preview, some features and instance types aren’t supported. For the list, see Automated internet firewall . Features, service quotas , and console labels can change during the preview. Your use of the preview is subject to the Betas and Previews section of the AWS Service Terms . Conclusion In this post, we showed you how automated internet firewall mode applies Network Firewall inspection and built-in NAT at the internet gateway of your VPCs. You define and control policies centrally in Network Security Manager. It is designed so that VPC owners without the proper privileges can’t route around it, and your policy applies to new VPCs in scope when teams create them. To learn more, see Automated internet firewall in the Network Firewall Developer Guide. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Lawton Pittenger Lawton is a Worldwide Security Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS, based in New York City. He helps customers design and implement effective network security controls, and works with AWS service teams to improve security services based on customer feedback. Outside of work, he enjoys skateboarding, snowboarding, and spending time in nature. Akshay Choudhry Akshay is a Principal Product Manager in the Networking and Security Services Team at Amazon Web Services. He’s focused on making virtual private clouds more intuitive and secure for the millions of customers running their workloads on AWS. In his free time, he enjoys exploring the outdoors, trying out new restaurants, and spending time with friends and family.

items.title: Understanding the Root Cause of CVE‑2026‑119618
items.summary: Investigating CVE‑2026‑119618 Recently, Apache released an advisory for CVE-2026-119618, an improper synchronization vulnerability in mod_http2 that causes heap corruption and, according to Apache, can lead to remote code execution. As soon as it was disclosed, we began analyzing the vulnerability to better understand the root cause and to build scanners and detections to identify vulnerable Apache hosts within the Guard platform. While we haven’t gotten a working remote code execution exploit yet, we feel we have a fairly solid understanding of the root cause and wanted to share our analysis with the broader security community, as we are not aware of any detailed public breakdown of the vulnerability so far. Our monitoring systems also picked up several repositories claiming to have exploits for the vulnerability. These repositories often receive very little quality assurance before release, and in one case, a repository claiming a working exploit turned out to have been generated by an agent that simply exposed a CGI script on the Apache server, allowing arbitrary shell commands to be run through a header with nothing to do with the actual vulnerability. Our goal in this article is to share the results of our initial analysis, discuss the Apache internals relevant to understanding how the vulnerability works, cover the temporal debugging setup we used, and walk through an example crash triggered within an Apache worker when reproducing the vulnerability. Our analysis focuses on the source code of Apache HTTPD version 2.4.70. Digging into the Root Cause of the Vulnerability For a rather complex usermode memory corruption vulnerability, the root cause and fix are fairly simple with each requiring only a single-line of code change to address the issue. If we examine the diff responsible for fixing the vulnerability we observe the following change made to the h2_request.c source file: If we dig more into the relevant code, we see that the change was made within the assign_headers function which runs within a mod_http2 worker thread when it is processing an HTTP2 request as shown in the image below. The root cause of the issue comes from modifying the req->headers table from a mod_http2 worker thread. For a non-CONNECT request whose HEADERS carry END_STREAM, if the request has Content-Type but no Content-Length, Apache inserts a Content-Length header with value zero into req->headers before processing it. The issue arises when apr_table_setn is invoked on req->headers to add Content-Length. If the table’s backing array is full (nelts == nalloc), the insertion doubles that array’s current capacity and requests a new backing allocation. The table growth alone is not enough: its apr_palloc must exhaust usable space in the stream pool’s nodes and reach the shared, mutex-free apr_allocator_t. A concurrent c1-side allocation or free through that same allocator can corrupt its free-list state or cause one memnode to be issued to multiple pools. Later destruction of either pool can return the node while the other pool still has live objects, producing use-after-free behavior and further corruption. The core issue is that req->headers is allocated from the stream pool, which inherits the mutex-free allocator used by the c1 connection/session and its stream pools. c1 owns HTTP/2 network and stream lifecycle work, while c2 workers normally process requests using private allocators. If an attacker sends another request to the server while assign_headers executes, c1-side stream work can access the same allocator that the c2 worker incorrectly reaches through req->headers. A race in that allocator’s free-list operations can leave two different pools owning the same memnode. The allocation in assign_headers begins when apr_table_setn inserts a new header into a full table and therefore grows its backing array. To reach the vulnerable shared-allocator operation, that new backing allocation must also exceed the space available from the stream pool’s existing nodes. We will delve into the source code of apr_table_setn in the subsequent section. The process that triggers the race condition is shown in the diagram below: Digging Into the Table Resize Operation Apache Portable Runtime (APR) provides a table implementation within apr_tables.c which is used by HTTPD for representing and requesting headers within an HTTP request. The primary structure used to represent the table is the apr_table_t structure which contains an apr_array_header_t structure. The definition of apr_table_t is shown below: If we dig into apr_array_header_t, we see that it records the number of active elements, the allocated capacity, the size of each element, the owning pool, and a pointer to the backing array of apr_table_entry_t structures, each representing a single header field. The image given below shows the apr_array_header_t structure definition: Each entry is an apr_table_entry_t structure containing a key, value, and checksum. The key is the header name, the value is the header value, and the checksum lets APR reject nonmatching keys before calling strcasecmp during a lookup. Below is an image showing the definition of the apr_table_entry_t structure: Now that we understand the core structures used to represent the request headers structure, we can start digging into how the apr_table_setn function can result in a new heap allocation being triggered. The image below shows the first part of the apr_table_setn function. When a key is set, APR selects one of 32 index buckets from the first byte of the header name and separately computes a case-insensitive checksum from the first four bytes of that name. The table is not partitioned into regions; index_first and index_last merely bound the range that may contain entries colliding in that bucket. The code then starts iterating over the existing elements in the array and checking if an existing header in the table with the same name already exists. In the case of assign_headers it would be checking if “Content-Length” already exists in the table. The more interesting case though is when an entry doesn’t exist in the table. In this case, we hit the add_new_elt (“add new element”) case. In this scenario, the table_push function is called to add a new entry to the table: Internally, the table_push function is an alias to the do_table_push function which wraps the apr_array_push_noclear function: Examining apr_array_push_noclear, we see that when the backing array is full the function doubles its capacity, allocates a new backing store from the table’s pool, and copies the old entries into it. Investigating CVE‑2026‑119618

Recently, Apache released an advisory for CVE-2026-119618, an improper synchronization vulnerability in mod_http2 that causes heap corruption and, according to Apache, can lead to remote code execution. As soon as it was disclosed, we began analyzing the vulnerability to better understand the root cause and to build scanners and detections to identify vulnerable Apache hosts within the Guard platform. While we haven’t gotten a working remote code execution exploit yet, we feel we have a fairly solid understanding of the root cause and wanted to share our analysis with the broader security community, as we are not aware of any detailed public breakdown of the vulnerability so far.

Our monitoring systems also picked up several repositories claiming to have exploits for the vulnerability. These repositories often receive very little quality assurance before release, and in one case, a repository claiming a working exploit turned out to have been generated by an agent that simply exposed a CGI script on the Apache server, allowing arbitrary shell commands to be run through a header with nothing to do with the actual vulnerability.

Our goal in this article is to share the results of our initial analysis, discuss the Apache internals relevant to understanding how the vulnerability works, cover the temporal debugging setup we used, and walk through an example crash triggered within an Apache worker when reproducing the vulnerability. Our analysis focuses on the source code of Apache HTTPD version 2.4.70.

Digging into the Root Cause of the Vulnerability

For a rather complex usermode memory corruption vulnerability, the root cause and fix are fairly simple with each requiring only a single-line of code change to address the issue. If we examine the diff responsible for fixing the vulnerability we observe the following change made to the h2_request.c source file:

If we dig more into the relevant code, we see that the change was made within the assign_headers function which runs within a mod_http2 worker thread when it is processing an HTTP2 request as shown in the image below.

The root cause of the issue comes from modifying the req->headers table from a mod_http2 worker thread. For a non-CONNECT request whose HEADERS carry END_STREAM, if the request has Content-Type but no Content-Length, Apache inserts a Content-Length header with value zero into req->headers before processing it.

The issue arises when apr_table_setn is invoked on req->headers to add Content-Length. If the table’s backing array is full (nelts == nalloc), the insertion doubles that array’s current capacity and requests a new backing allocation.

The table growth alone is not enough: its apr_palloc must exhaust usable space in the stream pool’s nodes and reach the shared, mutex-free apr_allocator_t. A concurrent c1-side allocation or free through that same allocator can corrupt its free-list state or cause one memnode to be issued to multiple pools. Later destruction of either pool can return the node while the other pool still has live objects, producing use-after-free behavior and further corruption.

The core issue is that req->headers is allocated from the stream pool, which inherits the mutex-free allocator used by the c1 connection/session and its stream pools. c1 owns HTTP/2 network and stream lifecycle work, while c2 workers normally process requests using private allocators.

If an attacker sends another request to the server while assign_headers executes, c1-side stream work can access the same allocator that the c2 worker incorrectly reaches through req->headers. A race in that allocator’s free-list operations can leave two different pools owning the same memnode.

The allocation in assign_headers begins when apr_table_setn inserts a new header into a full table and therefore grows its backing array. To reach the vulnerable shared-allocator operation, that new backing allocation must also exceed the space available from the stream pool’s existing nodes. We will delve into the source code of apr_table_setn in the subsequent section.

The process that triggers the race condition is shown in the diagram below:

The image given below shows the apr_array_header_t structure definition:

Each entry is an apr_table_entry_t structure containing a key, value, and checksum. The key is the header name, the value is the header value, and the checksum lets APR reject nonmatching keys before calling strcasecmp during a lookup. Below is an image showing the definition of the apr_table_entry_t structure:

Now that we understand the core structures used to represent the request headers structure, we can start digging into how the apr_table_setn function can result in a new heap allocation being triggered. The image below shows the first part of the apr_table_setn function.

This setup was incredibly powerful when used alongside our agents, such as GPT-5.6-Cyber through OpenAI’s Daybreak Red program. An important part of the exploit development process has been making sure the agents have access to the correct tools. A capable model with only basic tracing and a standard debugger will struggle with a bug like this one, but the same model with access to rr can replay the crash and work backwards through the program state just like a human researcher would.

For example, in the following screenshot, the model used rr to trace every reuse of the freed memnode after the race triggered, until the process eventually crashed in apr_pool_destroy() due to corrupted state. In this case, we were aggressively attempting to retrigger the race across multiple streams on the same TCP connection, and showed that the same physical memnode was reused eight times while a live apr_pool_t and h2_stream still pointed into that memory. It would have been extremely difficult to get this same level of detail on memory and node usage with traditional debugging methods.

Analyzing a Crash Using Temporal Debugging

In this section, we will walk through an example of how temporal debugging can be used to better understand a complex crash condition. In our lab environment, we wrote a basic script to trigger the race condition under httpd running under rr with chaos mode enabled. Ultimately, a segmentation fault was triggered within the strlen function in libc due to an invalid pointer being passed to strlen.

If we examine the stack trace we observe that the crash was related to reading the header fields associated with our request from the headers table. In this scenario, we were racing the creation of a new connection stream with the table resize operation. The race succeeded and both threads received the same underlying memory node.

The assign_headers operation completed first and then the resized headers elements table was overwritten by the other thread with an apr_pool_t and h2_stream structure. This caused corruption of the headers elements table and a crash when it was subsequently read by the HTTP/2 Server Push code which later processed the corrupted request header elements.

We confirm our suspicion by examining req->headers->a.elts and determining that the corrupted values came from an h2_stream structure written over the header-elements array, as shown below:

If we go back in time we can see that the 0x5e1974086258 pointer was allocated within the assign_headers function during the race when the req->headers table was being resized in apr_table_setn.

If we return to the strlen segmentation fault and examine the request memory, we see that req->headers->a.elts points to 0x5e1974086258 and belongs to req->headers->a.pool at 0x5e19741761b8.

At the same time, the memory at 0x5e1974086258 itself also contains a valid apr_pool_t structure which within itself also references 0x5e1974086230. This provides evidence that at the time of crash two live pools both shared the same memnode within their respective active lists and provides further evidence of the race condition triggering as expected.

Being able to trace backwards and forwards in time within an active debugging session has been invaluable to understanding the vulnerability. In this case, the crash itself happened in the HTTP/2 Server Push code, well after the race had already corrupted req->headers. For many race condition bugs, especially those involving internal allocator corruption, it’s often hard to correlate a crash back to the exact request or thread involved in the data race. Being able to step backwards from the crash to the write that corrupted the memory lets you see exactly which thread and request were responsible.

Lessons Learned from Agentic Vulnerability Research

There is a lot more we learned about this vulnerability that we haven’t yet included in this article. The purpose of this article was just to provide some more background context on this vulnerability and the relevant Apache internals, and to delve into some of the debugging techniques that we’ve found useful when analyzing this vulnerability. Our team has been working towards a full remote code execution chain, and while we haven’t gotten one working yet, we continue to improve our understanding of the vulnerability every day.

The hardest part of this vulnerability wasn’t the bug itself, but setting up a proper debugging environment to analyze and trigger it reliably. The root cause can be explained with a single-line diff, but understanding what actually happens when two threads walk away with the same memnode required being able to record the race, replay it, and work backwards from the crash to the moment the memory was corrupted. The key to agentic vulnerability research isn’t just the model that you are using, but constructing an environment and tooling that the agents can leverage in order to be successful.

The post Understanding the Root Cause of CVE‑2026‑119618 appeared first on Praetorian.

items.title: Delegate user access to AI agents with Amazon Cognito token exchange
items.summary: Suppose you use a restaurant review app to check reviews, book tables, and email invitations to your friends. With OAuth 2.0 , the app sends you to the authorization server that your email provider trusts, where you sign in and approve only the access the app requested, such as the contacts.read and messages.send scopes. The review app won’t sees your credentials. It only receives a short-lived access token limited to the scopes you approved, which it presents to your email provider’s API to read your contacts and send invitation emails on your behalf. That works while the app calls the email API directly, but many requests take a second hop to call downstream services. When you book a table, the app calls its reservation service with your token to email details to your friends, which token should the reservation service use to call the email API? Forwarding the access token issued to the review app hides the reservation service because the email API thinks the app sent the request. Using the reservation service’s own token from an OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant loses user identity, because the email API knows which service called, but not for which user. Figure 1 shows this second hop. Figure 1: The reservation service calling the email API for a signed-in user OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, defined in RFC 8693 , handles this second hop. Instead of forwarding your access token, the reservation service goes back to the authorization server with two things: your access token, which shows what you consented for, and its own credentials, which show who it is. The authorization server returns a new token for the email API, called issued token , which identifies the user, can also name the reservation service, and carries the same scopes or fewer. AI agents make this second hop more common and more important, for example when the review app adds an AI agent that reserves tables and invites friends for you. The agent picks its tools at run time, such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that sends invitations, and those tools call APIs for you. With token exchange, each hop gets only the scopes it needs, and the email API can see which service acted for you. In this post, we show you how to use the new OAuth token exchange feature in Amazon Cognito when services and AI agents call your APIs on behalf of users, and Cognito serves as the OAuth 2.0 authorization server. We explain the difference between impersonation and delegation, and show you examples of how the feature works with an MCP server and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity . How token exchange works in Amazon Cognito Every token exchange starts with a subject token that represents the user. In Amazon Cognito, the subject token can be an access token or ID token that your user pool issued to the app where the user signed in. The calling service sends the subject token to Cognito, and Cognito returns a new token for that service to use at the downstream resource server. Token exchange distinguishes two patterns, impersonation and delegation. The calling service chooses which pattern to use based on whether the downstream API needs to authorize the service that’s acting on behalf of the user: Impersonation – The calling service doesn’t identify itself as the actor. The issued token represents the user. Its client_id claim identifies the app client that performed the exchange, but it doesn’t have an act (actor) claim to show a service is acting for the user. Delegation – The calling service identifies itself as the actor by also sending an actor token . Amazon Cognito adds an act claim that names the calling service, so the resource server can see and log who authorized the action and who carried it out. Impersonation fits when the calling service only relays the user’s request and makes no decisions of its own, such as a backend for frontend (BFF) that forwards requests from a web app to your APIs. It also fits where a downstream API authorizes the user alone and doesn’t need to know which service relayed the call. For AI agents, delegation is the important pattern. If the agent used a token of its own, the record would show that an agent called the resource server, but not for whom. With impersonation, the record shows the user but not the agent acting for them. You need delegation to see both for proper authorization and audit trails. Figure 2: Delegated access across two service hops Figure 2 shows the flow for delegated access between services: The user signs in to your app through Amazon Cognito. Cognito issues the user’s access token to the client application. The client calls the downstream service, such as an MCP server, with the user’s access token. The service calls the Cognito /oauth2/token endpoint and authenticates with its own app client. It sends the user’s access token as the subject token and names the resource server as the audience. For delegation, it also sends its own token as the actor token. Cognito validates the request and returns an issued token. The issued token still identifies the user in sub . For delegation, it also identifies the service in the act claim. The service calls the resource server, such as an email API, with the issued token. The resource server checks that the token’s aud claim names itself, then authorizes the request for the user and returns the user’s data to the service. The calling service returns the result to the client. In addition to requesting a token exchange at the /oauth2/token endpoint on your user pool’s domain, you can call the GetDerivedToken API with an AWS SDK , which doesn’t require a user pool domain. Both accept the same subject token, actor token, audience and scopes, and return an issued token with the same claims. Here’s an example issued token from a delegation token exchange. The token keeps user’s identity in sub and names the calling service in the act claim. { "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_EXAMPLE", "sub": "c4b82478-5678-90ab-cdef-EXAMPLE11111", "username": "you@example.com", "client_id": "invitations-mcp-client-id", "version": 2, "token_use": "access", "scope": "email-api/messages.send", "aud": "email-api", "act": { "sub": "invitations-mcp-client-id", "client_id": "invitations-mcp-client-id", "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_EXAMPLE", "token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token" }, "exp": 1735689600, "iat": 1735686000 } The email API authorizes the user identified by sub , and act tells it which service is acting for that user. It can then decide whether it trusts that service, and its logs can show both the user and the service for each request. Accept a delegated token only when act.client_id reflects a service you trust, such as the invitations MCP server, and matches the token’s client_id meaning the trusted service requested the token itself. Security controls during an exchange Amazon Cognito checks every exchange before it issues a token. It validates the subject token’s signature and expiry, and refuses a token that has been revoked or that belongs to a disabled user in your user pool. If the request includes an audience, the issued token is bound to that resource server, and every requested scope must belong to it. The issued token carries only scopes that both the subject token and the app client allow, so an exchange can narrow your access but doesn’t add to it. It also doesn’t outlive the subject token, and the exchange doesn’t return a refresh token. For the full list of checks, see Security model in Exchanging tokens for downstream services in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide . Checks by Cognito don’t replace the resource server’s own: it should still verify the JWT tokens , including signature, issuer, expiry, audience and scopes, and for delegated requests, it should validate the act claim. Your user pool might have a pre token generation AWS Lambda trigger , which can add or suppress custom claims and scopes in your user pool’s tokens. Amazon Cognito also invokes this trigger during token exchange, with the trigger source TokenGeneration_TokenExchange . However, Cognito doesn’t add any scopes that the trigger returns for an exchange, so the calling service can’t gain more permissions than the user’s token already has. You can still use the trigger to remove scopes from the issued token. For more information, see Customize the exchanged token with a Lambda trigger . Enable token exchange in your Amazon Cognito user pool Token exchange is an OAuth 2.0 grant, and you can enable it for each application client as an authentication flow in your Amazon Cognito user pool. Check the prerequisites in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide. To enable token exchange for an app client: Open the AWS Management Console for Amazon Cognito , and choose your Cognito user pool. In the navigation pane, under Applications section, choose App clients , and then choose your app client. In App client information , choose Edit . Figure 3: Cognito token exchange app client On the Edit app client information page, under Authentication flows , go to Exchange OAuth 2 token for delegation and impersonation and select the following: For delegation, select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION . For impersonation, select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_IMPERSONATION . Figure 4: Amazon Cognito token exchange authentication flows Choose Save changes . Example token exchange use cases for agentic workload delegation Now that you’ve enabled token exchange, we show you two examples of how it works in an agentic workload. Both continue the review app story: its AI agent sends invitations for you by calling the email API, and the email API needs to know who you are and which component acted for you. The two examples differ in where the exchange happens. Amazon Cognito fills the act claim from the actor token, so act names whichever component sends its own actor token in the exchange. In Example 1, a shared intermediary—such as an MCP server or an AI gateway—performs the exchange for every agent that calls it, so act names the intermediary. In Example 2, the agent requests the exchange itself, so act names the agent. Example 1: A shared intermediary as the actor In this example, the intermediary sits in front of the email API. We show it two ways: an MCP server you build that performs the exchange in its own code, and an AI gateway in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway that performs it through configuration. Using your own MCP server: The MCP authorization specification doesn’t allow an MCP server to pass along the token it received from the MCP client. To call the email API for you, the invitations MCP server needs a token of its own. It uses its own app client in your user pool to perform a delegation token exchange. Figure 5 shows how the invitations MCP server sends invites for you. Figure 5: The invitations MCP server sending invites for a signed-in user The user signs in to the review app through Amazon Cognito. The review app’s AI agent calls the send_invites tool on the invitations MCP server with the user’s access token. { "sub": "c4b82478-...", "username": "you@example.com", "client_id": " ", "scope": "openid invitations-mcp/tools email-api/contacts.read email-api/messages.send", "token_use": "access", "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/ " } The MCP server authorizes the inbound request by checking the token’s client_id and the invitations-mcp/tools scope, then gets its own actor token with its client ID and secret in an OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant flow. The MCP server sends the user’s token as subject token and its actor token to the Cognito /oauth2/token endpoint in a delegation token exchange. It requests only email-api/messages.send , because sending invites doesn’t require reading your contacts. curl -X POST "https:// .auth.us-east-1.amazoncognito.com/oauth2/token" \ -u "$MCP_SERVER_CLIENT_ID:$MCP_SERVER_CLIENT_SECRET" \ -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange \ --data-urlencode "subject_token=$YOUR_TOKEN" \ -d subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \ --data-urlencode "actor_token=$ACTOR_TOKEN" \ -d actor_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \ -d audience=email-api \ -d scope=email-api/messages.send Cognito validates both tokens and returns the issued token, while keeping the user in sub claim and adding the MCP server’s app client to act claim. { "sub": "c4b82478-...", "username": "you@example.com", "client_id": " ", "aud": "email-api", "scope": "email-api/messages.send", "act": { "sub": " ", "client_id": " ", "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/ ", "token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token" }, "token_use": "access" } The MCP server calls the email API with the issued token. The email API checks aud=email-api and the messages.send scope, and it confirms that act.client_id matches client_id and names an MCP server it trusts. It then sends the invites from your account and records that the invitations MCP server sent them for you. To set up the MCP server: In Amazon Cognito user pool, register the email API ( email-api ) and the MCP server ( invitations-mcp ) as resource servers in your user pool, with the scopes used. Create an app client with a client secret for the MCP server in your user pool. Select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION in authentication flows, allow the client credentials grant so the MCP server can get its actor token, and allow the email-api/messages.send scope that it requests in the exchange. Have the review app request email-api/messages.send when you sign in, along with invitations-mcp/tools . The exchange can remove scopes from your token, but it can’t add any. Other AI agents can also sign you in through Amazon Cognito and call the invitations MCP server. They can register with your user pool through dynamic client registration (DCR) , or identify themselves with a client ID metadata document (CIMD) . Token exchange works the same way for these clients. They send your access token to the MCP server, and the MCP server performs the exchange with its own app client, so the issued token names you in sub and the MCP server in act . Using AgentCore Gateway: If you don’t want to write the exchange in your MCP server, AgentCore Gateway can perform it for you. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity can perform the same token exchange on behalf of AgentCore Gateway, so the gateway doesn’t store the OAuth client secret or build the request. Here, AgentCore Gateway replaces the invitations MCP server. It exposes the email API as an MCP tool through an OpenAPI target, and the review app’s AI agent calls that tool with your access token. Figure 6 shows how AgentCore Gateway sends invites for you. Figure 6: AgentCore Gateway sending invites through AgentCore Identity The agent calls the AgentCore Gateway invite tool with user’s access token. The AgentCore Gateway inbound JWT authorizer validates the token against your user pool and accepts only tokens issued to the review app. AgentCore Gateway passes user’s access token to AgentCore Identity and asks for a token for the email API target. AgentCore Identity uses the AgentCore Gateway app client in a client credentials grant to get an actor token. AgentCore Identity sends your token and the actor token in a delegation token exchange, adding the subject_token_type and audience values from the target’s custom parameters. Amazon Cognito validates the request and returns the issued token, with the user in sub , and the AgentCore Gateway app client in act . AgentCore Identity passes the issued token to AgentCore Gateway. AgentCore Gateway calls the email API with the issued token, and the email API applies the same checks as for the preceding MCP server setup. To set up AgentCore Gateway: In your Amazon Cognito user pool, create an app client for AgentCore Gateway in the same way as for the MCP server. In AgentCore Identity, create an AgentCore Identity credential provider for the AgentCore Gateway app client. A credential provider stores what AgentCore Identity needs to request tokens from Amazon Cognito: your user pool’s discovery URL and the app client’s ID and secret. Use the CustomOauth2 provider type, and enable delegation in its customOauth2ProviderConfig settings: { "oauthDiscovery": { "discoveryUrl": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/ /.well-known/openid-configuration" }, "clientId": " ", "clientSecret": " ", "clientAuthenticationMethod": "CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC", "onBehalfOfTokenExchangeConfig": { "grantType": "TOKEN_EXCHANGE", "tokenExchangeGrantTypeConfig": { "actorTokenContent": "M2M" } } } In AgentCore Gateway, configure the AgentCore Gateway inbound JWT authorizer with your user pool’s discovery URL, and set allowedClients to the review app’s client ID. In the AgentCore Gateway target’s outbound authorization, reference the credential provider and add subject_token_type and audience as custom parameters. Because your token is an access token, set subject_token_type to urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token . { "providerArn": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1: :token-vault/default/oauth2credentialprovider/cognito", "scopes": ["email-api/messages.send"], "grantType": "TOKEN_EXCHANGE", "customParameters": { "subject_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token", "audience": "email-api" } } AgentCore Gateway handles the exchange through configuration, so you don’t need to write agent or interceptor code for it. For more information, see Set up outbound authorization for your gateway . With either your own MCP server or an AI gateway, act names the intermediary rather than the agent that called it. Every agent behind it appears as the same app client. This design still protects the email API. It accepts only tokens with aud=email-api , and your original access token has no such audience, so an agent can’t bypass the intermediary by forwarding your token. Each call that reaches the email API carries a token with only the scope it needs. The agents don’t hold downstream credentials or exchange logic, and the email API trusts one intermediary instead of every agent. If the email API needs to tell agents apart, perform the exchange in the agent, as Example 2 shows. Example 2: The agent as the actor on AgentCore Runtime If the review app’s AI agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime , the agent can request the exchange itself through AgentCore Identity and call the email API directly. The issued token then names the agent in act, so the email API knows which agent sent the invites. Figure 7 shows how the agent sends invites for you. Figure 7: The AI agent on AgentCore Runtime sending invites through AgentCore Identity The review app invokes the agent on AgentCore Runtime with the user’s access token. Runtime validates your token with its inbound JWT authorizer , exchanges it for a workload access token from AgentCore Identity, and passes that token to the agent. A workload access token is an opaque token that proves which agent is calling. It carries the user’s access token, which AgentCore Identity uses as the subject token in step 4. The agent asks AgentCore Identity for a token for the email API by calling GetResourceOauth2Token with the workload access token. AgentCore Identity gets an actor token with the agent’s app client, then sends user’s token and the actor token to Cognito in a delegation token exchange. Amazon Cognito returns the issued token, with user in sub and the agent’s app client in act , and AgentCore Identity passes it to the agent. The agent calls the email API with the issued token. The email API applies the same checks as in Example 1, and confirms that act.client_id names an agent it trusts. The issued token has the same shape as in Example 1, but client_id and act name the agent’s app client. To set up the agent: In your Amazon Cognito user pool, create an app client for the agent in your user pool and select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION for it. To tell agents apart in act claim, give each agent its own app client and credential provider. In AgentCore Identity, create a credential provider for the agent’s app client in the same way as for AgentCore Gateway. In AgentCore Runtime, configure the inbound JWT authorizer on AgentCore Runtime to accept your user pool’s tokens, with allowedClients set to the review app’s client ID. In the agent’s code, request the issued token with the AgentCore SDK: from bedrock_agentcore.identity.auth import requires_access_token @requires_access_token( provider_name=" ", scopes=["email-api/messages.send"], audiences=["email-api"], auth_flow="ON_BEHALF_OF_TOKEN_EXCHANGE", custom_parameters={ "subject_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token" }, ) async def send_invites(friends: list[str], *, access_token: str): # Call the email API with access_token ... The decorator makes the GetResourceOauth2Token call in step 3 of Figure 7 and passes the issued token to your function as access_token . For more information, see On-behalf-of token exchange with AgentCore Identity . Conclusion Think back to the agent at the start of this post. The agent had to book a table and send invitations for you, and forwarding the user’s original access token would have hidden which service acted for you and given it more access than the job needed. With Amazon Cognito token exchange, each hop gets its own scoped-down token, bound to the resource server it calls and limited to the scopes it needs. Each issued token also expires no later than your own token and doesn’t come with a refresh token, so no service can keep access after your token expires. For AI agents, delegation adds a second identity to the token. The act claim names the service doing the work, so a downstream API can choose which agents it trusts. Your audit records can then show both the person who authorized a request and the agent that made it. You can try this on a new or existing Amazon Cognito user pool on the Essentials or Plus plan. Enable ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION for an app client, register the downstream API as a resource server, and call GetDerivedToken or the token endpoint. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Edward Sun Edward is a Senior Security Specialist Solutions Architect focused on identity and access management. He loves helping customers throughout their cloud transformation journey with architecture design, security best practices, migration, and cost optimizations. Outside of work, Edward enjoys hiking, golfing, and cheering for his alma mater, the Georgia Bulldogs. Owen Hawkins Owen is a Principal Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, working with independent software vendors in the UK. Building on more than 20 years in information security and digital banking, he now spends his time on agent identity and on helping engineering organizations improve their software development lifecycle with AI-driven approaches. Varun Sharma Varun is a Senior AWS Cloud Security Engineer who wears his security cape proudly. With a knack for unravelling the mysteries of Amazon Cognito and IAM, Varun is a go-to subject matter expert for these services. When he’s not busy securing the cloud, you’ll find him in the world of security penetration testing. And when the pixels are at rest, Varun switches gears to capture the beauty of nature through the lens of his camera.

Figure 2: Delegated access across two service hops

  1. The user signs in to your app through Amazon Cognito.

  3. The client calls the downstream service, such as an MCP server, with the user’s access token.

  8. The calling service returns the result to the client.

In addition to requesting a token exchange at the /oauth2/token endpoint on your user pool’s domain, you can call the GetDerivedToken API with an AWS SDK, which doesn’t require a user pool domain. Both accept the same subject token, actor token, audience and scopes, and return an issued token with the same claims.

Here’s an example issued token from a delegation token exchange. The token keeps user’s identity in sub and names the calling service in the act claim.

{
  "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_EXAMPLE",
  "sub": "c4b82478-5678-90ab-cdef-EXAMPLE11111",
  "username": "you@example.com",
  "client_id": "invitations-mcp-client-id",
  "version": 2,
  "token_use": "access",
  "scope": "email-api/messages.send",
  "aud": "email-api",
  "act": {
    "sub": "invitations-mcp-client-id",
    "client_id": "invitations-mcp-client-id",
    "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_EXAMPLE",
    "token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token"
  },
  "exp": 1735689600,
  "iat": 1735686000
}

The email API authorizes the user identified by sub, and act tells it which service is acting for that user. It can then decide whether it trusts that service, and its logs can show both the user and the service for each request. Accept a delegated token only when act.client_id reflects a service you trust, such as the invitations MCP server, and matches the token’s client_id meaning the trusted service requested the token itself.

Security controls during an exchange

Amazon Cognito checks every exchange before it issues a token. It validates the subject token’s signature and expiry, and refuses a token that has been revoked or that belongs to a disabled user in your user pool. If the request includes an audience, the issued token is bound to that resource server, and every requested scope must belong to it. The issued token carries only scopes that both the subject token and the app client allow, so an exchange can narrow your access but doesn’t add to it. It also doesn’t outlive the subject token, and the exchange doesn’t return a refresh token.

For the full list of checks, see Security model in Exchanging tokens for downstream services in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide. Checks by Cognito don’t replace the resource server’s own: it should still verify the JWT tokens, including signature, issuer, expiry, audience and scopes, and for delegated requests, it should validate the act claim.

Your user pool might have a pre token generation AWS Lambda trigger, which can add or suppress custom claims and scopes in your user pool’s tokens. Amazon Cognito also invokes this trigger during token exchange, with the trigger source TokenGeneration_TokenExchange. However, Cognito doesn’t add any scopes that the trigger returns for an exchange, so the calling service can’t gain more permissions than the user’s token already has. You can still use the trigger to remove scopes from the issued token. For more information, see Customize the exchanged token with a Lambda trigger.

Enable token exchange in your Amazon Cognito user pool

Token exchange is an OAuth 2.0 grant, and you can enable it for each application client as an authentication flow in your Amazon Cognito user pool. Check the prerequisites in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

To enable token exchange for an app client:

  1. Open the AWS Management Console for Amazon Cognito, and choose your Cognito user pool.
  2. In the navigation pane, under Applications section, choose App clients, and then choose your app client.
  3. In App client information, choose Edit.

    Figure 3: Cognito token exchange app client

  4. On the Edit app client information page, under Authentication flows, go to Exchange OAuth 2 token for delegation and impersonation and select the following:
    1. For delegation, select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION.
    2. For impersonation, select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_IMPERSONATION.

    Figure 4: Amazon Cognito token exchange authentication flows

  5. Choose Save changes.
Example token exchange use cases for agentic workload delegation

Now that you’ve enabled token exchange, we show you two examples of how it works in an agentic workload. Both continue the review app story: its AI agent sends invitations for you by calling the email API, and the email API needs to know who you are and which component acted for you.

The two examples differ in where the exchange happens. Amazon Cognito fills the act claim from the actor token, so act names whichever component sends its own actor token in the exchange. In Example 1, a shared intermediary—such as an MCP server or an AI gateway—performs the exchange for every agent that calls it, so act names the intermediary. In Example 2, the agent requests the exchange itself, so act names the agent.

Example 1: A shared intermediary as the actor

In this example, the intermediary sits in front of the email API. We show it two ways: an MCP server you build that performs the exchange in its own code, and an AI gateway in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway that performs it through configuration.

Using your own MCP server:

The MCP authorization specification doesn’t allow an MCP server to pass along the token it received from the MCP client. To call the email API for you, the invitations MCP server needs a token of its own. It uses its own app client in your user pool to perform a delegation token exchange.

Figure 5 shows how the invitations MCP server sends invites for you.

Figure 5: The invitations MCP server sending invites for a signed-in user

  1. The user signs in to the review app through Amazon Cognito.
  2. The review app’s AI agent calls the send_invites tool on the invitations MCP server with the user’s access token. 
    {
  "sub": "c4b82478-...",
  "username": "you@example.com",
  "client_id": "",
  "scope": "openid invitations-mcp/tools email-api/contacts.read email-api/messages.send",
  "token_use": "access",
  "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/"
}
  3. The MCP server authorizes the inbound request by checking the token’s client_id and the invitations-mcp/tools scope, then gets its own actor token with its client ID and secret in an OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant flow.
  4. The MCP server sends the user’s token as subject token and its actor token to the Cognito /oauth2/token endpoint in a delegation token exchange. It requests only email-api/messages.send, because sending invites doesn’t require reading your contacts. 
    curl -X POST "https://.auth.us-east-1.amazoncognito.com/oauth2/token" \
  -u "$MCP_SERVER_CLIENT_ID:$MCP_SERVER_CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange \
  --data-urlencode "subject_token=$YOUR_TOKEN" \
  -d subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \
  --data-urlencode "actor_token=$ACTOR_TOKEN" \
  -d actor_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \
  -d audience=email-api \
  -d scope=email-api/messages.send
  5. Cognito validates both tokens and returns the issued token, while keeping the user in sub claim and adding the MCP server’s app client to act claim. 
    {
  "sub": "c4b82478-...",
  "username": "you@example.com",
  "client_id": "",
  "aud": "email-api",
  "scope": "email-api/messages.send",
  "act": {
    "sub": "",
    "client_id": "",
    "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/",
    "token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token"
  },
  "token_use": "access"
}
  6. The MCP server calls the email API with the issued token. The email API checks aud=email-api and the messages.send scope, and it confirms that act.client_id matches client_id and names an MCP server it trusts. It then sends the invites from your account and records that the invitations MCP server sent them for you.

To set up the MCP server:

  1. In Amazon Cognito user pool, register the email API (email-api) and the MCP server (invitations-mcp) as resource servers in your user pool, with the scopes used.
  2. Create an app client with a client secret for the MCP server in your user pool. Select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION in authentication flows, allow the client credentials grant so the MCP server can get its actor token, and allow the email-api/messages.send scope that it requests in the exchange.
  3. Have the review app request email-api/messages.send when you sign in, along with invitations-mcp/tools. The exchange can remove scopes from your token, but it can’t add any.

Other AI agents can also sign you in through Amazon Cognito and call the invitations MCP server. They can register with your user pool through dynamic client registration (DCR), or identify themselves with a client ID metadata document (CIMD). Token exchange works the same way for these clients. They send your access token to the MCP server, and the MCP server performs the exchange with its own app client, so the issued token names you in sub and the MCP server in act.

Using AgentCore Gateway:

If you don’t want to write the exchange in your MCP server, AgentCore Gateway can perform it for you. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity can perform the same token exchange on behalf of AgentCore Gateway, so the gateway doesn’t store the OAuth client secret or build the request.

Here, AgentCore Gateway replaces the invitations MCP server. It exposes the email API as an MCP tool through an OpenAPI target, and the review app’s AI agent calls that tool with your access token.

Figure 6 shows how AgentCore Gateway sends invites for you.

Figure 6: AgentCore Gateway sending invites through AgentCore Identity

  1. The agent calls the AgentCore Gateway invite tool with user’s access token. The AgentCore Gateway inbound JWT authorizer validates the token against your user pool and accepts only tokens issued to the review app.
  2. AgentCore Gateway passes user’s access token to AgentCore Identity and asks for a token for the email API target.
  3. AgentCore Identity uses the AgentCore Gateway app client in a client credentials grant to get an actor token.
  4. AgentCore Identity sends your token and the actor token in a delegation token exchange, adding the subject_token_type and audience values from the target’s custom parameters.
  5. Amazon Cognito validates the request and returns the issued token, with the user in sub, and the AgentCore Gateway app client in act.
  6. AgentCore Identity passes the issued token to AgentCore Gateway.
  7. AgentCore Gateway calls the email API with the issued token, and the email API applies the same checks as for the preceding MCP server setup.

To set up AgentCore Gateway:

  1. In your Amazon Cognito user pool, create an app client for AgentCore Gateway in the same way as for the MCP server.
  2. In AgentCore Identity, create an AgentCore Identity credential provider for the AgentCore Gateway app client. A credential provider stores what AgentCore Identity needs to request tokens from Amazon Cognito: your user pool’s discovery URL and the app client’s ID and secret. Use the CustomOauth2 provider type, and enable delegation in its customOauth2ProviderConfig settings: 
    {
  "oauthDiscovery": { "discoveryUrl": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com//.well-known/openid-configuration" },
  "clientId": "",
  "clientSecret": "",
  "clientAuthenticationMethod": "CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC",
  "onBehalfOfTokenExchangeConfig": {
    "grantType": "TOKEN_EXCHANGE",
    "tokenExchangeGrantTypeConfig": { "actorTokenContent": "M2M" }
  }
}
  3. In AgentCore Gateway, configure the AgentCore Gateway inbound JWT authorizer with your user pool’s discovery URL, and set allowedClients to the review app’s client ID.
  4. In the AgentCore Gateway target’s outbound authorization, reference the credential provider and add subject_token_type and audience as custom parameters. Because your token is an access token, set subject_token_type to urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token. 
    {
  "providerArn": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1::token-vault/default/oauth2credentialprovider/cognito",
  "scopes": ["email-api/messages.send"],
  "grantType": "TOKEN_EXCHANGE",
  "customParameters": {
    "subject_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token",
    "audience": "email-api"
  }
}

AgentCore Gateway handles the exchange through configuration, so you don’t need to write agent or interceptor code for it. For more information, see Set up outbound authorization for your gateway.

With either your own MCP server or an AI gateway, act names the intermediary rather than the agent that called it. Every agent behind it appears as the same app client. This design still protects the email API. It accepts only tokens with aud=email-api, and your original access token has no such audience, so an agent can’t bypass the intermediary by forwarding your token. Each call that reaches the email API carries a token with only the scope it needs. The agents don’t hold downstream credentials or exchange logic, and the email API trusts one intermediary instead of every agent. If the email API needs to tell agents apart, perform the exchange in the agent, as Example 2 shows.

Example 2: The agent as the actor on AgentCore Runtime

If the review app’s AI agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, the agent can request the exchange itself through AgentCore Identity and call the email API directly. The issued token then names the agent in act, so the email API knows which agent sent the invites.

Figure 7 shows how the agent sends invites for you.

Figure 7: The AI agent on AgentCore Runtime sending invites through AgentCore Identity

  1. The review app invokes the agent on AgentCore Runtime with the user’s access token.
  2. Runtime validates your token with its inbound JWT authorizer, exchanges it for a workload access token from AgentCore Identity, and passes that token to the agent. A workload access token is an opaque token that proves which agent is calling. It carries the user’s access token, which AgentCore Identity uses as the subject token in step 4.
  3. The agent asks AgentCore Identity for a token for the email API by calling GetResourceOauth2Token with the workload access token.
  4. AgentCore Identity gets an actor token with the agent’s app client, then sends user’s token and the actor token to Cognito in a delegation token exchange.
  5. Amazon Cognito returns the issued token, with user in sub and the agent’s app client in act, and AgentCore Identity passes it to the agent.
  6. The agent calls the email API with the issued token. The email API applies the same checks as in Example 1, and confirms that act.client_id names an agent it trusts.

The issued token has the same shape as in Example 1, but client_id and act name the agent’s app client.

To set up the agent:

  1. In your Amazon Cognito user pool, create an app client for the agent in your user pool and select ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION for it. To tell agents apart in act claim, give each agent its own app client and credential provider.
  2. In AgentCore Identity, create a credential provider for the agent’s app client in the same way as for AgentCore Gateway.
  3. In AgentCore Runtime, configure the inbound JWT authorizer on AgentCore Runtime to accept your user pool’s tokens, with allowedClients set to the review app’s client ID.
  4. In the agent’s code, request the issued token with the AgentCore SDK: 
    from bedrock_agentcore.identity.auth import requires_access_token

@requires_access_token(
    provider_name="",
    scopes=["email-api/messages.send"],
    audiences=["email-api"],
    auth_flow="ON_BEHALF_OF_TOKEN_EXCHANGE",
    custom_parameters={
        "subject_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token"
    },
)
async def send_invites(friends: list[str], *, access_token: str):
    # Call the email API with access_token
    ...

The decorator makes the GetResourceOauth2Token call in step 3 of Figure 7 and passes the issued token to your function as access_token.

For more information, see On-behalf-of token exchange with AgentCore Identity.

Conclusion

Think back to the agent at the start of this post. The agent had to book a table and send invitations for you, and forwarding the user’s original access token would have hidden which service acted for you and given it more access than the job needed. With Amazon Cognito token exchange, each hop gets its own scoped-down token, bound to the resource server it calls and limited to the scopes it needs. Each issued token also expires no later than your own token and doesn’t come with a refresh token, so no service can keep access after your token expires.

For AI agents, delegation adds a second identity to the token. The act claim names the service doing the work, so a downstream API can choose which agents it trusts. Your audit records can then show both the person who authorized a request and the agent that made it.

You can try this on a new or existing Amazon Cognito user pool on the Essentials or Plus plan. Enable ALLOW_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_DELEGATION for an app client, register the downstream API as a resource server, and call GetDerivedToken or the token endpoint.

items.title: AWS completed its second ISO/IEC 42001:2023 surveillance audit
items.summary: In November 2024, Amazon Web Services (AWS) was the first major cloud service provider to announce the ISO/IEC 42001 accredited certification for AI services, covering Amazon Bedrock , Amazon Q Business , Amazon Textract , and Amazon Transcribe . In November 2026, AWS successfully completed its second surveillance audit for ISO 42001:2023 , Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS), with no findings and added AWS DevOps Agent as a new service now covered under its ISO 42001:2023 certification program. This demonstrates the continuous commitment by AWS to responsible AI practices. With this independent validation, our customers can gain assurances on our commitment to responsible AI that enables customers to build and operate AI applications responsibly using AWS services. For a full list of AWS services that are certified under ISO and CSA STAR, see the AWS ISO and CSA STAR Certified page. Customers can also access the certifications through the AWS Management Console for AWS Artifact. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Basit Janjua Basit is a Senior Security Industry Specialist at AWS. He leads the AWS assurance delivery strategy for security assurance audits and engagements across the globe. Basit has nearly 20 years of experience in information security engineering and assurance. He holds a Bachelor’s degree in Computer Science and a Master’s degree in Telecommunications, along with professional certifications including CISSP and CCSP. Shalini Mishra Shalini is a Compliance Program Manager at AWS. She has over 5 years of experience leading end-to-end compliance programs across ISO, SOC, and cloud security frameworks, with deep expertise in third-party risk management and enterprise governance, driving measurable improvements in security posture and audit readiness. Shalini holds a Master of Science degree in Information Systems, CRISC and ISO 27001 lead auditor certification.
