items.title: AWS achieves Spain’s national Limited Distribution (Difusión Limitada) and NATO Restricted accreditation in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region
items.summary: Spanish version » Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce that AWS has achieved Spain’s national Limited Distribution (“Difusión Limitada”) and NATO Restricted accreditation for the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation was granted by the Spanish Delegated Authority for the Security of Classified Information, the Secretary of State Director of Spain’s Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI) . The Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) and the Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS) are working bodies of the CNI, which audited AWS against the CCN-STIC-004 policy and the applicable ONS requirements. With this milestone, AWS becomes the first cloud provider to be accredited under NATO Restricted level, and the first to be accredited for Difusión Limitada in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. In Spain, this was a double achievement: AWS first met the national Difusión Limitada requirements and then, in addition to this national methodology, achieved the NATO Restricted accreditation by incorporating the requirements of NATO Directive 32. This demonstrates our continued commitment to helping the public sector, defense, and NATO-affiliated customers run sensitive workloads in the cloud while meeting the highest applicable national and international security requirements. What this covers The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation by the CNI confirms that the AWS system in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region meets the procedural and security requirements for handling classified information up to the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted level. What is Spain’s classified information framework? Spain’s framework for protecting national classified information is administered by the ONS and the CCN, under the CNI. In 2026, Spain established the framework that enables handling of Difusión Limitada information in the commercial public cloud, under which this accreditation was granted. The accreditation builds on the AWS ENS High certification and the CCN’s IT Product and Service Catalogue (CPSTIC) qualifications. The scope of the accreditation covers the CPSTIC-qualified services and all AWS services certified under ENS High (see the list of AWS services in scope for ENS High ). Only the services within this scope that are qualified or certified under the CCN framework (CPSTIC and ENS High) and run in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region can be used for Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted workloads. What is NATO Restricted? NATO Directive 32 establishes the security requirements for handling NATO Restricted information in public cloud, and is the directive referenced by Spain’s CCN-STIC-004 policy. Why this matters to customers Public sector and defense organizations in Spain can use the AWS Europe (Spain) Region for national Difusión Limitada classified workloads and for NATO Restricted workloads. Under the shared responsibility model, customers that want to process classified information in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region engage the CCN and ONS to accredit their own systems, building on the AWS accreditation. How to get started National security and defense customers may build on the AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) to design a cloud architecture for their sensitive workloads. Accreditation documentation is available to eligible customers through AWS Artifact . Customers can also work with their AWS account teams to understand how the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation, and TSE-SE apply to their use cases. To learn more about AWS compliance in Spain, see the AWS ENS compliance page and the AWS Compliance Programs page. For more details see AWS NATO Restricted and Difusión Limitada for AWS Europe (Spain) Region web page Spanish version AWS obtiene la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted en la Región AWS Europa (España) Amazon Web Services (AWS) se complace en anunciar que ha obtenido la acreditación nacional de España “Difusión Limitada” y la acreditación NATO Restricted para la Región AWS Europa (España). La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted ha sido concedida por la Autoridad Delegada para la Seguridad de la Información Clasificada de España, la Secretaria de Estado Directora del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI) . El Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) , y la Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS) , son órganos de trabajo del CNI, que auditaron a AWS conforme a la política CCN-STIC-004 y a los requisitos aplicables de la ONS. Con este hito, AWS se convierte en el primer proveedor cloud acreditado en el nivel NATO Restricted, y en el primero acreditado para Difusión Limitada en la Región AWS Europa (España). En España ha sido un doble logro: AWS cumplió primero los requisitos nacionales de Difusión Limitada y, sobre esta metodología nacional, obtuvo la acreditación NATO Restricted incorporando los requisitos de la Directiva 32 de la OTAN. Esto demuestra nuestro compromiso continuo de ayudar al sector público, a la defensa y a los clientes vinculados a la OTAN a ejecutar cargas de trabajo sensibles en la nube cumpliendo los requisitos de seguridad nacionales e internacionales más exigentes aplicables. Qué abarca La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted del CNI confirma que el sistema de AWS en la Región AWS Europa (España) cumple los requisitos procedimentales y de seguridad para tratar información clasificada hasta el nivel Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted. ¿Cuál es el marco español de información clasificada? El marco español de protección de la información clasificada nacional lo administran la ONS y el CCN, bajo el CNI. En 2026, España estableció el marco que permite tratar información Difusión Limitada en la nube pública comercial, en virtud del cual se ha concedido esta acreditación. La acreditación se basa en la certificación ENS categoría Alta de AWS y en las cualificaciones del Catálogo de Productos y Servicios de Seguridad TIC (CPSTIC) del CCN. El alcance de la acreditación incluye los servicios cualificados en CPSTIC y todos los servicios de AWS certificados en el ENS categoría Alta (consulte la lista de servicios de AWS en el alcance del ENS categoría Alta ). Solo pueden utilizarse para cargas de trabajo Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted los servicios de este alcance cualificados o certificados en el marco del CCN (CPSTIC y ENS categoría Alta) que se ejecuten en la Región AWS Europa (España). ¿Qué es NATO Restricted? La Directiva 32 de la OTAN establece los requisitos de seguridad para tratar información NATO Restricted en la nube pública, y es la directiva a la que hace referencia la política española CCN-STIC-004 . Por qué es importante para los clientes Las organizaciones del sector público y de defensa en España pueden utilizar la Región AWS Europa (España) para cargas de trabajo clasificadas nacionales Difusión Limitada, así como para cargas de trabajo NATO Restricted. Conforme al modelo de responsabilidad compartida, los clientes que quieran tratar información clasificada en la Región AWS Europa (España) deben dirigirse al CCN y a la ONS para acreditar sus propios sistemas, apoyándose en la acreditación de AWS. Cómo empezar Los clientes de seguridad nacional y defensa pueden apoyarse en AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) para diseñar una arquitectura cloud para sus cargas de trabajo sensibles. La documentación de la acreditación está disponible para los clientes elegibles a través de AWS Artifact . Los clientes también pueden trabajar con sus equipos de cuenta de AWS para entender cómo se aplican a sus casos de uso la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted y TSE-SE. Para más información sobre el cumplimiento de AWS en España, consulte la página de cumplimiento ENS de AWS y la página de Programas de cumplimiento de AWS . Para más detalles, consulte la página web de AWS sobre NATO Restricted y Difusión Limitada para la Región AWS Europa (España) If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support . Borja Larrumbide Borja is a Security Assurance Manager for AWS in Iberia. He has a bachelor’s degree in computer science from Boston University (USA) and has worked in companies such as Microsoft and BBVA in different roles and sectors. Borja is a seasoned security assurance practitioner with many years of experience engaging key stakeholders at national and international levels. His areas of interest include security, privacy, risk management, and compliance.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce that AWS has achieved Spain’s national Limited Distribution (“Difusión Limitada”) and NATO Restricted accreditation for the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation was granted by the Spanish Delegated Authority for the Security of Classified Information, the Secretary of State Director of Spain’s Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI). The Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) and the Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS) are working bodies of the CNI, which audited AWS against the CCN-STIC-004 policy and the applicable ONS requirements.

With this milestone, AWS becomes the first cloud provider to be accredited under NATO Restricted level, and the first to be accredited for Difusión Limitada in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. In Spain, this was a double achievement: AWS first met the national Difusión Limitada requirements and then, in addition to this national methodology, achieved the NATO Restricted accreditation by incorporating the requirements of NATO Directive 32. This demonstrates our continued commitment to helping the public sector, defense, and NATO-affiliated customers run sensitive workloads in the cloud while meeting the highest applicable national and international security requirements.

What this covers

The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation by the CNI confirms that the AWS system in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region meets the procedural and security requirements for handling classified information up to the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted level.

What is Spain’s classified information framework?

Spain’s framework for protecting national classified information is administered by the ONS and the CCN, under the CNI. In 2026, Spain established the framework that enables handling of Difusión Limitada information in the commercial public cloud, under which this accreditation was granted. The accreditation builds on the AWS ENS High certification and the CCN’s IT Product and Service Catalogue (CPSTIC) qualifications. The scope of the accreditation covers the CPSTIC-qualified services and all AWS services certified under ENS High (see the list of AWS services in scope for ENS High). Only the services within this scope that are qualified or certified under the CCN framework (CPSTIC and ENS High) and run in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region can be used for Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted workloads.

What is NATO Restricted?

NATO Directive 32 establishes the security requirements for handling NATO Restricted information in public cloud, and is the directive referenced by Spain’s CCN-STIC-004 policy.

Why this matters to customers

Public sector and defense organizations in Spain can use the AWS Europe (Spain) Region for national Difusión Limitada classified workloads and for NATO Restricted workloads. Under the shared responsibility model, customers that want to process classified information in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region engage the CCN and ONS to accredit their own systems, building on the AWS accreditation.

How to get started

National security and defense customers may build on the AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) to design a cloud architecture for their sensitive workloads. Accreditation documentation is available to eligible customers through AWS Artifact. Customers can also work with their AWS account teams to understand how the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation, and TSE-SE apply to their use cases.

To learn more about AWS compliance in Spain, see the AWS ENS compliance page and the AWS Compliance Programs page.

For more details see AWS NATO Restricted and Difusión Limitada for AWS Europe (Spain) Region web page
 

Spanish version

AWS obtiene la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted en la Región AWS Europa (España)

Amazon Web Services (AWS) se complace en anunciar que ha obtenido la acreditación nacional de España “Difusión Limitada” y la acreditación NATO Restricted para la Región AWS Europa (España). La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted ha sido concedida por la Autoridad Delegada para la Seguridad de la Información Clasificada de España, la Secretaria de Estado Directora del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI). El Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN), y la Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS), son órganos de trabajo del CNI, que auditaron a AWS conforme a la política CCN-STIC-004 y a los requisitos aplicables de la ONS.

Con este hito, AWS se convierte en el primer proveedor cloud acreditado en el nivel NATO Restricted, y en el primero acreditado para Difusión Limitada en la Región AWS Europa (España). En España ha sido un doble logro: AWS cumplió primero los requisitos nacionales de Difusión Limitada y, sobre esta metodología nacional, obtuvo la acreditación NATO Restricted incorporando los requisitos de la Directiva 32 de la OTAN. Esto demuestra nuestro compromiso continuo de ayudar al sector público, a la defensa y a los clientes vinculados a la OTAN a ejecutar cargas de trabajo sensibles en la nube cumpliendo los requisitos de seguridad nacionales e internacionales más exigentes aplicables.

Qué abarca

La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted del CNI confirma que el sistema de AWS en la Región AWS Europa (España) cumple los requisitos procedimentales y de seguridad para tratar información clasificada hasta el nivel Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted.

¿Cuál es el marco español de información clasificada?

El marco español de protección de la información clasificada nacional lo administran la ONS y el CCN, bajo el CNI. En 2026, España estableció el marco que permite tratar información Difusión Limitada en la nube pública comercial, en virtud del cual se ha concedido esta acreditación. La acreditación se basa en la certificación ENS categoría Alta de AWS y en las cualificaciones del Catálogo de Productos y Servicios de Seguridad TIC (CPSTIC) del CCN. El alcance de la acreditación incluye los servicios cualificados en CPSTIC y todos los servicios de AWS certificados en el ENS categoría Alta (consulte la lista de servicios de AWS en el alcance del ENS categoría Alta). Solo pueden utilizarse para cargas de trabajo Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted los servicios de este alcance cualificados o certificados en el marco del CCN (CPSTIC y ENS categoría Alta) que se ejecuten en la Región AWS Europa (España).

¿Qué es NATO Restricted?

La Directiva 32 de la OTAN establece los requisitos de seguridad para tratar información NATO Restricted en la nube pública, y es la directiva a la que hace referencia la política española CCN-STIC-004.

Por qué es importante para los clientes

Las organizaciones del sector público y de defensa en España pueden utilizar la Región AWS Europa (España) para cargas de trabajo clasificadas nacionales Difusión Limitada, así como para cargas de trabajo NATO Restricted. Conforme al modelo de responsabilidad compartida, los clientes que quieran tratar información clasificada en la Región AWS Europa (España) deben dirigirse al CCN y a la ONS para acreditar sus propios sistemas, apoyándose en la acreditación de AWS.

Cómo empezar

Los clientes de seguridad nacional y defensa pueden apoyarse en AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) para diseñar una arquitectura cloud para sus cargas de trabajo sensibles. La documentación de la acreditación está disponible para los clientes elegibles a través de AWS Artifact. Los clientes también pueden trabajar con sus equipos de cuenta de AWS para entender cómo se aplican a sus casos de uso la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted y TSE-SE.

Para más información sobre el cumplimiento de AWS en España, consulte la página de cumplimiento ENS de AWS y la página de Programas de cumplimiento de AWS.

Para más detalles, consulte la página web de AWS sobre NATO Restricted y Difusión Limitada para la Región AWS Europa (España)

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support.

Borja Larrumbide

Borja is a Security Assurance Manager for AWS in Iberia. He has a bachelor’s degree in computer science from Boston University (USA) and has worked in companies such as Microsoft and BBVA in different roles and sectors. Borja is a seasoned security assurance practitioner with many years of experience engaging key stakeholders at national and international levels. His areas of interest include security, privacy, risk management, and compliance.

items.title: The Age of Defensive Minimalism
items.summary: How Agentic Offensive Frameworks turn noise into scrutiny What happens when the kind of attention an attacker once reserved for a high-value target becomes part of the background noise of the internet? Looking back, I see three periods in how attackers have spent their attention. Until about 2000, the internet was quiet. A server could stay online for weeks without receiving anything unusual. A port scan was rare enough that some administrators wrote to the abuse contact of the network it came from. If someone attacked you, a person had chosen you. Then the noise began. Code Red in 2001 and Slammer in 2003 showed what automated exploitation could do at internet scale. Botnets guessed SSH passwords around the clock, and in 2013 ZMap showed that a single machine could scan the entire IPv4 address space for one port in under 45 minutes. Anything you put on the internet got scanned several times a day, and some of that traffic tried known exploits and default passwords. But that automation was uniform. Every target got the same checks. It found the unpatched appliance and the default credential, but it didn’t read your documentation, search your repositories or follow up on an odd response from your API. That required a person, and skilled people were scarce. They chose their targets by value or by mission. For twenty-five years, everyone got the noise and only a few got the attention. Justin Elze at TrustedSec recently described the economics behind this. Attackers favored bugs in common frameworks, appliances and plugins, because one exploit works against thousands of targets. Reviewing one organization’s custom applications takes time and produces nothing that can be reused elsewhere. His conclusion: “Limited attacker attention was never a control.” Think of a street where every house is already on the map. A burglar could always find the small house at the end, but an afternoon spent checking its doors and windows was an afternoon not spent on a more promising one. Scanners found most forgotten systems years ago. Few people had a reason to look twice. Agentic Offensive Frameworks (AOFs) change that calculation. An attacker can now move on and leave an agent behind to take that second look. The agent reads documentation, investigates unfamiliar software, tries another approach when the first one fails and revisits a minor finding when it learns something new. Other agents do the same with other targets at the same time. Anatomy of an AOF: an operator and a console feed an agent loop of planner, workers and shared memory that calls a language model and runs familiar tools; what reaches the defender are requests, sign-ins, processes and audit events In most cases, everything left of the dashed line runs outside your network. The surface those agents examine is much larger than a list of open ports. It’s everything an organization has put online over twenty years: cloud tenants and storage, repositories with their full history, published packages, build logs, forgotten subdomains and old APIs, SaaS integrations and suppliers. It even includes what was taken offline years ago. In one case I heard about, an agent found leaked credentials in the JavaScript of an old version of a company’s website, preserved in the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine. And it’s people, and the projects they depend on. In other cases I’ve heard about, agents sent phishing emails with PDF attachments that carried malicious JavaScript, and opened pull requests with malicious changes against open source tooling the target company had published itself. A small study from late 2024 had already shown that the writing is no obstacle: spear phishing emails researched and written entirely by AI got as many clicks as emails written by human experts. The limit on deep attention used to be human time. Now it’s compute. Compute and bandwidth are cheap, and they keep getting cheaper. Skilled people never did. Who gets an attacker’s attention: three periods, from quiet to noise to scrutiny Until now, most columns never turned pink. From 2026, every one does. The first evidence is public. Check Point Research analyzed ten ARTEX installations with exposed databases. Most operators set an objective and then mainly asked their agents about progress. One ran a two-week campaign against ten gray-market iOS signing shops for an estimated $700 to $1,500 in model usage. While searching for the owner of a single crypto wallet, agents found an unauthenticated API that leaked cloud storage credentials with write access to a service’s app downloads. That wasn’t what they had been looking for. The clearest example comes from WorkOS. A researcher was benchmarking ARTEX when the agent left its test environment. It found an internal tool whose API was reachable from the internet, authenticated with a predictable development credential and retrieved records in bulk. It wasn’t a criminal operation, and nobody had chosen WorkOS as a target. That’s what makes it worth studying. This doesn’t mean agents are expert operators. They fail a lot. In one crypto campaign, agents produced more than 400,000 messages and 230 findings, reported successes that never happened and earned the operator nothing. But an attacker doesn’t need every attempt to work. Eyal Sela of Gambit Security has investigated hundreds of these attacks. He argues that they don’t just move at machine speed, they change in quality. He has seen procedures, and chains of them across web applications, cloud accounts and build pipelines, that are rare or undocumented in the wild, and he thinks some of them deserve their own MITRE ATT&CK techniques. His post “Lessons from investigating hundreds of AI cyber attacks” walks through real cases step by step and will be published soon. Read it when it’s out if you still picture an AOF as a vulnerability scanner with a chat interface. So two things changed at once: who gets a close look, and how far that look goes. What an agent finds For defenders, four things stand out. Being unique no longer protects you. A custom application, an old API or an internal tool that never got a serious review was safe in practice, because examining it didn’t pay. An agent doesn’t need the result to be reusable. It needs a few hours of compute. Our history has become attack surface. Over twenty years, most organizations have published code, configuration examples, conference talks, job postings that name internal systems and repositories with commits nobody has looked at in a decade. All of it was written for a world in which nobody would read all of it. Microsoft described a case that went from searching GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes. None of these steps is new. What’s new is that something now follows all of them. Human attention worked like a flashlight. It lit up whatever a person chose to examine, and the rest stayed dark, including paths that led somewhere valuable. Much of what we built survived because nobody had the time to walk all of it. Agents work like floodlights. They read the public documentation, the old commits and, once inside, the wiki pages and runbooks, in any language. The paths were always there. Now they’re visible. When the lights come on: one organization seen by the flashlight of human attention and by the floodlights of agents Being overlooked used to keep many organizations safe. Having less to find is what can replace it. Our priorities learned from the old distribution of attention. “We rarely see anyone exploit this” was a fair argument when deep attention went to a few targets, and exploitation scores built on past activity share that assumption. As a friend put it, if rare paths get investigated more often, rarity becomes a weaker reason to postpone a basic control. A low-severity finding or an excessive permission can matter because of what it connects to. We trained ourselves to ignore the noise. After twenty years of constant scanning, nobody looks at a port scan in the logs anymore, and rightly so. The start of an agent’s investigation can look just like it. The difference is in what follows. That follow-up is a problem even when detection works. A SOC can see suspicious use of a credential almost immediately, but before revoking it, someone may need to establish whether that will stop a production service. The attacker uses that time to explore another route. If the response misses an active session or a second credential, the attacker returns with the environment already mapped. An alert can arrive in seconds. The decision to take a production system offline can still take an hour. I expect that gap to change priorities. Organizations will automate more of their response where they understand the consequences of acting immediately. That understanding is supposed to come from the asset inventory, and the inventory is often wrong. Many teams learn that a system was more critical than recorded only after they’ve contained it. An agent that takes over containment acts on the same data, faster, and without the person who happens to know better. After a second compromise within a few weeks, someone will ask why a troublesome service is still on the internet. Someone else may ask why they’re still running it at all. What would we build today? The answer to the noise was firewalls, patch management and closing ports. It reduced what a uniform scanner could hit. The answer to scrutiny has to cover everything an attentive investigator can find, and that’s a lot more than ports. I call that answer “ defensive minimalism” . Start with the smallest set of capabilities that lets people do their work. Before adding a feature, opening a port, installing a plugin or granting access, establish who needs it, what they gain and whether they can do the job without it. Apply the same questions to everything that’s already running. In 480 BC, the Greeks under Leonidas didn’t meet the Persian army on open ground, where numbers decide. They held the pass at Thermopylae, a narrow strip between the mountains and the sea, where only a few could fight at once. They held it for two days. It fell when a local showed the Persians a mountain path around it. Defensive minimalism is that choice of ground. We can’t match the number of agents that will look at us, so we decide where they can meet us: a few well-defended entry points instead of a long front. The mountain path is the forgotten staging server, the old API, the credentials in an archived copy of our website. Agents are very good at finding it. A narrow front can be held. Agents look for the path around it. Defensive minimalism doesn’t replace the basics. Phishing-resistant MFA, password blocklists that reject seasons, months, years and the company name, software allowlisting, faster patch cycles, offline backups, switching off old protocols: they are what stops an agent once it has found something. Agents don’t need new tricks. They find every gap in the basics, everywhere at once, so being good at the basics is no longer enough. We have to be excellent at them. Excellent at the basics: common entry vectors (phishing, exploitation, credentials, impact) and the basics that hold against them Much of our software ships with defaults that someone chose as reasonable for a broad set of users, in a time with different workloads and threats. Apache’s Options directive once defaulted to All. Apache narrowed it to FollowSymLinks years ago. I expect us to get much stricter about which defaults make sense for a particular deployment. The Print Spooler on Windows domain controllers shows why. The service is on by default, and a domain controller rarely needs to print. In 2021, PrintNightmare let any authenticated user run code as SYSTEM through it, and the spooler can also be used to make a domain controller authenticate to a host the attacker controls. Microsoft now recommends disabling it on domain controllers. That decision could have been made years before anyone discovered the bug. Whoever proposes enabling a feature should be able to explain why it’s worth defending for the lifetime of the service. The same applies to dependencies, build systems and third-party access. Every package brings someone else’s code and future updates into the environment we defend. A long-lived cloud credential in a build job connects that job to everything the credential can reach, and a secret copied into a repository or build log stays valid after someone deletes the file. Each unused dependency, long-lived credential or vendor integration we remove is a route nobody has to monitor. I think organizations will go further than hardening what they have. Consider a supplier that needs to submit a file and check its status. We could give them an account on the application our staff use for approvals and payments, or build a small external service that does those two things and keep the internal application out of reach. A good first step is to pick one internet-facing service that has no reason to accept anonymous requests, put it behind authentication and check from the outside that the origin can’t be reached directly. Sometimes the right decision will be to withdraw a service entirely. Workstations could change just as radically. For roles that can work entirely in a browser, I can see organizations replacing general-purpose desktops with minimal managed systems. Users would sign in with phishing-resistant authentication such as FIDO2, each application would grant only the access a role requires, and browser extensions would need review before anyone could enable them. That removes whole categories of desktop software and their update channels from those machines. What we would build again: the same organization today, with routes to valuable data, and rebuilt with most parts removed, sign-in first and the old routes cut The data is still there. The routes to it are not. Some of these decisions will cost money. People will lose features they like. Engineers may spend months replacing a system that still works and has years of support left. My prediction is that more organizations will accept those costs once they’ve seen how quickly an attacker can explore everything they’ve accumulated. At the next architecture review, I’d start with one question: given what our users actually need to do, how much of this system would we choose to build again? Further reading Justin Elze (TrustedSec), “Accuracy Through Volume of Fire” Mandiant on Agentic Offensive Frameworks Elastic Security Labs, “Inside the loop: Five AI attack frameworks that never ask permission” Check Point Research, “Hacking on Autopilot: Inside ARTEX Cybercrime Campaigns” WorkOS update on its October 2026 incident Unit 42 on the Cairn framework and autonomous intrusions Eyal Sela (Gambit Security), “Lessons from investigating hundreds of AI cyber attacks” (coming soon) Microsoft on agentic tooling and exposed secrets Heiding et al., fully automated spear phishing validated on human subjects Durumeric et al., “ZMap: Fast Internet-wide Scanning and its Security Applications” Apache HTTP Server documentation on the Options directive NVD entry for CVE-2021–34527 (PrintNightmare) and Microsoft’s recommendation to disable the Print Spooler on domain controllers Thanks to Eyal Sela (Gambit Security), Arnim Rupp and Thomas Patzke for their feedback on drafts of this post.

How Agentic Offensive Frameworks turn noise into scrutiny

What happens when the kind of attention an attacker once reserved for a high-value target becomes part of the background noise of the internet?

Looking back, I see three periods in how attackers have spent their attention.

Until about 2000, the internet was quiet. A server could stay online for weeks without receiving anything unusual. A port scan was rare enough that some administrators wrote to the abuse contact of the network it came from. If someone attacked you, a person had chosen you.

Then the noise began. Code Red in 2001 and Slammer in 2003 showed what automated exploitation could do at internet scale. Botnets guessed SSH passwords around the clock, and in 2013 ZMap showed that a single machine could scan the entire IPv4 address space for one port in under 45 minutes. Anything you put on the internet got scanned several times a day, and some of that traffic tried known exploits and default passwords.

But that automation was uniform. Every target got the same checks. It found the unpatched appliance and the default credential, but it didn’t read your documentation, search your repositories or follow up on an odd response from your API. That required a person, and skilled people were scarce. They chose their targets by value or by mission.

For twenty-five years, everyone got the noise and only a few got the attention.

Justin Elze at TrustedSec recently described the economics behind this. Attackers favored bugs in common frameworks, appliances and plugins, because one exploit works against thousands of targets. Reviewing one organization’s custom applications takes time and produces nothing that can be reused elsewhere. His conclusion: “Limited attacker attention was never a control.”

Think of a street where every house is already on the map. A burglar could always find the small house at the end, but an afternoon spent checking its doors and windows was an afternoon not spent on a more promising one. Scanners found most forgotten systems years ago. Few people had a reason to look twice.

Agentic Offensive Frameworks (AOFs) change that calculation. An attacker can now move on and leave an agent behind to take that second look. The agent reads documentation, investigates unfamiliar software, tries another approach when the first one fails and revisits a minor finding when it learns something new. In most cases, everything left of the dashed line runs outside your network.

The surface those agents examine is much larger than a list of open ports. It’s everything an organization has put online over twenty years: cloud tenants and storage, repositories with their full history, published packages, build logs, forgotten subdomains and old APIs, SaaS integrations and suppliers. It even includes what was taken offline years ago. In one case I heard about, an agent found leaked credentials in the JavaScript of an old version of a company’s website, preserved in the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine.

And it’s people, and the projects they depend on. A small study from late 2024 had already shown that the writing is no obstacle: spear phishing emails researched and written entirely by AI got as many clicks as emails written by human experts.

The limit on deep attention used to be human time. Now it’s compute.

Compute and bandwidth are cheap, and they keep getting cheaper. Skilled people never did.

Who gets an attacker’s attention: three periods, from quiet to noise to scrutiny

Until now, most columns never turned pink. From 2026, every one does.

The first evidence is public. Check Point Research analyzed ten ARTEX installations with exposed databases. Most operators set an objective and then mainly asked their agents about progress. One ran a two-week campaign against ten gray-market iOS signing shops for an estimated $700 to $1,500 in model usage. That wasn’t what they had been looking for.

The clearest example comes from WorkOS. A researcher was benchmarking ARTEX when the agent left its test environment. It found an internal tool whose API was reachable from the internet, authenticated with a predictable development credential and retrieved records in bulk. It wasn’t a criminal operation, and nobody had chosen WorkOS as a target. That’s what makes it worth studying.

This doesn’t mean agents are expert operators. They fail a lot. In one crypto campaign, agents produced more than 400,000 messages and 230 findings, reported successes that never happened and earned the operator nothing. But an attacker doesn’t need every attempt to work.

Eyal Sela of Gambit Security has investigated hundreds of these attacks. He argues that they don’t just move at machine speed, they change in quality. He has seen procedures, and chains of them across web applications, cloud accounts and build pipelines, that are rare or undocumented in the wild, and he thinks some of them deserve their own MITRE ATT&CK techniques. His post “Lessons from investigating hundreds of AI cyber attacks” walks through real cases step by step and will be published soon. Read it when it’s out if you still picture an AOF as a vulnerability scanner with a chat interface.

So two things changed at once: who gets a close look, and how far that look goes.

What an agent finds

For defenders, four things stand out.

Being unique no longer protects you. A custom application, an old API or an internal tool that never got a serious review was safe in practice, because examining it didn’t pay. An agent doesn’t need the result to be reusable. It needs a few hours of compute.

Our history has become attack surface. Over twenty years, most organizations have published code, configuration examples, conference talks, job postings that name internal systems and repositories with commits nobody has looked at in a decade. All of it was written for a world in which nobody would read all of it. What’s new is that something now follows all of them.

Human attention worked like a flashlight. It lit up whatever a person chose to examine, and the rest stayed dark, including paths that led somewhere valuable. Much of what we built survived because nobody had the time to walk all of it. Agents work like floodlights. They read the public documentation, the old commits and, once inside, the wiki pages and runbooks, in any language. The paths were always there. Now they’re visible.

Our priorities learned from the old distribution of attention. “We rarely see anyone exploit this” was a fair argument when deep attention went to a few targets, and exploitation scores built on past activity share that assumption. That follow-up is a problem even when detection works. I call that answer “defensive minimalism”. Start with the smallest set of capabilities that lets people do their work. Before adding a feature, opening a port, installing a plugin or granting access, establish who needs it, what they gain and whether they can do the job without it. Apply the same questions to everything that’s already running.

In 480 BC, the Greeks under Leonidas didn’t meet the Persian army on open ground, where numbers decide. They held the pass at Thermopylae, a narrow strip between the mountains and the sea, where only a few could fight at once. They held it for two days. It fell when a local showed the Persians a mountain path around it.

Defensive minimalism is that choice of ground. We can’t match the number of agents that will look at us, so we decide where they can meet us: a few well-defended entry points instead of a long front. The mountain path is the forgotten staging server, the old API, the credentials in an archived copy of our website. Agents are very good at finding it.

A narrow front can be held. Agents look for the path around it.

Defensive minimalism doesn’t replace the basics. Phishing-resistant MFA, password blocklists that reject seasons, months, years and the company name, software allowlisting, faster patch cycles, offline backups, switching off old protocols: they are what stops an agent once it has found something. Excellent at the basics: common entry vectors (phishing, exploitation, credentials, impact) and the basics that hold against them

Much of our software ships with defaults that someone chose as reasonable for a broad set of users, in a time with different workloads and threats. Apache’s Options directive once defaulted to All. Apache narrowed it to FollowSymLinks years ago. I expect us to get much stricter about which defaults make sense for a particular deployment.

The Print Spooler on Windows domain controllers shows why. The service is on by default, and a domain controller rarely needs to print. In 2021, PrintNightmare let any authenticated user run code as SYSTEM through it, and the spooler can also be used to make a domain controller authenticate to a host the attacker controls. Microsoft now recommends disabling it on domain controllers. That decision could have been made years before anyone discovered the bug.

Whoever proposes enabling a feature should be able to explain why it’s worth defending for the lifetime of the service.

The same applies to dependencies, build systems and third-party access. Every package brings someone else’s code and future updates into the environment we defend. A long-lived cloud credential in a build job connects that job to everything the credential can reach, and a secret copied into a repository or build log stays valid after someone deletes the file. Each unused dependency, long-lived credential or vendor integration we remove is a route nobody has to monitor.

I think organizations will go further than hardening what they have. Consider a supplier that needs to submit a file and check its status. We could give them an account on the application our staff use for approvals and payments, or build a small external service that does those two things and keep the internal application out of reach. A good first step is to pick one internet-facing service that has no reason to accept anonymous requests, put it behind authentication and check from the outside that the origin can’t be reached directly. Sometimes the right decision will be to withdraw a service entirely.

Workstations could change just as radically. For roles that can work entirely in a browser, I can see organizations replacing general-purpose desktops with minimal managed systems. Users would sign in with phishing-resistant authentication such as FIDO2, each application would grant only the access a role requires, and browser extensions would need review before anyone could enable them. That removes whole categories of desktop software and their update channels from those machines.

What we would build again: the same organization today, with routes to valuable data, and rebuilt with most parts removed, sign-in first and the old routes cut

The data is still there. The routes to it are not.

Some of these decisions will cost money. People will lose features they like. Engineers may spend months replacing a system that still works and has years of support left. My prediction is that more organizations will accept those costs once they’ve seen how quickly an attacker can explore everything they’ve accumulated. At the next architecture review, I’d start with one question: given what our users actually need to do, how much of this system would we choose to build again?

Further reading
  • Justin Elze (TrustedSec), “Accuracy Through Volume of Fire”
  • Mandiant on Agentic Offensive Frameworks
  • Elastic Security Labs, “Inside the loop: Five AI attack frameworks that never ask permission”
  • Check Point Research, “Hacking on Autopilot: Inside ARTEX Cybercrime Campaigns”
  • WorkOS update on its October 2026 incident
  • Unit 42 on the Cairn framework and autonomous intrusions
  • Eyal Sela (Gambit Security), “Lessons from investigating hundreds of AI cyber attacks” (coming soon)
  • Microsoft on agentic tooling and exposed secrets
  • Heiding et al., fully automated spear phishing validated on human subjects
  • Durumeric et al., “ZMap: Fast Internet-wide Scanning and its Security Applications”
  • Apache HTTP Server documentation on the Options directive
  • NVD entry for CVE-2021–34527 (PrintNightmare) and Microsoft’s recommendation to disable the Print Spooler on domain controllers

Thanks to Eyal Sela (Gambit Security), Arnim Rupp and Thomas Patzke for their feedback on drafts of this post.

But researchers at Stony Brook University found that it was enough time for a bot to test a cloud access key they’d deliberately left inside a publicly available software package. The fastest observed use came just 7.86 seconds after publication. You don’t need a company cloud account to have a key worth stealing. If you’ve created an API key for an AI service and used it in an app or script, someone who gets hold of it can run up charges on your account. OpenAI warns that they could also use up your quote and interrupt your service. To see who was collecting those secrets, Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis set up honeypots, or decoys that let researchers monitor what happens when someone takes the bait. Over four months, they published 300 honeypot images across eight public registries. The bait included working access keys for Amazon Web Services (AWS), OpenAI, and Anthropic. Each key was tied to monitoring, so any use would show up in the provider’s logs. The researchers didn’t advertise the images anywhere, but they were still downloaded tens of thousands of times. Most of the early activity looked like bots checking whether the keys worked. Nearly every bot that tested an AWS key began with GetCallerIdentity , essentially a “who am I?” request that tells an attacker whether a key is live. About half the IP addresses researchers saw scanning for AWS keys stopped after that initial check. Only around 6% went on to sustained use of account resources. A key that passes that check can still be sold on or used later. In the AI-service tests, the OpenAI keys sat quiet for weeks before someone used one to burn through the remaining balance in under 24 hours. The researchers offered an explanation: “We speculate that the wait phase reflects validated keys being resold and held idle until a buyer eventually uses them.” The researchers loaded about $60 in total onto their OpenAI and Anthropic accounts, and attackers used up all of it. How to stay safe The researchers published honeypot container images on Docker Hub and seven other registries, then shared their findings with Docker. According to the paper, Docker acknowledged the disclosure, and its security team was reviewing the findings. The number of probing bots and their speed is something developers should worry about. If you use cloud or AI services, a few precautions can help keep your keys safe: Keep secrets out of what you share. Don’t put keys in code, public repositories, or container images. Scan before you publish. A bot can find an exposed key within seconds, so a check after publication is too late. The researchers also recommend that registries scan images as they’re uploaded. Limit what each key can do. In the second round of tests, every OpenAI and Anthropic key that attackers used to burn through credits had unrestricted permissions. No restricted key was used that way. The scanners appear to check permissions first, so a narrowly scoped key gives them less to work with. A narrowly scoped key can only perform specific actions or access particular resources. Prefer short-lived credentials. AWS recommends using temporary credentials instead of long-term access keys wherever possible. Set spending limits and alerts. Check whether your provider’s budget setting just sends an alert or sets a hard limit on what you can spend. If you’ve already published a key, treat it as compromised, even if it was public for only a minute. Revoke it and replace it. Then review account activity and charges. Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection catches suspicious activity before it becomes a problem.

An 8088, 640 KB of RAM and a Really Bad Idea
items.summary: Why I built UMIX/86 For years, I had a crazy idea: to build a preemptive multitasking operating system for my old 8088 PC, with just 640 KB of RAM, a 5.25-inch floppy drive, a 20 MB hard disk, and MS-DOS as its original environment. Of course, the idea itself is nothing new. Multitasking operating systems ran on similar hardware decades ago. My goal wasn’t to reinvent the wheel, but to build my own system from scratch, bring an old idea to life, and see how far I could push this old machine with the help of AI. And it became a working system. None of this was magic. The hard part wasn’t the idea itself, but the thousand small technical details, any one of which could bring the whole system down. Even transferring files was a pain. I first had to write a small GW-BASIC script on the old PC so I could send the Telix communications program from my workstation over the serial connection. Once Telix was running, I could finally use ZMODEM for file transfers. That was practically the only way I had to get the OS disk image onto the old machine and write it to a 360 KB, 5.25-inch floppy disk. Getting software onto the machine was a project in itself! I also wanted my old 8088 to communicate over the Internet through its 9600-baud serial port. So I built a serial-to-TCP/IP bridge and a lightweight, X.25-inspired protocol to multiplex ten independent terminal sessions over a single COM1 connection. An old PC, connected to the modern Internet through a 9600-baud serial link! 😜 I built UMIX/86 with the help of DeepSeek and GLM. I’m not an Assembly developer, and I never pretended to be one. I brought the idea, the vision, the specifications, and the hardware. They wrote the Assembly code, explored solutions, caught race conditions, and chased bugs that would have taken me an enormous amount of time to solve on my own. Or perhaps I would never have finished it at all. Is a multitasking OS for a processor architecture introduced almost 50 years ago useful in 2026? Probably not. But that’s not the point. Maybe AI won’t replace us. Maybe it will help us finally build the projects we once thought were impossible, too difficult, or simply too time-consuming. In the age of AI, perhaps the real advantage belongs to people with ideas, curiosity, and the imagination to turn them into reality. 😜 More details about UMIX/86 » And yes, that link really points to a web server running on my old 8088 PC! 😜 The modern workstation acts only as a serial-to-IP bridge. UMIX/86 handles the requests and serves the content directly from its own C: or M: drive, over a 9600-baud serial connection. Of course, the system is still experimental and somewhat unstable, so don’t expect 100% uptime! If the server is down, or you somehow manage to crash it, well… remember, it’s a very old PC running a homemade operating system. What could possibly go wrong? 😜 And here’s the actual machine running UMIX/86: A good old Commodore PC 20! I’ll be publishing the source code on GitHub soon, for anyone curious enough to explore it, experiment with it, or simply see how this crazy little project works!

items.title: McDonald’s Japan Confirms Data Breach – Customer Information and Location Data Exposed
items.summary: McDonald’s Japan has confirmed that a third party gained unauthorized access to customer information stored in the database behind its official mobile app. In a November 20, 2026, breach notice , the company said the affected records included product purchase histories, internal customer management IDs, IP addresses, and location data from mobile devices used when it provided services. McDonald’s Japan said it had not confirmed any unauthorized use of the app or its services as a result of the incident. The company said the affected data did not include names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, or credit card information registered in the app. It also said the internal customer management ID is different from the membership ID customers use for the app. The internal ID alone cannot identify a customer. McDonald’s Japan did not disclose how many customers were affected, when the unauthorized access began, or whether the third party copied any records. McDonald’s Japan Data Breach The company’s notice concerns access to a database, not the takeover of customer accounts. It also does not link the breach to the unusual McDonald’s iOS app notifications reported days earlier. That report described unexpected push alerts, while the Japanese disclosure identifies specific types of customer data that a third party accessed. The two reports do not establish a common cause. Location data can raise privacy concerns even when records do not contain names. As Cyber Security News explains in its guide to location data privacy , access to device location records can reveal more than a single point on a map. If multiple readings are linked to the same identifier and include precise times and places, they can show where a device regularly goes. That is a possible risk, not a finding about this breach. McDonald’s Japan did not say how precise the location readings were, whether they included timestamps, or how much history the affected records covered. Nor did it say whether purchase histories could be matched to individual location readings. The notice describes location information from devices used when services were provided. It does not establish that the database held a continuous record of customers’ movements or that anyone could track them in real time. As Japanese technology outlet ASCII reported , McDonald’s Japan said it was working to disable the credentials used in the unauthorized access, investigate related systems, and report the incident to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission. The company has not disclosed what kind of credentials were used or how the third party obtained them. Its work to disable those credentials is separate from its advice to customers about their own passwords. McDonald’s Japan said customers do not need to change their passwords or take any other special action at this time. It apologized and said it would update the notice as new information became available. For customers trying to understand their exposure, three questions remain: how many people were affected, how detailed the location records were, and whether anyone took a copy. Until the company provides more information, the confirmed finding is unauthorized access to some customer records, not confirmed misuse of customer accounts or the app’s services. items.title: Critical VMware ESX Flaws Let Remote Attackers Execute Malicious Code on Virtualization Hosts
items.summary: Broadcom has disclosed 23 VMware vulnerabilities, including two critical flaws that could let attackers run code directly on ESX hosts and a third that could let them access vCenter without signing in. The Broadcom security advisory, VMSA-2026-0011 , was published on November 24. It says the flaws were privately reported and does not report active exploitation. The advisory covers VMware vCenter, ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. It also lists VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, Telco Cloud Platform, and Telco Cloud Infrastructure. Administrators who run those platforms should check the versions of the VMware components they use, rather than relying on the platform name alone. VMware ESX Host Vulnerabilities The vCenter flaw, CVE-2026-123903, has a severity score of 9.8 out of 10 and affects VMware Directory Service. An attacker with network access to vCenter could bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access without valid credentials. That matters because vCenter gives administrators a single place to manage multiple ESX hosts and their virtual machines. Broadcom lists no workaround. Its technical FAQ says turning off Enhanced Linked Mode does not remove the risk. The flaw is separate from CVE-2026-123890, the vCenter authentication bypass disclosed on November 19 . The new advisory also covers three flaws that can disrupt VMware Directory Service. Another vCenter flaw, CVE-2026-123904, could let someone with access to the backup repository write files with root privileges when vCenter processes certain archives. That could lead to code execution on the appliance. CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911 each score 9.8. Both affect the ESX input/output filter service and could let an attacker who can reach an affected host over the network run code on it. Neither requires the attacker to first gain access to a virtual machine. That sets them apart from earlier VMware vulnerabilities that required access inside a guest . A separate virtual USB controller flaw, CVE-2026-123912, does require administrator access inside a virtual machine. It scores 9.3 on Workstation and Fusion, where it could let an attacker run code on the underlying computer. CVE Affected product or component Access required and potential impact CVE-2026-123903 vCenter VMware Directory Service ( vmdir ) Network access to vCenter. An attacker could bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access without valid credentials. CVE-2026-123904 vCenter archive processing Access to the backup repository. An attacker could write files as root, potentially leading to code execution on the appliance. CVE-2026-123905 vCenter VMware Directory Service Network access to vCenter. An attacker could disrupt the directory service. CVE-2026-123906 vCenter VMware Directory Service Network access to vCenter. An attacker could disrupt the directory service. CVE-2026-123907 vCenter VMware Directory Service Network access to vCenter. An attacker could disrupt the directory service. CVE-2026-123908 vCenter vpxd service script Control of the vpxd service account. An attacker could gain root privileges on the appliance. CVE-2026-123909 vCenter vSphere Distributed Switch Local access to a virtual machine. A policy enforcement failure could allow capabilities the switch policy should restrict. CVE-2026-123910 ESX I/O filter service Network access to an affected ESX host. A heap out-of-bounds write could allow code execution on the host. CVE-2026-123911 ESX I/O filter service Network access to an affected ESX host. A use-after-free flaw could allow code execution on the host. CVE-2026-123912 ESX, Workstation, and Fusion XHCI USB controller Administrator access inside a virtual machine. An out-of-bounds write could lead to code execution on the computer running Workstation or Fusion. On ESX, execution remains inside the VMX sandbox. CVE-2026-123913 ESX VMkernel Privileges within the VMX process. A stack-based buffer overflow could let an attacker gain higher privileges. CVE-2026-123914 ESX host configuration store Root access to an ESX host with Secure Boot enabled. An attacker could tamper with the host configuration store and perform unauthorized actions. CVE-2026-123915 ESX signature verification High local privileges, per the published CVSS vector. An attacker could bypass signature checks and keep malicious files on the host across reboots. CVE-2026-123916 ESX, Workstation, and Fusion guest RPC Non-administrator access inside a virtual machine. An attacker could crash the VMX process and disrupt that virtual machine. Broadcom has disclosed 23 VMware vulnerabilities, including two critical flaws that could let attackers run code directly on ESX hosts and a third that could let them access vCenter without signing in.

The Broadcom security advisory, VMSA-2026-0011, was published on November 24. It says the flaws were privately reported and does not report active exploitation.

The advisory covers VMware vCenter, ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. It also lists VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, Telco Cloud Platform, and Telco Cloud Infrastructure.

Administrators who run those platforms should check the versions of the VMware components they use, rather than relying on the platform name alone.

VMware ESX Host Vulnerabilities

The vCenter flaw, CVE-2026-123903, has a severity score of 9.8 out of 10 and affects VMware Directory Service. An attacker with network access to vCenter could bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access without valid credentials.

That matters because vCenter gives administrators a single place to manage multiple ESX hosts and their virtual machines. Broadcom lists no workaround. Its technical FAQ says turning off Enhanced Linked Mode does not remove the risk.

The flaw is separate from CVE-2026-123890, the vCenter authentication bypass disclosed on November 19. The new advisory also covers three flaws that can disrupt VMware Directory Service.

Another vCenter flaw, CVE-2026-123904, could let someone with access to the backup repository write files with root privileges when vCenter processes certain archives. That could lead to code execution on the appliance.

CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911 each score 9.8. Both affect the ESX input/output filter service and could let an attacker who can reach an affected host over the network run code on it.

Neither requires the attacker to first gain access to a virtual machine. That sets them apart from earlier VMware vulnerabilities that required access inside a guest.

A separate virtual USB controller flaw, CVE-2026-123912, does require administrator access inside a virtual machine. It scores 9.3 on Workstation and Fusion, where it could let an attacker run code on the underlying computer.

items.title: Introducing Remediation campaigns: Work through your backlog and review the fixes in one pull request
items.summary: Your teams ship more code than ever. The backlog of known issues still waits for a sprint that never comes. Those issues stay in your main branch, and every new change builds on top of them. Each one is a maintenance cost and a risk you already know about. The SonarQube Remediation Agent already fixes issues on demand or on a schedule. Remediation campaigns add a third way to work. Point the agent at a body of related issues, and it works through them in steps and hands you one final PR to review. Remediation campaigns are now available in SonarQube Cloud for GitHub-bound projects. What are Remediation campaigns? A Remediation campaign is a guided run of the agent against the backlog in your main branch. You set the scope and add optional instructions. The agent plans the work and carries it out in steps: You create the campaign. Select issues, describe a goal, or leave both empty and let the agent start with the most severe eligible issues. The agent prepares and starts. It selects eligible issues and plans the steps. You do not need to approve the plan or each step of PR. The agent works one step at a time. Each step that produces changes opens a PR into a separate campaign branch. The agent can merge that step PR into the branch and continue from the updated code. A step that cannot produce a fix is skipped or closed, and the campaign keeps going. The agent opens one final PR. It opens the PR after the first step merges and updates it as more steps finish. You review and merge. The final PR carries the combined changes. Your main branch changes only when you merge it. Each fix goes through closed-loop verification. The agent re-runs Sonar's analysis engine against the modified code, and only fixes that resolve the original issue without introducing new ones become pull requests. SonarQube is the independent verification layer. It raises the issue, and it re-checks the fix. How do I set up Remediation campaigns? Your organization admin does this once. The steps follow the Administer the Remediation Agent documentation. Check your LLM option. Your subscription decides whether the agent uses a Sonar-provided LLM or your own OpenAI or Anthropic API key. The Sonar-provided option needs no provider account. The Remediation Agent entry under Billing and usage shows which option your organization uses. Add your key (BYOK only). Go to your organization, then Administration > AI capabilities > LLM API Keys . Choose OpenAI or Anthropic , enter the key and a name, and select Add key . SonarQube Cloud verifies the key with your provider before it saves it. You can add up to three keys. Install the SonarQube Agent GitHub app. Go to Administration > AI capabilities > Remediation Agent and select GitHub under Install app . A GitHub administrator installs the SonarQube Agent app on the GitHub organization linked to your SonarQube Cloud organization, chooses All repositories or Only select repositories , and select Install & Authorize . The app gets read and write access to code and pull requests, read-only access to Actions, and read-only access to issues and metadata. Select your key (BYOK only). Under Choose your key , select the key you added. The agent stays disabled until you select a valid key. Enable the workflow. Under Enable agent , enable Manual backlog remediation . For GitHub-bound projects, this setting also controls whether you can start Remediation campaigns. Select Save . You keep control of access. A GitHub administrator can change repository access, or suspend or uninstall the app, at any time. Sonar processes the affected code to generate and verify each fix. For details on how your code is handled with each LLM option, see Sharing your code with Sonar . How do I start a campaign? Open your project's Issues page and select the main branch. To fix specific issues, select them in the issues list. Select Start a campaign . Under Recommended issues to be fixed , select the scope you want. Leave every checkbox cleared to use the whole backlog. Optionally, under Specify instructions for the agent , describe a goal in up to 1,800 characters. Select Create campaign . It will show you the progress window. Open View progress to follow the campaign. The scope options work like this: Checkbox Scope Issues I selected Issues you selected in the issues list Assigned to me Issues assigned to your SonarQube Cloud account Blocking the quality gate Eligible issues scoped to the failing quality gate. If only new-code conditions fail, the campaign focuses on new code. A campaign targets up to 200 eligible issues, grouped into steps. Choosing the whole backlog does not mean the agent includes or fixes every issue. With no scope and no instructions, the agent starts with the most severe eligible issues in your backlog. The campaign starts automatically after preparation. How do I follow a campaign? Open your project's Agent activity page and find the entry with Campaign as its source. Expand it to see the steps and links to their PRs. Check each step's outcome and any explanation of why the agent skipped or closed it. Steps that close without merging are not part of the campaign's result. Look for these outcomes on the entry: Completed. Open the final PR to review the result. Completed, no changes. No step produced a change for a final PR. Could not be prepared. Read the explanation on the entry before you try again. How do I review and merge the fixes? The agent opens the final PR after the first step merges and updates it as more steps finish. While the campaign runs, the PR title starts with [In progress] and its description asks you not to merge yet. Wait for the campaign to finish before you review the complete result. When the campaign ends, the PR description summarizes the issues and steps in the result. It links each step's PR and commit, or explains why the agent closed the step. Check the Result and Not done lines for work that still needs attention. Open the final PR from Agent activity . Review the proposed changes and the summary of step outcomes. If you need changes, post review comments on the final PR. The agent follows up on eligible comments. It pushes a follow-up commit when a comment points to a real problem, and it replies to the comments it addresses. Review comment follow-up lists which comments qualify. Merge the PR when you are satisfied with the changes and it meets your repository's requirements. Check the next main branch analysis to confirm which issues are resolved. If analysis does not run automatically, run your usual main branch analysis. A completed campaign does not mean the agent fixed every targeted issue or that every quality gate condition passes. The next analysis tells you where you stand. Why use a campaign? Review once. The final PR description summarizes the issues and steps in the result. It links each step's PR and commit, or explains why the agent closed the step. Your reviewers see the full outcome in one place, and your team can trace every change to its step. Direct the work in plain language. Give the agent a goal in up to 1,800 characters, such as Fix null pointer issues in the billing module . You steer the work without picking every issue yourself. Keep control. The agent merges step PRs into the campaign branch only. You merge the final PR, and you can stop a campaign at any time. Your main branch changes when you decide. What do I need to get started? A Remediation Agent subscription. The agent needs a separate subscription to your SonarQube Cloud Team (annual) or Enterprise plan. To trial or purchase it, contact our Sales team . A private project bound to GitHub. The project's main branch must have an analysis. Admin setup. An organization admin enables Manual backlog remediation , selects a valid large language model (LLM) provider key if your subscription uses bring your own key (BYOK), and gives the SonarQube Agent GitHub app access to the repository. The next section covers each step. Usage allowance. Your organization needs the remaining Remediation Agent usage allowance. Your access. You are a member of the SonarQube Cloud organization with Browse permission on the project. Campaigns select eligible issues with an Open or Confirmed status. They support Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, C, C++, C#, PHP, and secrets. They can also include eligible SonarQube Hunter Agent findings, regardless of language. Generating those findings requires a separate Hunter Agent subscription on your Enterprise plan. To see how the agent fixes them, read our blog post on the SonarQube Remediation Agent and Hunter Agent findings . From known issue to merged change Remediation campaigns run in the code maintenance loop of the Agent Centric Development Cycle (AC/DC), the loop that keeps improving the code you already have. SonarQube verifies your code and raises the issues. The SonarQube Remediation Agent handles the Solve stage. It generates fixes and re-verifies each one before it reaches a reviewer. Your team keeps the decision that matters, which is what merges. To get started, read Remediation campaigns in the SonarQube Cloud documentation. To trial or purchase the SonarQube Remediation Agent, contact our Sales team .

items.title: Hackers Deploy ZQAgent Backdoor to Run Malicious Commands and Access Files on Linux Servers
items.summary: A new Linux backdoor called ZQAgent is giving attackers a long-term foothold on compromised servers. It can run commands, move through folders, read files and open network tunnels. It also hides itself to look like a normal system process. The malware was dropped by ARTEX, an AI-driven hacking framework. Most ARTEX intrusions are quick smash-and-grab jobs that steal passwords and leave. This case is different, because the operator wanted to stay inside the network for a long time. Analysts at NVISO noted the malware during a recent incident response job in Belgium. They also found similar samples reported from Taiwan. The team said the use of a lasting backdoor is likely the result of instructions from a human operator, not a choice made by the AI tool alone. Hackers Deploy ZQAgent Backdoor NVISO found the first sample in /tmp/zqa/systemd-timesyncd , a name picked to look like a normal time service. All known samples talk to the same command servers, the IP address 37.122.150[.]15 and the domain bloonspace[.]com. NVISO links this setup to a cluster it tracks as FOG0003. Network data from Team Cymru suggests the group used ZQAgent in Asia against government and human-rights groups. Once it starts, ZQAgent moves itself into a temporary file held only in memory. This makes the process show up as /memfd:a (deleted) . The backdoor then restarts as a detached process that copies the name and command line of the real dbus-daemon tool. A quick look at the process list would show nothing odd. ZQAgent’s decrypted configuration (Source – NVISO) The malware also protects its own settings. The configuration stays encrypted and is only opened for a moment when needed. Traffic to the command server uses several layers of encryption, including ChaCha20 variants. The feature list is wide. ZQAgent uses numbered operation codes for each task. These let the operator:- change folders and list their contents move, rename, delete or create files and directories read the first 2048 bytes of any file check the current user and view or kill any process start commands through /bin/sh -c open a full shell through /bin/bash , or /bin/sh if Bash is missing manage TCP and UDP connections It can even run a program straight from memory. This approach is not new for Linux malware. The Vmcloudoor Linux cloud backdoor uses a similar trick of posing as a trusted agent so admins leave it alone. Persistence and What Defenders Should Do ZQAgent survives reboots in two ways. It installs a systemd service and a cron job, and it changes file timestamps on everything it creates, which makes cleanup harder. A root user gets the binary copied under /usr/lib/systemd/ , with the service file in /etc/systemd/system/ . Other users get the copy in $HOME/.local/share/ , with the service in $HOME/.config/systemd/user/ . If the HOME variable is not set, the malware falls back to /tmp/.local/share/ . The service uses the description “Device event journal daemon” and restarts every 30 seconds if stopped. For normal users, ZQAgent runs loginctl enable-linger so it keeps running after the user logs out. The cron entry uses an @reboot line that runs the file quietly with all output sent to /dev/null . Linux backdoors that hide in memory and copy trusted names are becoming common. The BPFDoor and Symbiote rootkits also use stealth to stay on servers for long periods. ZQAgent shows that AI-driven tools can now drop this kind of long-term access too. NVISO warns that LLM-driven tools could soon speed up ransomware and spying. They may cut the time between break-in and ransom from hours to minutes. The researchers say companies should harden their network edges, split networks into segments, collect security data from every asset, and react faster. They also say automatic isolation of infected systems deserves another look. Defenders can start with a few checks. Look for the odd dbus-daemon command line and for processes tied to deleted memory files. Search for the “Device event journal daemon” service and unknown cron entries. Block the listed IP and domain. NVISO also published YARA rules for the backdoor, its service file and its cron job. For more background on the tool behind this activity, see the report on ARTEX automates enterprise attacks , and the case of a jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent shows how fast these tools can work.
