items.summary_html:
A new Linux backdoor called ZQAgent is giving attackers a long-term foothold on compromised servers.

It can run commands, move through folders, read files and open network tunnels. It also hides itself to look like a normal system process.

The malware was dropped by ARTEX, an AI-driven hacking framework. Most ARTEX intrusions are quick smash-and-grab jobs that steal passwords and leave.

This case is different, because the operator wanted to stay inside the network for a long time. Analysts at NVISO noted the malware during a recent incident response job in Belgium. They also found similar samples reported from Taiwan.

The team said the use of a lasting backdoor is likely the result of instructions from a human operator, not a choice made by the AI tool alone.

Hackers Deploy ZQAgent Backdoor

NVISO found the first sample in /tmp/zqa/systemd-timesyncd, a name picked to look like a normal time service. All known samples talk to the same command servers, the IP address 37.122.150[.]15 and the domain bloonspace[.]com.

NVISO links this setup to a cluster it tracks as FOG0003. Network data from Team Cymru suggests the group used ZQAgent in Asia against government and human-rights groups.

Once it starts, ZQAgent moves itself into a temporary file held only in memory. This makes the process show up as /memfd:a (deleted).

The backdoor then restarts as a detached process that copies the name and command line of the real dbus-daemon tool. A quick look at the process list would show nothing odd.

ZQAgent’s decrypted configuration (Source – NVISO)

The malware also protects its own settings. The configuration stays encrypted and is only opened for a moment when needed. Traffic to the command server uses several layers of encryption, including ChaCha20 variants.

The feature list is wide. ZQAgent uses numbered operation codes for each task. These let the operator:-

  • change folders and list their contents
  • move, rename, delete or create files and directories
  • read the first 2048 bytes of any file
  • check the current user and view or kill any process
  • start commands through /bin/sh -c
  • open a full shell through /bin/bash, or /bin/sh if Bash is missing
  • manage TCP and UDP connections

It can even run a program straight from memory. This approach is not new for Linux malware. The Vmcloudoor Linux cloud backdoor uses a similar trick of posing as a trusted agent so admins leave it alone.

Persistence and What Defenders Should Do

ZQAgent survives reboots in two ways. It installs a systemd service and a cron job, and it changes file timestamps on everything it creates, which makes cleanup harder.

A root user gets the binary copied under /usr/lib/systemd/, with the service file in /etc/systemd/system/. Other users get the copy in $HOME/.local/share/, with the service in $HOME/.config/systemd/user/.

If the HOME variable is not set, the malware falls back to /tmp/.local/share/. The service uses the description “Device event journal daemon” and restarts every 30 seconds if stopped.

For normal users, ZQAgent runs loginctl enable-linger so it keeps running after the user logs out. The cron entry uses an @reboot line that runs the file quietly with all output sent to /dev/null.

Linux backdoors that hide in memory and copy trusted names are becoming common. The BPFDoor and Symbiote rootkits also use stealth to stay on servers for long periods. ZQAgent shows that AI-driven tools can now drop this kind of long-term access too.

NVISO warns that LLM-driven tools could soon speed up ransomware and spying. They may cut the time between break-in and ransom from hours to minutes.

The researchers say companies should harden their network edges, split networks into segments, collect security data from every asset, and react faster. They also say automatic isolation of infected systems deserves another look.

Defenders can start with a few checks. Look for the odd dbus-daemon command line and for processes tied to deleted memory files. Search for the “Device event journal daemon” service and unknown cron entries.

Block the listed IP and domain. NVISO also published YARA rules for the backdoor, its service file and its cron job.

For more background on the tool behind this activity, see the report on ARTEX automates enterprise attacks, and the case of a jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent shows how fast these tools can work.

items.title: LDAP Enumeration Cheatsheet
items.summary: LDAP enumeration is a key part of a Windows Active Directory assessment. It can do so much, it’s hard to know exactly what to check. It typically requires some auth on the domain, but any user can get almost all of the information. This is the checklist I work through each time I get creds on a domain, starting with quick checks for things like roastable accounts, gMSA passwords, and deleted objects, then looking at ADCS, collecting and analyzing BloodHound data, finding objects I can write to, and digging into individual objects. I’ll also show what’s worth trying when I don’t have creds yet.

items.title: Critical ASP.NET AntiCsrf Flaw Exploited in Attacks by triggering a web redirect on vulnerable apps
items.summary: Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-131914 , a critical flaw in Idunno: AntiCsrf, an old third-party library used by ASP.NET WebForms applications. watchTowr Intel reports that it saw attackers trigger web redirects on vulnerable applications to check whether exploitation worked. The flaw allows attackers to run code on an affected server without signing in. ASP.NET AntiCsrf Flaw The report follows Mandiant’s November 18 disclosure of active exploitation. As Cyber Security News previously reported, the flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 severity score of 9.3 out of 10. The National Vulnerability Database lists versions through 0.9.1 Beta, including DLL version 0.9.1.0, as affected. The issue is in the optional library, not ASP.NET WebForms itself. The redirect let attackers check the result, not the weakness that let them run code. A redirect alone does not prove a server was compromised because web applications also redirect visitors during normal use. watchTowr’s public report did not name the affected organizations, disclose the redirect destinations, or say what attackers did after the probes. Idunno.AntiCsrf was built to prevent cross-site request forgery, where a site tricks a signed-in browser into sending an unwanted request. The flaw lies in how the library reads a security token. It reconstructs .NET objects from untrusted data before checking whether the token is valid, a weakness known as insecure deserialization. Code that runs through the flaw inherits the permissions of the IIS worker process (w3wp). No fixed release is listed, so teams should check deployed applications for Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll and review web.config for references to the module. watchTowr Intel has observed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-131914, a Remote Code Execution vulnerability in Idunno.AntiCsrf, a legacy https://t.co/hvvX7CNams anti-CSRF library. Attacker probes were observed validating exploitation by triggering a web redirect on… pic.twitter.com/wGaQGHn5Yi — watchTowr (@watchtowrcyber) November 24, 2026 Prioritize internet-facing applications. Replace the library with a maintained CSRF defense and test that forms still reject requests without valid tokens. If replacement cannot happen immediately, restrict access to the affected application while the work is underway. For exposed applications, preserve IIS and reverse proxy logs and compare unexpected redirects with endpoint alerts, new files, or unusual processes started by w3wp.exe. Earlier reporting on attacks against IIS servers covered a separate route involving exposed ASP.NET machine keys. That distinction matters here: rotating keys does not remove the vulnerable library, and removing the library does not tell defenders whether attackers already ran code. items.title: CVE-2026-134401: Critical Google Chrome Flaw Can Enable Code Execution Outside the Sandbox
items.summary: Google has released an emergency security update addressing CVE-2026-134401, a Critical vulnerability in Google Chrome that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code outside the browser sandbox after a victim loads a specially crafted HTML page. The vulnerability is caused by improper input validation in Chrome’s Variations component and is classified as CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.6 (Critical). Google has not yet disclosed the precise vulnerable function, malformed input structure, or technical exploitation chain because access to the underlying Chromium bug remains restricted while the majority of users receive the security update. The Chrome Stable channel was updated on November 23, 2026 to versions 158.0.8127.88/.89 for Windows and macOS and 158.0.8127.88 for Linux . Chrome 158.0.8127.92 for Android contains the corresponding security fixes, while the Extended Stable channel for Windows and macOS received version 156.0.8078.114 . The vulnerability is particularly serious because Google’s CVE description states that successful exploitation can potentially execute code outside the Chrome sandbox . Browser sandboxing normally restricts compromised rendering processes from directly accessing the wider operating system, so a flaw capable of bypassing that boundary can significantly increase the impact of a malicious web page. As of November 24, 2026, Google and the available public reports have not confirmed exploitation in real-world attacks. No campaign-specific attacker infrastructure, malware payloads, or exploit chain has been disclosed. Contact Sales Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize emerging vulnerability intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. SOC Prime is a cybersecurity company that delivers machine-speed detection intelligence, helping security teams uncover cyber attacks, including AI-powered ones. All SOC Prime products run on Prime Core , a detection intelligence dataset of more than 1 million curated, Sigma-based detection rules and 13,000 cyber domain labels, built over a decade and updated daily. LogTotal provides private security log analysis at machine speed, handling up to 60 million events per analysis. Log files are sanitized in the browser, checked against Prime Core detection rules, and correlated into Attack Chains, which reveal sequences of adversary activity. AI adds context to each finding, but raw payloads never go to a model. Prime Hunt scans SIEM, EDR, and Data Lake environments through API access, on demand or on a schedule, without moving data. It forms Attack Chains from historical data to find attacks that were missed. Prime Detect runs detections directly in the data pipeline, before data reaches the SIEM, and works with Kafka, Flink, Cribl, Vector, and more. It reveals Attack Chains in real time with sub-minute mean time to detect and decides which telemetry goes to the SIEM and which goes to cheaper storage. Prime Architect is SOC Prime’s first-party agentic AI for detection engineers. It combines tools, skills, and prompts with web search, image recognition, Attack Flow understanding, and translation of Sigma rules into multiple detection languages. It is available as a UI and via MCP and has no token fees. CVE-2026-134401 analysis CVE-2026-134401 affects Google Chrome releases prior to version 158.0.8127.88. Google’s CNA record describes the vulnerability as improper input validation in the browser’s Variations component and states that a remote attacker can potentially achieve arbitrary code execution outside the sandbox through a crafted HTML page. Chrome Variations is part of Chromium’s infrastructure for configuring and testing browser field trials and experiments. Chromium documentation describes the Variations framework as supporting feature and field-trial configuration across platforms. However, Google has not stated which specific Variations code path is vulnerable or how malicious HTML reaches the affected input-validation logic. This limitation is important for defenders. The publicly available description establishes the security boundary being crossed but does not yet provide enough technical detail to build a reliable network signature for the exploit itself. Google frequently restricts vulnerability details until a significant percentage of the user base has upgraded. The company also keeps restrictions in place when an issue affects third-party components that other projects may not yet have fixed. In this case, Chromium issue 554051967 remains the referenced underlying bug. The vulnerability is classified as: CWE-20: Improper Input Validation Improper input validation occurs when software fails to adequately verify data before processing it. Depending on where that validation failure occurs, attackers may be able to create unexpected object states, corrupt data, bypass security assumptions, or reach dangerous execution paths. Google has not said which of those mechanisms applies here. It would therefore be premature to characterize CVE-2026-134401 as a use-after-free, type confusion, buffer overflow, integer issue, or another specific memory-safety condition without additional technical disclosure. What is confirmed is the outcome described by Chrome’s CVE record: malicious HTML can potentially enable arbitrary code execution beyond the normal Chrome sandbox boundary. The attack requires a user to load attacker-controlled web content. This could theoretically occur through a malicious website, compromised legitimate site, phishing link, malvertising redirect, or another mechanism capable of causing Chrome to process a crafted HTML document. The currently available sources do not identify a specific delivery campaign. Unlike a vulnerability requiring browser extension privileges, local access, or an authenticated account, the attack surface is ordinary web content. The victim does, however, need to interact with or navigate to content containing the exploit. A successful sandbox escape dramatically changes the potential security impact of a browser vulnerability. A renderer compromise normally remains confined by Chrome’s sandbox architecture. Execution outside that sandbox can expose the operating system and user context to further compromise, although Google has not disclosed the precise privilege level obtained through this flaw. The CVE-2026-134401 PoC status remains favorable for defenders at the time of writing. PoC or public exploit is not available, the underlying Chromium issue remains restricted, and publicly tracked vulnerability sources do not currently identify a validated proof-of-concept exploit. Similarly, there is no confirmation that attackers discovered the vulnerability independently or used it before Google’s November update. BigGo’s report specifically notes that exploitation has not been confirmed. Google states that the security issue was reported by Google on August 28, 2026 , indicating that the vulnerability was internally identified months before public disclosure. The Stable security update was released on November 23, and the CVE record was published at approximately the same time. For CVE-2026-134401 detection, organizations should first identify vulnerable Chrome installations. Browser inventory is particularly important during staged rollouts because Google notes that the Stable update will reach users gradually over the following days and weeks. Security teams should hunt for suspicious behavior originating from Chrome rather than relying solely on web-request signatures while exploit details remain private. High-value behavioral indicators include: Chrome processes unexpectedly spawning command interpreters or scripting engines. Browser processes launching PowerShell, cmd.exe, shell utilities, Python, or similar tooling. Executable or script files appearing shortly after suspicious web browsing activity. Unexpected persistence changes following a Chrome session. Chrome or unusual descendant processes establishing previously unseen outbound connections. Endpoint protection alerts indicating browser sandbox violations, exploit behavior, or unexpected memory activity. Browser crashes followed by unusual process execution or file creation. Organizations using EDR should pay particular attention to the Chrome process tree. Normal Chrome installations create multiple renderer, GPU, utility, and network processes, so simply observing many child processes is not suspicious. Detection should focus on descendants that are inconsistent with standard browser behavior. Traditional CVE-2026-134401 IOCs such as malicious domains, IP addresses, payload hashes, or filenames have not been published because no exploitation campaign has been confirmed. Static IOC matching therefore provides little coverage at this stage. Instead, defenders should combine software inventory, browser telemetry, endpoint behavior, DNS and proxy logs, and exploit-prevention alerts. Once Google makes the restricted bug details public, more precise exploit-oriented hunting may become possible. Security teams looking for additional details for CVE-2026-134401 should monitor Google’s Chrome Releases page and Chromium issue 554051967. Google explicitly notes that bug access may remain restricted until most users have received the update. CVE-2026-134401 Mitigation The primary remediation is to update Google Chrome immediately. Google lists the following Stable releases: Platform Fixed Chrome version Windows 158.0.8127.88/.89 macOS 158.0.8127.88/.89 Linux 158.0.8127.88 Android 158.0.8127.92 Extended Stable Windows/macOS 156.0.8078.114 For CVE-2026-134401 mitigation, organizations should verify that browser updates have actually been installed rather than relying solely on automatic-update policies. Desktop users can check the installed browser version through: chrome://settings/help Chrome will normally check for updates from this page. A browser restart is required to activate the new version after it has been downloaded. Enterprise administrators should use browser-management or endpoint-management platforms to identify machines running Chrome versions below the fixed threshold and prioritize externally exposed user workstations. Organizations should also verify systems where Chrome remains open continuously. An update may have downloaded without replacing the active browser processes until the user restarts Chrome. The rollout is gradual, so some devices may not receive the update immediately through the standard automatic process. Where organizational policy permits, administrators should manually trigger or centrally deploy the patched build rather than waiting for the staged rollout to complete. Google Chrome for Android 158.0.8127.92 contains the same security fixes as the corresponding desktop release unless otherwise noted. Mobile-device administrators should therefore ensure Android devices receive the updated browser through Google Play or enterprise mobile management. For organizations using Chromium packages supplied by Linux distributions, do not assume that updating Google Chrome automatically updates a separately installed Chromium package. Distribution maintainers may ship fixes on different timelines, so administrators should verify their specific package source. Browser hardening can provide additional risk reduction but should not replace patching. Security teams should continue using web filtering, endpoint exploit prevention, restricted execution policies, and attack-surface reduction controls to limit the consequences of malicious browser content. Organizations should also enforce least privilege for everyday users. Although the confirmed CVE description states that code execution can occur outside the sandbox, the eventual impact of post-exploitation activity can still be influenced by the privileges available to the compromised user context. Since Google has not confirmed exploitation, large-scale incident response is not warranted solely because a device was running a vulnerable browser. However, systems showing suspicious browser-originated execution, unusual downloads, or endpoint security alerts during the vulnerable period should receive additional investigation. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. FAQ What is CVE-2026-134401 and how does it work? CVE-2026-134401 is a Critical improper input validation vulnerability in Google Chrome’s Variations component. Google states that a remote attacker can potentially exploit the flaw through a specially crafted HTML page and execute arbitrary code outside the browser sandbox. The company has not yet publicly disclosed the precise technical mechanism because the underlying Chromium bug remains restricted. When was CVE-2026-134401 first discovered? Google’s Chrome release announcement states that the issue was reported by Google on August 28, 2026. The precise internal discovery date has not been disclosed. Google publicly released the Chrome security update on November 23, 2026, with the CVE record published at approximately the same time. What is the impact of CVE-2026-134401 on systems? Successful exploitation can potentially allow arbitrary code execution outside Chrome’s sandbox after a victim loads a crafted HTML page. Escaping the sandbox can expose the wider operating system to follow-on activity, although Google has not disclosed the exact privilege level, exploit chain, or post-exploitation capabilities associated with the vulnerability. Google has released an emergency security update addressing CVE-2026-134401, a Critical vulnerability in Google Chrome that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code outside the browser sandbox after a victim loads a specially crafted HTML page.

The vulnerability is caused by improper input validation in Chrome’s Variations component and is classified as CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.6 (Critical). Google has not yet disclosed the precise vulnerable function, malformed input structure, or technical exploitation chain because access to the underlying Chromium bug remains restricted while the majority of users receive the security update.

The Chrome Stable channel was updated on November 23, 2026 to versions 158.0.8127.88/.89 for Windows and macOS and 158.0.8127.88 for Linux. Chrome 158.0.8127.92 for Android contains the corresponding security fixes, while the Extended Stable channel for Windows and macOS received version 156.0.8078.114.

The vulnerability is particularly serious because Google’s CVE description states that successful exploitation can potentially execute code outside the Chrome sandbox. Browser sandboxing normally restricts compromised rendering processes from directly accessing the wider operating system, so a flaw capable of bypassing that boundary can significantly increase the impact of a malicious web page.

As of November 24, 2026, Google and the available public reports have not confirmed exploitation in real-world attacks. No campaign-specific attacker infrastructure, malware payloads, or exploit chain has been disclosed.

It is available as a UI and via MCP and has no token fees.

CVE-2026-134401 analysis

CVE-2026-134401 affects Google Chrome releases prior to version 158.0.8127.88. Google’s CNA record describes the vulnerability as improper input validation in the browser’s Variations component and states that a remote attacker can potentially achieve arbitrary code execution outside the sandbox through a crafted HTML page.

Chrome Variations is part of Chromium’s infrastructure for configuring and testing browser field trials and experiments. Chromium documentation describes the Variations framework as supporting feature and field-trial configuration across platforms. However, Google has not stated which specific Variations code path is vulnerable or how malicious HTML reaches the affected input-validation logic.

This limitation is important for defenders. The publicly available description establishes the security boundary being crossed but does not yet provide enough technical detail to build a reliable network signature for the exploit itself.

Google frequently restricts vulnerability details until a significant percentage of the user base has upgraded. The company also keeps restrictions in place when an issue affects third-party components that other projects may not yet have fixed. In this case, Chromium issue 554051967 remains the referenced underlying bug.

The vulnerability is classified as:

CWE-20: Improper Input Validation

Improper input validation occurs when software fails to adequately verify data before processing it. Depending on where that validation failure occurs, attackers may be able to create unexpected object states, corrupt data, bypass security assumptions, or reach dangerous execution paths.

Google has not said which of those mechanisms applies here. It would therefore be premature to characterize CVE-2026-134401 as a use-after-free, type confusion, buffer overflow, integer issue, or another specific memory-safety condition without additional technical disclosure.

What is confirmed is the outcome described by Chrome’s CVE record: malicious HTML can potentially enable arbitrary code execution beyond the normal Chrome sandbox boundary.

The attack requires a user to load attacker-controlled web content. This could theoretically occur through a malicious website, compromised legitimate site, phishing link, malvertising redirect, or another mechanism capable of causing Chrome to process a crafted HTML document. The currently available sources do not identify a specific delivery campaign.

Unlike a vulnerability requiring browser extension privileges, local access, or an authenticated account, the attack surface is ordinary web content. The victim does, however, need to interact with or navigate to content containing the exploit.

A successful sandbox escape dramatically changes the potential security impact of a browser vulnerability. A renderer compromise normally remains confined by Chrome’s sandbox architecture. Execution outside that sandbox can expose the operating system and user context to further compromise, although Google has not disclosed the precise privilege level obtained through this flaw.

The CVE-2026-134401 PoC status remains favorable for defenders at the time of writing. PoC or public exploit is not available, the underlying Chromium issue remains restricted, and publicly tracked vulnerability sources do not currently identify a validated proof-of-concept exploit.

Similarly, there is no confirmation that attackers discovered the vulnerability independently or used it before Google’s November update. BigGo’s report specifically notes that exploitation has not been confirmed.

Google states that the security issue was reported by Google on August 28, 2026, indicating that the vulnerability was internally identified months before public disclosure. The Stable security update was released on November 23, and the CVE record was published at approximately the same time.

For CVE-2026-134401 detection, organizations should first identify vulnerable Chrome installations. Browser inventory is particularly important during staged rollouts because Google notes that the Stable update will reach users gradually over the following days and weeks.

Security teams should hunt for suspicious behavior originating from Chrome rather than relying solely on web-request signatures while exploit details remain private. High-value behavioral indicators include:

  • Chrome processes unexpectedly spawning command interpreters or scripting engines.
  • Browser processes launching PowerShell, cmd.exe, shell utilities, Python, or similar tooling.
  • Executable or script files appearing shortly after suspicious web browsing activity.
  • Unexpected persistence changes following a Chrome session.
  • Chrome or unusual descendant processes establishing previously unseen outbound connections.
  • Endpoint protection alerts indicating browser sandbox violations, exploit behavior, or unexpected memory activity.
  • Browser crashes followed by unusual process execution or file creation.

Organizations using EDR should pay particular attention to the Chrome process tree. Normal Chrome installations create multiple renderer, GPU, utility, and network processes, so simply observing many child processes is not suspicious. Detection should focus on descendants that are inconsistent with standard browser behavior.

Traditional CVE-2026-134401 IOCs such as malicious domains, IP addresses, payload hashes, or filenames have not been published because no exploitation campaign has been confirmed. Static IOC matching therefore provides little coverage at this stage.

Instead, defenders should combine software inventory, browser telemetry, endpoint behavior, DNS and proxy logs, and exploit-prevention alerts. Once Google makes the restricted bug details public, more precise exploit-oriented hunting may become possible.

Security teams looking for additional details for CVE-2026-134401 should monitor Google’s Chrome Releases page and Chromium issue 554051967. Google explicitly notes that bug access may remain restricted until most users have received the update.

CVE-2026-134401 Mitigation

The primary remediation is to update Google Chrome immediately.

Google lists the following Stable releases:

PlatformFixed Chrome versionWindows158.0.8127.88/.89macOS158.0.8127.88/.89Linux158.0.8127.88Android158.0.8127.92Extended Stable Windows/macOS156.0.8078.114

For CVE-2026-134401 mitigation, organizations should verify that browser updates have actually been installed rather than relying solely on automatic-update policies.

Desktop users can check the installed browser version through:

chrome://settings/help

Chrome will normally check for updates from this page. A browser restart is required to activate the new version after it has been downloaded.

Enterprise administrators should use browser-management or endpoint-management platforms to identify machines running Chrome versions below the fixed threshold and prioritize externally exposed user workstations.

Organizations should also verify systems where Chrome remains open continuously. An update may have downloaded without replacing the active browser processes until the user restarts Chrome.

The rollout is gradual, so some devices may not receive the update immediately through the standard automatic process. Where organizational policy permits, administrators should manually trigger or centrally deploy the patched build rather than waiting for the staged rollout to complete.

Google Chrome for Android 158.0.8127.92 contains the same security fixes as the corresponding desktop release unless otherwise noted. Mobile-device administrators should therefore ensure Android devices receive the updated browser through Google Play or enterprise mobile management.

For organizations using Chromium packages supplied by Linux distributions, do not assume that updating Google Chrome automatically updates a separately installed Chromium package. Distribution maintainers may ship fixes on different timelines, so administrators should verify their specific package source.

Browser hardening can provide additional risk reduction but should not replace patching. Security teams should continue using web filtering, endpoint exploit prevention, restricted execution policies, and attack-surface reduction controls to limit the consequences of malicious browser content.

Organizations should also enforce least privilege for everyday users. Although the confirmed CVE description states that code execution can occur outside the sandbox, the eventual impact of post-exploitation activity can still be influenced by the privileges available to the compromised user context.

Since Google has not confirmed exploitation, large-scale incident response is not warranted solely because a device was running a vulnerable browser. However, systems showing suspicious browser-originated execution, unusual downloads, or endpoint security alerts during the vulnerable period should receive additional investigation.

Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added.

CVE-2026-134401 is a Critical improper input validation vulnerability in Google Chrome’s Variations component. With the feature expected to become generally available in 2027, Microsoft wants to make a familiar Windows security problem less confusing. Your PC has a collection of built-in protections, but working out which ones are enabled and what to do when they aren’t can take some digging. Windows baseline protection will show you what’s missing and help you fix it. It will also give software developers a simpler way to check whether your computer meets their requirements and decide whether to let an app run at all. On the positive side, that could make security easier to manage. But it could also mean more encounters with software that says your PC isn’t secure enough to use it. The protections already exist in Windows. What’s new is the way Windows evaluates them together and shares the result. For people using personal or unmanaged PCs, the most immediately useful change may be the explanation that comes with the result. Preview of Windows baseline protection in Settings (image courtesy of Microsoft) Where possible, a single button will enable the missing protections and restart the computer. The first version checks these eight requirements: Security processor : Dedicated hardware, such as a TPM, that helps protect sensitive information. Secure Boot : Protection against malicious software loading during startup. Virtualization-based security : Hardware-assisted isolation that helps protect critical processes. Memory integrity : Protection against malicious code running in protected parts of Windows. Signed drivers only : A requirement that drivers have digital signatures. Windows-certified drivers : A requirement that drivers meet Windows hardware signing requirements. An application that wants to check a computer’s security configuration can use Windows’ baseline protection signal instead of maintaining its own collection of checks. The intended uses are straightforward. An exam service might want to verify a student’s device before a test. A game might check protections relevant to anti-cheat measures. An organization might require a device to meet its security requirements before granting access. Main takeaways Windows baseline protection brings existing safeguards together into a common, hardware-backed security assessment and helps users enable any missing protections. That could make Windows security less confusing, but it also gives software vendors a simpler way to warn users, restrict features, or deny access when a computer falls short. The developer decides what happens next. Will they require the entire baseline, or only the protections their application actually needs? Windows baseline protection and security software such as Malwarebytes address different parts of the problem. Microsoft’s checks establish whether a set of underlying Windows safeguards is enabled. Malwarebytes Premium Plus adds protection against threats such as malware, ransomware, exploits, and malicious websites, along with browser protection and a VPN. Neither replaces the other: Installing security software does not switch on a missing Windows safeguard, and passing Microsoft’s checklist is not a guarantee that your PC is free of malware. The feature is still in preview, and Microsoft says feedback will shape it before general availability. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. Read their review →

In this article
  • Microsoft plans to bring eight Windows security checks together in 2027
  • Windows baseline protection will flag missing safeguards and let you turn some on with one click
  • Apps could use the result to warn you, limit features, or block access

Microsoft announced plans to introduce Windows baseline protection, a feature that brings eight existing safeguards together into a single, verifiable security status.

With the feature expected to become generally available in 2027, Microsoft wants to make a familiar Windows security problem less confusing. Your PC has a collection of built-in protections, but working out which ones are enabled and what to do when they aren’t can take some digging.

Windows baseline protection will show you what’s missing and help you fix it. It will also give software developers a simpler way to check whether your computer meets their requirements and decide whether to let an app run at all.

On the positive side, that could make security easier to manage. But it could also mean more encounters with software that says your PC isn’t secure enough to use it.

The protections already exist in Windows. What’s new is the way Windows evaluates them together and shares the result. For people using personal or unmanaged PCs, the most immediately useful change may be the explanation that comes with the result.

Microsoft says the new baseline protection page in Windows Settings will show which protections are missing.

Preview of Windows baseline protection in Settings (image courtesy of Microsoft)

Where possible, a single button will enable the missing protections and restart the computer. If you need to change your PC’s firmware settings, for example to enable Secure Boot or the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), Windows will provide guidance.

The first version checks these eight requirements:

  • Security processor: Dedicated hardware, such as a TPM, that helps protect sensitive information.
  • Secure Boot: Protection against malicious software loading during startup.
  • Virtualization-based security: Hardware-assisted isolation that helps protect critical processes.
  • Memory integrity: Protection against malicious code running in protected parts of Windows.
  • Signed drivers only: A requirement that drivers have digital signatures.
  • Windows-certified drivers: A requirement that drivers meet Windows hardware signing requirements.
  • Kernel debugger protection: Restrictions that help prevent debugging tools from bypassing Windows security protections.
  • Vulnerable driver protection: Protection against known vulnerable drivers that could weaken the system’s security.

An application that wants to check a computer’s security configuration can use Windows’ baseline protection signal instead of maintaining its own collection of checks.

The intended uses are straightforward. An exam service might want to verify a student’s device before a test. A game might check protections relevant to anti-cheat measures. An organization might require a device to meet its security requirements before granting access.

Main takeaways

Windows baseline protection brings existing safeguards together into a common, hardware-backed security assessment and helps users enable any missing protections. That could make Windows security less confusing, but it also gives software vendors a simpler way to warn users, restrict features, or deny access when a computer falls short.

The developer decides what happens next. Will they require the entire baseline, or only the protections their application actually needs?

Windows baseline protection and security software such as Malwarebytes address different parts of the problem. Microsoft’s checks establish whether a set of underlying Windows safeguards is enabled. Malwarebytes Premium Plus adds protection against threats such as malware, ransomware, exploits, and malicious websites, along with browser protection and a VPN. Neither replaces the other: Installing security software does not switch on a missing Windows safeguard, and passing Microsoft’s checklist is not a guarantee that your PC is free of malware.

The feature is still in preview, and Microsoft says feedback will shape it before general availability.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” 

According to CNET. Read their review →

items.title: We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
items.summary: This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?” Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly. There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream of the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problem lies. Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, recoverability—these are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are inefficient: costs that feel wasteful until something bad happens. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, squeeze all inefficiencies out of a company in pursuit of near-term profits. Competition, with multiple companies competing to do the same thing, is another inefficiency. Monopolization removes that in pursuit of near-term profits. The result is brittle systems, single points of failure. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures. Fixing this is technical, but it’s political first. It requires changing incentives, and that involves regulation and control. “What to do” is easy; finding the political will to stand up to moneyed interests and do it is hard.

items.title: Autonomous AI Attack Tools Target Coding Agents, Chatbots and Retail Payment Systems, Infrawatch Finds
items.summary: New research from Infrawatch has revealed how threat actors are using autonomous offensive frameworks (AOFs) to launch attacks against organisations, with AI coding agents, customer-facing chatbots, fintech platforms and retail payment systems among the targets. The findings highlight an emerging dimension of AI security risk: not only are threat actors using AI to facilitate cyberattacks, but they are increasingly targeting AI infrastructure itself, exploiting the autonomy and permissions granted to these systems. The research , The Autonomy of the Autonomous Intrusions , analysed 128 AI-assisted intrusions and identified 10,848 services running autonomous offensive frameworks across 8,105 hosts globally. The number of servers hosting these frameworks has more than doubled since 6 November 2026. Researchers also identified more than 130 variants of ARTEX, the most widely used autonomous offensive framework, highlighting the rapid evolution of the AI-powered offensive ecosystem. AI infrastructure becomes a target In at least 24 of the attacks analysed, threat actors targeted other organisations’ AI infrastructure. In one instance, an attacker targeted exposed AI coding agents, redirecting them to an attacker-controlled language model and harvesting 77 credentials from compromised machines. Elsewhere, an autonomous offensive framework testing a fintech company’s production AI service introduced a malicious tool via its Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint. Worryingly, the company’s own AI agent discovered, approved and executed the malicious tool without human intervention. Customer-facing chatbots were also targeted, with attackers extracting an online retailer’s internal chatbot instructions and information about the tools it could access. In another instance, a hotel booking assistant was manipulated into revealing details of its internal functionality. The research also uncovered attempts to compromise publicly accessible image-generation and local AI inference services, demonstrating the breadth of the emerging AI attack surface. From cyberattacks to financial fraud The use of autonomous offensive frameworks extends beyond traditional network intrusions. Infrawatch identified a modified version of ARTEX being used in a fraud campaign targeting a multinational retailer’s payment and gift-card infrastructure. Researchers also observed attacks against cryptocurrency exchanges, government databases and e-commerce platforms. Where researchers could establish the level of human involvement, AI agents were responsible for driving more than 70% of intrusions, either autonomously or under supervision. However, the technology remains imperfect, with hallucinations contributing to unsuccessful attacks. Familiar vulnerabilities, unprecedented scale Despite the technological sophistication of autonomous offensive frameworks, the underlying security weaknesses being exploited are largely familiar. Unsecured databases, insufficient authentication and longstanding software vulnerabilities continue to provide opportunities for attackers. The difference lies in the speed and scale at which these weaknesses can now be identified and exploited, without requiring continuous human involvement. However, the infrastructure supporting autonomous attacks presents an opportunity for defenders. Infrawatch found that 45% of observed intrusions originated directly from servers hosting autonomous offensive frameworks, making infrastructure intelligence a potentially valuable tool for disrupting malicious activity. The researchers recommend incorporating infrastructure intelligence into wider cybersecurity strategies, alongside behavioural monitoring, authentication controls and risk-based blocking. As autonomous offensive frameworks proliferate, organisations face the dual challenge of defending against increasingly automated attacks while ensuring that their own AI deployments do not become new avenues for compromise.

items.title: Hackers Bypass Alpine Linux SSH Authentication Using Just a 257-Byte Password
items.summary: A flaw in OpenSSH lets remote attackers sign in to certain Alpine Linux accounts without knowing a valid password or holding an SSH key. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 and known as SSHole, affects unpatched servers that use the musl C library, run without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), and allow SSH password logins. OpenSSH released a fix on November 5, and Alpine shipped patched packages the same day. Hackers Bypass Alpine Linux SSH Authentication According to IOTSEC Forum , the 257-byte figure comes from a November 23 lab report. A researcher showed that an unpatched OpenSSH build on Alpine Linux 3.24 accepted a password login for an account with no usable password. The patched Alpine package rejected the login. The lab result is separate from Cyber Security News’ earlier reporting on active exploitation . OpenSSH normally checks a password by comparing its hash, a one-way representation of the password, with the value stored for the account. On affected systems, musl’s crypt() function can return an error marker instead of a hash. That marker can look identical to the stored value that tells Linux an account has no usable password. The unpatched server treated the match as a successful login. It did not recover or guess anyone’s password. CVE-2026-123158 Bypassed Output (Source: iotsec) The fix blocks that false match by rejecting stored values that are too short to be valid password hashes. It also changes how OpenSSH copies account data so a later lookup cannot overwrite the value being checked. The OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes credit Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield with reporting the flaw. An Alpine base image alone does not make a system vulnerable. The risk is on hosts and containers running an affected SSH server with password authentication enabled and the account conditions described in the Alpine Linux security advisory . Containers that do not run sshd and servers that use PAM for authentication are outside this attack path. Alpine also flagged older tiny-cloud images, covered in our initial OpenSSH bypass report . Those images shipped with an alpine user that could gain root privileges through doas without a password. Alpine said the images were not exposed on first boot, but later account changes could make them vulnerable. Blocking direct root login does not protect a separate account that can become root. Check the installed server package revision, not just the upstream version shown in an SSH banner. The first fixed Alpine packages include 10.3_p1-r2 for 3.24, 10.2_p1-r1 for 3.23, and 10.0_p1-r11 for 3.22. After upgrading, restart the running server with rc-service sshd restart. If patching must wait, verify that key-based access works, set PasswordAuthentication no, and restart sshd. Keep the current session open until a fresh login succeeds. On exposed systems, review /var/log/messages for Accepted password entries involving accounts meant to use SSH keys only. Compare each event with the account’s settings at the time. Review doas activity and look for newly created users, unfamiliar files, or changes to authorized_keys. A failed login followed by a success is not proof of exploitation. A password login to an account that should never accept one warrants immediate investigation. Alpine advises treating the system as compromised if you cannot rule out unauthorized access. items.title: Hackers Bypass MFA Through Phone Scams to Access Microsoft 365, OneDrive and SharePoint Data
items.summary: Cybercriminals posing as corporate IT support are calling employees and tricking them into handing over access to Microsoft 365 accounts, even when multifactor authentication (MFA) is enabled. The attackers have used compromised accounts to steal email and files from OneDrive and SharePoint, then contacted employees through Microsoft Teams or email to demand payment. The calls are a form of voice phishing, or vishing. The caller claims an account setting needs attention and directs the employee to a fake sign-in page made to look like a company portal. As earlier reporting on Microsoft 365 session theft explains, a successful MFA prompt does not guarantee that the person who approved it is the only one who can use the resulting session. Researchers at Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 identified malware in a related investigation: a browser extension masquerading as Google Chrome. The team found it while investigating an activity cluster it calls Helix. The extension was not available through the Chrome Web Store, and Unit 42 did not find evidence that other Com-affiliated groups used it. Hackers Bypass MFA Through Phone Scams Unit 42 identified two activity clusters, Vortex and Cinder, in September 2026. Vortex primarily targeted healthcare, pharmaceutical and other medical organizations. Its callers posed as internal IT support and directed employees to sign-in pages tailored to their employer. The pages acted as a relay between the employee and the real login service, allowing the attackers to intercept authentication information as the employee signed in. The approach, known as adversary-in-the-middle phishing, does not require the attackers to crack MFA. Instead, the victim completes authentication and the attacker takes advantage of the authenticated session. Related reporting on passkey-themed Microsoft 365 phishing shows how a supposed security update can make an unexpected call sound like routine IT work. Vortex targeted employees on both corporate computers and personal phones. Flow chart (Source – Unit42) Within minutes of signing in, Vortex operators enrolled an unauthorized MFA device. Unit 42 saw a device named Pixel 10a reused across multiple compromised accounts. The attackers then used scripts to collect Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive and SharePoint data. The device enrollment gave them a way to maintain access beyond the original sign-in. Cinder took a different route. Unit 42 found that it reused a persistent “keep me signed in” session token without triggering another Duo MFA prompt. The group used Microsoft Graph, an interface for accessing Microsoft cloud services, to collect SharePoint and OneDrive files. The findings echo earlier coverage of UNC6671 cloud data theft , where automated collection followed employee session hijacking. Cinder later used a compromised account to send extortion messages by email and Teams. What Security Teams Should Look For In the Helix investigation, Unit 42 found that the fake Chrome extension could log keystrokes, steal authentication cookies, read clipboard contents and capture screenshots. Researchers identified two versions, 1.6.111 and 1.6.112 , that communicated with the same remote server. An organization investigating a suspicious call should therefore check browser extensions as well as cloud sign-ins, particularly if an employee recalls being asked to install software. The timing of events can be more useful than any single alert. Microsoft’s cloud compromise research describes unusual sign-ins followed by new authentication methods, heavy Microsoft Graph activity and bursts of file downloads. A phone model or software identifier may be legitimate on its own. An unexpected enrollment followed by bulk downloads from the same account deserves closer scrutiny. Organizations should require employees to verify unexpected support calls through a help desk number they already know. Unit 42 recommends phishing-resistant MFA, tighter help desk verification, browser extension allowlists and alerts for unauthorized exports. Earlier coverage of Microsoft Entra passkey enrollment highlights why enrollment itself needs protection: a strong sign-in method does not help if the attacker persuades an employee to register it on the attacker’s behalf. When a takeover is suspected, responders should revoke active sessions, remove unauthorized authentication methods and review mailbox, OneDrive and SharePoint audit records to determine what the account accessed. Check outbound email and Teams messages as well: both featured in the extortion activity, and a message sent from a real employee account can look trustworthy to colleagues. items.title: CISA Warns of VMware vCenter, SAP NetWeaver, Cisco Expressway, and Apache Roller Flaws Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added four vulnerabilities affecting VMware vCenter, SAP NetWeaver, Cisco Expressway, and Apache Roller to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on November 20, 2026. In its November 20 alert, the agency confirmed all four flaws were exploited and gave federal civilian agencies until November 23 to patch them, noting that their impact varies. Three carry a critical severity score of 9.8, while the SAP flaw is rated 6.5. Its inclusion shows why security teams should weigh evidence of real attacks alongside severity scores when deciding which systems to patch first. VMware vCenter Server flaw CVE-2026-123890 affects the VMware Directory Service. An attacker who can reach a vulnerable vCenter server over the network can bypass its login checks and gain unauthorized access. Because vCenter manages multiple virtual hosts, a breach can put more than one system at risk. Broadcom released fixes on November 19. As Cyber Security News reported in its VMware vCenter zero-day coverage , Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant traced attacks to early September, before a patch was available. CVE-2026-76466 affects Cisco Expressway-C and E clusters, allowing unauthenticated root command execution through hardcoded credentials. Cisco patched the flaw in October 2026 before CISA added it to its catalog. CVE ID Product Vulnerability / Impact CVE-2026-123890 VMware vCenter Server Zero-day authentication bypass. CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal JNDI injection flaw. CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Remote code execution in clustered deployments. CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Unauthenticated remote code execution under active exploitation. Apache Roller, an open-source blogging platform, fixed CVE-2026-129448, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw caused by processing untrusted data before authentication, in version 6.1.5. SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal flaw CVE-2025-42884 can let an attacker without an account redirect a Java lookup and potentially read or change server information. SAP addressed the issue in its November 2025 security updates under Security Note 3660969. This is separate from the SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer zero-day that CISA listed in April 2025. CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 26-04 guidance tells federal civilian agencies to prioritize fixes for internet-facing systems when a known exploited flaw can give attackers full control. The directive also requires agencies to check for signs of earlier breaches and encourages other organizations to use CISA’s KEV catalog to prioritize patches. Administrators should confirm which versions they run, check which systems are reachable from the internet, and apply the fixes listed in vendor advisories. For systems that were exposed before patching, security teams should preserve and review available logs for unusual sign-ins, new accounts, or unexpected changes. Installing an update closes the flaw, but it does not tell defenders whether someone used it before the fix went in. CVE-2026-76466 affects Cisco Expressway-C and E clusters, allowing unauthenticated root command execution through hardcoded credentials. Cisco patched the flaw in October 2026 before CISA added it to its catalog.

Apache Roller, an open-source blogging platform, fixed CVE-2026-129448, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw caused by processing untrusted data before authentication, in version 6.1.5.

Administrators should confirm which versions they run, check which systems are reachable from the internet, and apply the fixes listed in vendor advisories.

For systems that were exposed before patching, security teams should preserve and review available logs for unusual sign-ins, new accounts, or unexpected changes. Installing an update closes the flaw, but it does not tell defenders whether someone used it before the fix went in.

items.title: Critical Google Chrome Flaw Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code Outside Browser Sandbox
items.summary: Google released a desktop Chrome security update on November 23, 2026, to fix CVE-2026-134401. This critical flaw could let a remote attacker run malicious code outside the browser sandbox. The Stable update covers Windows, macOS, and Linux. It contains one security fix, and Google says the rollout will take place over the coming days and weeks. The update follows the initial Chrome 158 release, which fixed 204 security flaws . Users who installed that earlier release still need the new update. The full build number matters: the National Vulnerability Database lists Chrome versions before 158.0.8127.88 as affected. Critical Google Chrome Flaw Google traced the flaw to improper input validation in Variations, a Chrome component that lets the company test changes with groups of users before a wider rollout. Input validation is the process of checking that data meets expected rules before software uses it. Google reported the issue internally on August 28, 2026, and rated it critical. The sandbox limits what code handling web content can access on a device. The [National Vulnerability Database record] says a specially crafted HTML page could let a remote attacker run code outside that boundary. Our earlier coverage of a separate Chrome sandbox escape flaw gives readers more context on why that boundary matters. Google’s release notes do not indicate that the flaw has been exploited in attacks. Additionally, the public record does not clarify whether successful exploitation would grant administrator access. Running code outside the sandbox is a serious issue, but it does not, on its own, prove that an attacker could gain full control of the device. Google is rolling out Chrome version 158.0.8127.88 or 158.0.8127.89 for Windows and macOS, and 158.0.8127.88 for Linux. To check for updates, open the Chrome menu, select Help, and click on About Google Chrome. After the update installs, select Relaunch. Reopen the About page to ensure that Chrome is running the updated version. Note that an update downloaded in the background does not protect a browser session that hasn’t been restarted. For IT teams, the currently running version is a more reliable reference than whether the update was offered. After Chrome restarts, verify the full build number on managed devices, and check again on devices that are still waiting for the staged rollout. items.title: Suzlon Energy Cyberattack – Company Confirms Critical Infrastructure Operational
items.summary: Suzlon Energy disclosed a cyber incident on November 23, 2026. It said it had seen no impact on its business-critical applications at the time of reporting. In a filing with India’s stock exchanges, the wind turbine maker said it took immediate steps to limit the impact, activated its incident response procedures, and notified the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In). Suzlon Energy Cyberattack According to Economic Times , the company did not say when it first detected the incident, how it began or which systems were affected. It also did not say whether anyone accessed or stole customer or employee data. Suzlon urged stakeholders to avoid speculation. Its statement covers the business applications it relies on. However, it does not separately address the status of turbine controls, remote monitoring systems or power generation. That distinction matters in the energy sector. Business applications support company workflows, while operational technology, or OT, monitors and controls physical equipment such as wind turbines. As our coverage of CISA’s guide to tracking industrial equipment explains, keeping an accurate record of these systems helps operators identify what could be affected during an incident. Suzlon has not said whether the incident reached its industrial networks. Separately, India’s Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has tightened cybersecurity requirements for approved wind turbine manufacturers. An August ministry notice asked manufacturers to show that they store turbine data in India, keep operational control within the country and prevent live operational data from being sent abroad. The rules predate Suzlon’s disclosure. Our reporting on internet-exposed solar equipment shows why securing connected devices matters across renewable energy. A separate case involving cyberattacks on Polish wind and solar farms illustrates why operators track communications and generation separately. In that incident, some facilities lost communications with the distribution network operator, but electricity generation continued. That case is not linked to Suzlon. It shows how one part of an energy network can be disrupted while another keeps working. For energy operators, guidance on isolating critical systems recommends identifying where business and industrial networks connect and testing whether essential equipment can keep running if those links are cut. Those are general safeguards, not steps Suzlon said it took. The company’s filing leaves three questions open: which systems were affected, whether any data was exposed, and whether industrial networks were involved. items.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot Flaw Lets Attackers Gain Elevated Privileges Without User Interaction
items.summary: Microsoft disclosed a critical Microsoft 365 Copilot vulnerability that could let an attacker with limited privileges gain higher permissions over a network without any action from another user. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-50691, was released on November 19, 2026, and received a CVSS 3.1 base score of 9.9 out of 10. Microsoft says customers do not need to take any action to resolve it. Microsoft 365 Copilot Flaw The distinction is that no user interaction does not mean no initial access. The attacker needs some permissions before exploiting the flaw, but does not need another user to click a link, open a file, or approve a request. That separates this issue from SearchLeak, a one-click Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw that Cyber Security News covered in June. Microsoft classified the weakness as improper authorization, or CWE-285. Authorization is the check that decides what someone can do after the service knows who they are. When that check is missing or applied incorrectly, a user can gain access to a resource or action that their existing permissions should block. Microsoft’s assessment describes a network-reachable flaw with low attack complexity. It also rates the potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability as high. In plain terms, a successful attack could put protected data, its accuracy, and access to affected resources at risk. The score also reflects a change in scope, meaning the impact could extend beyond the security boundary of the affected component. These ratings describe potential impact, not confirmed customer harm. Microsoft’s assessment listed the flaw as not exploited at publication. The Microsoft Security Response Center advisory says no customer action is required, so administrators do not need to install a local update for this CVE. This flaw is separate from EchoLeak , an earlier Copilot issue that could expose information without user interaction and did not require an attacker to have prior access. Here, the reported impact is higher privileges for an attacker who already has limited access. The update does not eliminate the necessity of reviewing existing permissions. Microsoft’s Copilot security guidance advises checking SharePoint sites for files shared too broadly and restricting access to only those who need it. This review addresses a separate risk: even if Copilot enforces permissions accurately, it can still make files easier to find for users who already have more access than intended. items.title: Critical N-able Mail Assure SSRF Vulnerability Allows Attackers to Reach Internal Systems via LDAP Sync
items.summary: N-able has patched a critical vulnerability in MailAssure, also known as SpamExperts, that lets an attacker with privileged API access reach internal network services through the email security platform. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3. N-able’s November 22 security advisory identifies build 20261121.1943 as the fix and lists all earlier builds as affected. N-able Mail Assure SSRF Vulnerability The disclosure follows a November 16 service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of the N-able server breach , the company confirmed unauthorized access to one hosted server and disabled management access while it responded. Dashboard and API access returned late on November 21. The advisory does not establish how the attacker first gained access to the hosted environment. The flaw affects a connection check that MailAssure runs for LDAP synchronization when a mail relay is configured. As N-able’s LDAP mailbox sync guide explains, LDAP, short for Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, lets MailAssure query an organization’s directory and keep its mailbox and alias lists up to date. The problem was not with LDAP itself. MailAssure failed to limit where its server could connect during the check. That makes the flaw a server-side request forgery, or SSRF, classified as CWE-918. A user with the required API privileges can make the MailAssure server connect to internal hosts and ports, learn which services are reachable, and send specially prepared data to them. The distinction matters: internal services do not need to be exposed to the internet for the MailAssure server to reach them. The risk is similar to that described in Cyber Security News’ coverage of the Zimbra SSRF vulnerability : a trusted server can reach systems that an outside user cannot contact directly. In this case, the severity rating specifies that high privileges are required, but no other user needs to take action. N-able’s advisory describes internal network access, not remote code execution. Organizations running MailAssure or SpamExperts should verify that their service is on build 20261121.1943 or later. Customers who cannot check the build themselves should ask their provider to confirm that the fix is in place. The National Vulnerability Database entry records the flaw, which CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 23. Administrators should review who holds privileged API credentials and check available logs for unexpected relay changes or connections from MailAssure to systems outside its normal directory setup. The patch closes the vulnerable connection check, but it cannot show whether someone misused it beforehand. Hosted customers without access to those logs may need help from their provider.
