items.title: Patching vCenter Zero-Day Is Only Step One
items.summary: CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter's directory service, rated 9.8 out of 10. An attacker who can reach vCenter on the network can become administrator@vsphere.local without a password. A suspected China-nexus espionage group, ARMORY CASTLE, exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. Broadcom patched it on Nov. 19, and CISA gave U.S. federal agencies until Nov. 23 to fix it. Install the patch today. Then plan for the harder job. If anything that could reach your vCenter was compromised at any point since September, the patch closes the door but doesn't take back what went through it. In the intrusion researchers investigated, that included vCenter's SAML signing key, its master encryption key and Active Directory credentials copied straight out of virtual machine disks. Let's see how the attackers used this flaw, which builds fix it, and the hunting and credential rotation that should follow the patch. What Is CVE-2026-123890 Broadcom disclosed the flaw last week, in advisory VMSA-2026-0009 , which fixes five vulnerabilities across vCenter, SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows. CVE-2026-123890 is the critical one. An authentication bypass using an alternate path (CWE-288) in the VMware Directory Service, the component behind vCenter's single sign-on. Mandiant found it and reported it privately. The bug lives in a remote procedure call interface that vCenter's directory service exposes on TCP port 2012. Its Secure Remote Password login generates predictable identifiers based on timestamps, and according to researchers, an attacker can use that to recover the shared session key without knowing any password. The result is an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local , the most powerful account in a vSphere environment. From there, an attacker can run commands and copy files through the directory service, including data.mdb , the database that holds the SSO domain's accounts and the private key vCenter uses to sign SAML login tokens. It is not a virtual machine escape. It's worse in a different way - it hands over the console that manages every host and VM. Two things make it easy to get wrong: It's a different bug from CVE-2026-59309, the vCenter authentication bypass Broadcom fixed in July. Mandiant observed attackers using CVE-2026-123890 against a vCenter that was already patched for the July flaw. There is no workaround. Broadcom's only fix is the update, which its own FAQ treats as an emergency change. How ARMORY CASTLE used it from a support box to domain credentials Mandiant's write-up shows why vCenter being reachable only from the internal network didn't protect it. The attackers never touched vCenter from the internet. They worked their way to it from the inside. ARMORY CASTLE's path from a remote-support appliance to Active Directory credentials Break in at the edge. The group, formerly tracked as UNC5221, first exploited a separate zero-day in BeyondTrust Remote Support, CVE-2026-102764. Find the VMware estate. From the support appliance, it scanned the internal network for VMware ports, including 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080, then moved to internal Linux appliances that had no endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. It dropped two web shells and became root by setting the SUID bit on /bin/env with the gdb debugger. Take vCenter. A custom Go tool Mandiant calls BONESAW exploited CVE-2026-123890 over port 2012, created a new SSO administrator account, copied the directory database and extracted the token-signing key. Forge logins. A second tool, SAWSNAKE, used the stolen key to sign SAML tokens as the administrator, a "Golden SAML" attack that bypasses passwords and MFA. Drop into the appliance. The group switched on SSH through vCenter's appliance management API, logged in with its new account, stole vCenter's master encryption key and its PostgreSQL database password, then switched SSH off again. Reach the hosts and the domain. It logged in to ESXi hosts as vpxuser and root, added its own SSH key, and used a Python tool to extract the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) and registry hives straight from a virtual machine's disk. The files left through the original support appliance. Two backdoors kept the door open: BEARBONES, a modified Dropbear SSH server that accepts a hardcoded password, and LAZYBONES, which takes commands through Slack. The timing matters too. BONESAW's build timestamp is July 13, 2026, and the attackers used it in early September. Go build timestamps can be faked, but Mandiant reads it as a tool built for broader operations, not a one-off. Which vCenter versions fix CVE-2026-123890? Product line Affected Fixed in vCenter in VCF / vSphere Foundation 9.1 9.1.x 9.1.1.0200 vCenter in VCF / vSphere Foundation 9.0 9.0.x 9.0.2.0200 vCenter Server 8.0 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x 5.x 5.2.5 vCenter Server 7.0 7.0 No public fix; extended-support customers go through Broadcom Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure Listed versions See Broadcom KB463116 A few details that trip people up: Patched in July doesn't mean patched now. Every vCenter below the builds in the table needs this update, including systems that already have the CVE-2026-59309 fix. vCenter 7.0 is the hard case. vSphere 7.0 reached the end of general support on Oct. 2, 2025, so there's no public fix. Broadcom's supplemental FAQ also says to presume versions 6.5 and 6.7 are affected. If you're on any of these, restricting network access to port 2012 is your main protection until you can upgrade or obtain a fix. ESXi isn't in the advisory. The flaw is in vCenter. ESXi hosts still matter for the cleanup, because the attackers used vCenter to reach them. Don't run the GitHub "proof of concept." A repository that appeared on Nov. 20 claiming exploit code describes the wrong advisory and fixed versions. As of Nov. 21, Rapid7 had opened a Metasploit module titled as an authentication bypass to root, so expect working public exploit code soon, if it isn't out already. Why patching isn't enough The patch fixes the login flaw. It does nothing about what an attacker took while the flaw was open, and in this case the stolen items are exactly the kind that keep working: The token-signing key. Anyone holding vCenter's SAML signing key can mint valid administrator logins until that certificate is replaced. A patched vCenter will accept them. New accounts. The attackers created an SSO administrator named sps- followed by random characters in vsphere.local. BONESAW can also add a machine account and grant Global Administrator rights on the vCenter root folder. Appliance secrets. vCenter's master encryption key and PostgreSQL password were copied over SSH. Host access. An SSH key was added to the ESXi root account. Active Directory. A copy of NTDS.dit plus the SYSTEM hive is enough to recover the password hashes of every account in the domain, offline. The exposure window also runs further back than most patch plans assume. Exploitation started in early September, more than 10 weeks before the fix. If any system that could reach your vCenter's management ports was compromised in that time, treat vCenter as possibly compromised too until you've checked. After the patch: what to hunt for Search logs back to at least early September 2026. These come from Mandiant's analysis; ARMORY CASTLE deletes its tools after use, so absence of files doesn't prove absence of compromise. On the network Connections to TCP 2012 on vCenter from anything other than your documented management hosts, especially Linux appliances or remote-support servers. Internal scans for VMware ports 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080. Servers calling the Slack API, and SSH services announcing the banner SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345, often on high, non-standard ports. Traffic to the 11 suspected obfuscation-network IPs in GTIG's report, such as 103.147.251[.]5 and 176.9.89[.]66. On vCenter SSO accounts you didn't create, especially names starting with sps- in vsphere.local, and unexpected members of the Administrators group. A PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh call to the appliance management API, particularly SSH being enabled and disabled again shortly after. SSH logins to the appliance, and reads of the master key or PostgreSQL password files. On ESXi hosts ESXi Host Client logins as vpxuser and root SSH sessions you can't explain. New entries in root's authorized_keys. Hidden directories such as .a on VMFS volumes, and the files vmfs-pydist.tar.gz or vmfs_browser.py. On internal Linux appliances The files /tmp/123 (BONESAW), /tmp/sss (SAWSNAKE), /tmp/dbr (BEARBONES), /tmp/123.key and /tmp/gdb_file. /usr/bin/vmtoolscs (LAZYBONES) running as a systemd service that restarts every 50 minutes. Web shells named ActiveSer.jsp or u.jsp, and the SUID bit set on /bin/env. GTIG has published YARA rules for BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES and both web shells in the same report. After the patch: what to rotate and reset If you find signs of compromise, or can't rule it out because logs don't reach back to September, work through this in order. Patch and lock down access first, or the attacker can simply take the new secrets too. These steps reflect the consensus among incident responders building on Mandiant's findings; follow Broadcom's knowledge base procedures for each vCenter task. Patch, then close the paths in. Install the fixed build, patch BeyondTrust Remote Support if you run it, and restrict ports 2012, 443, 5480 and 22 on vCenter to named management hosts. Rebuild what you can't trust. Where compromise is confirmed, rebuild vCenter and the affected Linux appliances rather than cleaning them. The attackers had root and deleted their tools as they went. Replace the STS signing certificate. This is the step that kills forged SAML tokens, and no other step does. Plan for the knock-on effect: products that trust vCenter single sign-on may need to be re-registered. Afterwards, confirm that sessions created with the old key fail. Reset vSphere identities. Reset administrator@vsphere.local and every other SSO and local account, remove accounts and Administrators-group members you didn't create, and rotate solution-user certificates, service-account passwords and third-party integration tokens tied to vsphere.local. Clean up the hosts. Reset ESXi root passwords and remove any SSH keys you didn't add to authorized_keys. Treat Active Directory as exposed if a domain controller ran there. If a domain controller's virtual disk sat on a host the attackers reached, assume every domain password hash was taken. That means resetting privileged and service accounts and resetting the krbtgt account twice, with time for replication in between, the standard response to a stolen NTDS.dit. Step 6 is the one that turns a VMware incident into a company-wide one, so decide early whether it applies to you. Harden the vCenter control plane This is ARMORY CASTLE's second zero-day in one intrusion, and Mandiant's point is that patching alone can't keep up with that. Its hardening advice centers on making vCenter hard to reach and noisy when someone tries. Don't rely on the built-in appliance firewall. Mandiant notes that the firewall managed through vCenter's appliance management interface can't restrict access port by port, so trusting a backup server for the API trusts it for SSH and management too. It's managed from the same interface an attacker would take over, it doesn't log blocked connections remotely, and it doesn't control outbound traffic. Enforce rules below the application. CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter's directory service, rated 9.8 out of 10. An attacker who can reach vCenter on the network can become administrator@vsphere.local without a password. A suspected China-nexus espionage group, ARMORY CASTLE, exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. Broadcom patched it on Nov. 19, and CISA gave U.S. federal agencies until Nov. 23 to fix it.

Install the patch today. Then plan for the harder job. If anything that could reach your vCenter was compromised at any point since September, the patch closes the door but doesn't take back what went through it. In the intrusion researchers investigated, that included vCenter's SAML signing key, its master encryption key and Active Directory credentials copied straight out of virtual machine disks.

Let's see how the attackers used this flaw, which builds fix it, and the hunting and credential rotation that should follow the patch.

What Is CVE-2026-123890

Broadcom disclosed the flaw last week, in advisory VMSA-2026-0009, which fixes five vulnerabilities across vCenter, SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows. CVE-2026-123890 is the critical one. An authentication bypass using an alternate path (CWE-288) in the VMware Directory Service, the component behind vCenter's single sign-on. Mandiant found it and reported it privately.

The bug lives in a remote procedure call interface that vCenter's directory service exposes on TCP port 2012. Its Secure Remote Password login generates predictable identifiers based on timestamps, and according to researchers, an attacker can use that to recover the shared session key without knowing any password. The result is an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local, the most powerful account in a vSphere environment.

From there, an attacker can run commands and copy files through the directory service, including data.mdb, the database that holds the SSO domain's accounts and the private key vCenter uses to sign SAML login tokens. It is not a virtual machine escape. It's worse in a different way - it hands over the console that manages every host and VM.

Two things make it easy to get wrong:

  • It's a different bug from CVE-2026-59309, the vCenter authentication bypass Broadcom fixed in July. Mandiant observed attackers using CVE-2026-123890 against a vCenter that was already patched for the July flaw.

  • There is no workaround. Broadcom's only fix is the update, which its own FAQ treats as an emergency change.

How ARMORY CASTLE used it from a support box to domain credentials

Mandiant's write-up shows why vCenter being reachable only from the internal network didn't protect it. The attackers never touched vCenter from the internet. They worked their way to it from the inside.

ARMORY CASTLE's path from a remote-support appliance to Active Directory credentials

  1. Break in at the edge. The group, formerly tracked as UNC5221, first exploited a separate zero-day in BeyondTrust Remote Support, CVE-2026-102764.

  2. Find the VMware estate. From the support appliance, it scanned the internal network for VMware ports, including 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080, then moved to internal Linux appliances that had no endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. It dropped two web shells and became root by setting the SUID bit on /bin/env with the gdb debugger.

  3. Take vCenter. A custom Go tool Mandiant calls BONESAW exploited CVE-2026-123890 over port 2012, created a new SSO administrator account, copied the directory database and extracted the token-signing key.

  4. Forge logins. A second tool, SAWSNAKE, used the stolen key to sign SAML tokens as the administrator, a "Golden SAML" attack that bypasses passwords and MFA.

  5. Drop into the appliance. The group switched on SSH through vCenter's appliance management API, logged in with its new account, stole vCenter's master encryption key and its PostgreSQL database password, then switched SSH off again.

  6. Reach the hosts and the domain. It logged in to ESXi hosts as vpxuser and root, added its own SSH key, and used a Python tool to extract the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) and registry hives straight from a virtual machine's disk. The files left through the original support appliance.

Two backdoors kept the door open: BEARBONES, a modified Dropbear SSH server that accepts a hardcoded password, and LAZYBONES, which takes commands through Slack. The timing matters too. BONESAW's build timestamp is July 13, 2026, and the attackers used it in early September. Go build timestamps can be faked, but Mandiant reads it as a tool built for broader operations, not a one-off.

Which vCenter versions fix CVE-2026-123890?

Product line Affected Fixed in vCenter in VCF / vSphere Foundation 9.1 9.1.x 9.1.1.0200 vCenter in VCF / vSphere Foundation 9.0 9.0.x 9.0.2.0200 vCenter Server 8.0 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x 5.x 5.2.5 vCenter Server 7.0 7.0 No public fix; extended-support customers go through Broadcom Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure Listed versions See Broadcom KB463116

A few details that trip people up:

  • Patched in July doesn't mean patched now. Every vCenter below the builds in the table needs this update, including systems that already have the CVE-2026-59309 fix.

  • vCenter 7.0 is the hard case. vSphere 7.0 reached the end of general support on Oct. 2, 2025, so there's no public fix. Broadcom's supplemental FAQ also says to presume versions 6.5 and 6.7 are affected. If you're on any of these, restricting network access to port 2012 is your main protection until you can upgrade or obtain a fix.

  • ESXi isn't in the advisory. The flaw is in vCenter. ESXi hosts still matter for the cleanup, because the attackers used vCenter to reach them.

  • Don't run the GitHub "proof of concept." A repository that appeared on Nov. 20 claiming exploit code describes the wrong advisory and fixed versions. As of Nov. 21, Rapid7 had opened a Metasploit module titled as an authentication bypass to root, so expect working public exploit code soon, if it isn't out already.

Why patching isn't enough

The patch fixes the login flaw. It does nothing about what an attacker took while the flaw was open, and in this case the stolen items are exactly the kind that keep working:

  • The token-signing key. Anyone holding vCenter's SAML signing key can mint valid administrator logins until that certificate is replaced. A patched vCenter will accept them.

  • New accounts. The attackers created an SSO administrator named sps- followed by random characters in vsphere.local. BONESAW can also add a machine account and grant Global Administrator rights on the vCenter root folder.

  • Appliance secrets. vCenter's master encryption key and PostgreSQL password were copied over SSH.

  • Host access. An SSH key was added to the ESXi root account.

  • Active Directory. A copy of NTDS.dit plus the SYSTEM hive is enough to recover the password hashes of every account in the domain, offline.

The exposure window also runs further back than most patch plans assume. Exploitation started in early September, more than 10 weeks before the fix. If any system that could reach your vCenter's management ports was compromised in that time, treat vCenter as possibly compromised too until you've checked.

After the patch: what to hunt for

Search logs back to at least early September 2026. These come from Mandiant's analysis; ARMORY CASTLE deletes its tools after use, so absence of files doesn't prove absence of compromise.

On the network

  • Connections to TCP 2012 on vCenter from anything other than your documented management hosts, especially Linux appliances or remote-support servers.

  • Internal scans for VMware ports 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080.

  • Servers calling the Slack API, and SSH services announcing the banner SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345, often on high, non-standard ports.

  • Traffic to the 11 suspected obfuscation-network IPs in GTIG's report, such as 103.147.251[.]5 and 176.9.89[.]66.

On vCenter

  • SSO accounts you didn't create, especially names starting with sps- in vsphere.local, and unexpected members of the Administrators group.

  • A PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh call to the appliance management API, particularly SSH being enabled and disabled again shortly after.

  • SSH logins to the appliance, and reads of the master key or PostgreSQL password files.

On ESXi hosts

  • ESXi Host Client logins as vpxuser and root SSH sessions you can't explain.

  • New entries in root's authorized_keys.

  • Hidden directories such as .a on VMFS volumes, and the files vmfs-pydist.tar.gz or vmfs_browser.py.

On internal Linux appliances

  • The files /tmp/123 (BONESAW), /tmp/sss (SAWSNAKE), /tmp/dbr (BEARBONES), /tmp/123.key and /tmp/gdb_file.

  • /usr/bin/vmtoolscs (LAZYBONES) running as a systemd service that restarts every 50 minutes.

  • Web shells named ActiveSer.jsp or u.jsp, and the SUID bit set on /bin/env.

GTIG has published YARA rules for BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES and both web shells in the same report.

After the patch: what to rotate and reset

If you find signs of compromise, or can't rule it out because logs don't reach back to September, work through this in order. Patch and lock down access first, or the attacker can simply take the new secrets too. These steps reflect the consensus among incident responders building on Mandiant's findings; follow Broadcom's knowledge base procedures for each vCenter task.

  1. Patch, then close the paths in. Install the fixed build, patch BeyondTrust Remote Support if you run it, and restrict ports 2012, 443, 5480 and 22 on vCenter to named management hosts.

  2. Rebuild what you can't trust. Where compromise is confirmed, rebuild vCenter and the affected Linux appliances rather than cleaning them. The attackers had root and deleted their tools as they went.

  3. Replace the STS signing certificate. This is the step that kills forged SAML tokens, and no other step does. Plan for the knock-on effect: products that trust vCenter single sign-on may need to be re-registered. Afterwards, confirm that sessions created with the old key fail.

  4. Reset vSphere identities. Reset administrator@vsphere.local and every other SSO and local account, remove accounts and Administrators-group members you didn't create, and rotate solution-user certificates, service-account passwords and third-party integration tokens tied to vsphere.local.

  5. Clean up the hosts. Reset ESXi root passwords and remove any SSH keys you didn't add to authorized_keys.

  6. Treat Active Directory as exposed if a domain controller ran there. If a domain controller's virtual disk sat on a host the attackers reached, assume every domain password hash was taken. That means resetting privileged and service accounts and resetting the krbtgt account twice, with time for replication in between, the standard response to a stolen NTDS.dit.

Step 6 is the one that turns a VMware incident into a company-wide one, so decide early whether it applies to you.

Harden the vCenter control plane

This is ARMORY CASTLE's second zero-day in one intrusion, and Mandiant's point is that patching alone can't keep up with that. Its hardening advice centers on making vCenter hard to reach and noisy when someone tries.

Don't rely on the built-in appliance firewall. Mandiant notes that the firewall managed through vCenter's appliance management interface can't restrict access port by port, so trusting a backup server for the API trusts it for SSH and management too. It's managed from the same interface an attacker would take over, it doesn't log blocked connections remotely, and it doesn't control outbound traffic.

Enforce rules below the application. Mandiant recommends its VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool, which applies default-deny iptables rules at the operating-system level, filters outbound traffic and forwards blocked connections and shell commands to a SIEM. By Mandiant's analysis, those rules would have blocked the exploit on port 2012, the forged logins on 443, the SSH pivot and the Slack command channel. Test any such rules under change control before production.

Close the visibility gaps. The attackers chose Linux appliances with no EDR as their staging ground. Inventory every appliance that can reach vCenter or ESXi, and get logs off them if you can't run an agent. Manage vSphere only from privileged access workstations, as set out in Mandiant's vSphere defender's guide.

Yes. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say the suspected China-nexus group ARMORY CASTLE exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 20, 2026, with a Nov. 23 remediation deadline for federal agencies.

vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m, and VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.5. vCenter 7.0 has no public fix; extended-support customers must go through Broadcom. There is no workaround.

I installed the July fix for CVE-2026-59309. Am I protected?

No. CVE-2026-123890 is a separate flaw, and Mandiant observed it being exploited against a vCenter already patched for CVE-2026-59309. You need the November builds.

As of Nov. 21, 2026, the attackers' tool hadn't been released, and a GitHub repository claiming a proof of concept was fake. Rapid7 had opened a Metasploit module, so working public exploit code is expected soon.

items.title: AI-Powered Hackers Gain Access to 3,392 User Accounts and Decrypt 50 SSH Private Keys
items.summary: An attacker using the CyberStrikeAI framework gained access to 3,392 user accounts and their active session tokens during a four-day cloud intrusion in October 2026. The operator also decrypted a bastion host’s database to recover 50 SSH private keys. The activity spanned two Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts and seven Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) clusters, according to a November 23 disclosure. The scale became clear only after investigators compared the victim’s security logs with more than 3,000 files left exposed on the attacker’s server. The logs showed activity inside AWS and Kubernetes, while the exposed files revealed what happened in the identity system and on other hosts. A separate investigation into exposed ARTEX operator servers showed how similar mistakes have helped researchers reconstruct AI-assisted attacks. Researchers at Wiz identified a custom rootkit, malware designed to hide and maintain access, on compromised Kubernetes nodes. It masqueraded as a font configuration service and used DNS traffic to communicate. The sample had zero detections on VirusTotal at the time Wiz examined it, but the public report did not disclose a file hash that defenders could use to identify it. AI-Powered Hackers Gain Access to 3,392 User Accounts The intruder entered with a stolen session tied to a Terraform runner, a service used to manage cloud infrastructure. That access led to elevated Kubernetes privileges. Wiz also documented a compromise of the Jenkins build controller and the use of stolen cloud credentials from the attacker’s own server. Those credentials exposed infrastructure records and cloud secrets beyond the systems where they were originally issued. The attacker’s files showed that forged administrator tokens opened access to the identity provider’s 3,392 users and their live session tokens. The tokens matter because they can let someone act as an already signed-in user without knowing the password. The figure describes the accounts the attacker could access; the report does not say the operator individually signed in as all 3,392 users. The operator decrypted the database of a bastion host, a controlled entry point for administrators connecting to private systems, and recovered 50 SSH private keys. Artex harvester agentic attacks walkthrough (Source – Wiz) The files also showed that the attacker placed beacons, which can signal back to an operator, on 19 hosts. Wiz did not say that each recovered key was used or that the 50 keys corresponded to 50 separate machines. The breach also reached the systems that build and deploy software. The attacker extracted GitHub Actions secrets and changed the production Jenkins configuration to run before its approval check, exposing production secrets. Separate reporting on GitHub Actions credential theft shows why build systems are valuable targets: a single workflow can have access to credentials for several services. Wiz also found that the operator collected Anthropic API keys from 50 hosts and searched employees’ AI coding-assistant histories for production sign-on credentials. CyberStrikeAI as the framework The original Wiz Research report identifies CyberStrikeAI as the framework that ran the operation. Investigators found a copy of ARTEX on the same server, but that does not make the intrusion part of the same campaign as the other attacks discussed in the report. Seeing both sides of an attack (Source – Wiz) Wiz also noted csai-escape , csai-pentest-role , and csai-probe as names the operator left on resources in this case. Those strings can help narrow a search, but they are not unique fingerprints. In a separate campaign, Wiz saw more than 220 proxy IPs used against a single target. That churn helps explain why FBI guidance on ARTEX is more useful alongside behavioral monitoring than as a reason to rely on static blocklists. For defenders, the strongest leads are unusual administrative sessions, sudden spikes in secret retrieval, and cloud credentials used from unexpected locations. If the logs confirm exposure, invalidate affected sessions and replace the stolen SSH keys and other secrets. Then review which systems still trust those keys, which build jobs can reach production, and whether any workloads gained privileges they did not need. A password reset alone does not address a stolen SSH key or a compromised build credential. items.title: Hackers Plant Backdoors in 6 WordPress Plugins to Steal Passwords and Take Over Websites
items.summary: Hackers planted a remote-control backdoor in nine versions of six WordPress plugins from WP connect on November 22, 2026. The malware could let an attacker steal password hashes, run commands, and take over a website. But WordPress.org blocked the tainted versions before distributing them and closed all six plugins that evening. The advisory does not report confirmed password theft or website takeovers from the incident. Wordfence estimated that the six plugins had more than 3,600 active installations combined. That figure describes the plugins’ reach, not the number of compromised sites. The malicious versions were committed through the developer’s own WordPress.org account. WP connect reported that its account had been compromised, but how the attackers gained access was not clear when the advisory was published. Researchers at Wordfence identified the malware independently of the WordPress.org Plugins Team. Wordfence’s PRISM monitoring system flagged suspicious changes in two plugins within a minute of each other, and analysts traced the same module to four more. A researcher known as Computeronfire separately reported the backdoor in Air WP Sync. Hackers Plant Backdoors in 6 WordPress Plugins The affected releases were Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress 2.9.1–2.9.4, WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress 1.7.4, Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms 2.6.3, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable 2.5.4, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion 1.6.4, and Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce 1.0.2. The release immediately preceding each plugin’s affected version or range did not contain the backdoor. Each tainted release loaded a new PHP file that passed itself off as an analytics and update module. An earlier WordPress plugin backdoor case also hid malicious code behind an update-related feature. In the WP connect incident, Wordfence found the same module across all six plugins, with a slightly earlier draft in Air WP Sync 2.9.1. The module ran during normal site requests and used WP-Cron, WordPress’s scheduler, to check in every 30 minutes as a fallback. It sent the site URL, software versions, server account name, and previous command output to a remote server. The module could execute PHP sent back by that server without a WordPress login. It also disabled verification of the server’s TLS certificate. Backdoor offers multiple capabilities The backdoor could run shell commands, read or change files, query database tables, and extract usernames, email addresses, and password hashes. A hash is not a plaintext password, but a stolen hash can be used to test password guesses offline. The malware could also plant a webshell, a script that provides remote access, or set up an hourly task to run malicious code. As earlier reporting on self-rebuilding WordPress backdoors showed, removing the original plugin does not necessarily remove everything it installed. WordPress.org’s release hold kept the versions out of the update channel while Gandalf, its automated reviewer, independently detected the malicious code and stopped the rollout. The incident shows why automated plugin update reviews matter even when a commit comes from a trusted developer account. Wordfence tracks the backdoor as CVE-2026-135202, with a critical CVSS score of 9.8. No patched versions were available at disclosure. Wordfence estimated that the six plugins had more than 3,600 active installations combined. That figure describes the plugins’ reach, not the number of compromised sites.

The malicious versions were committed through the developer’s own WordPress.org account. WP connect reported that its account had been compromised, but how the attackers gained access was not clear when the advisory was published.

Researchers at Wordfence identified the malware independently of the WordPress.org Plugins Team. Wordfence’s PRISM monitoring system flagged suspicious changes in two plugins within a minute of each other, and analysts traced the same module to four more. A researcher known as Computeronfire separately reported the backdoor in Air WP Sync.

Hackers Plant Backdoors in 6 WordPress Plugins

The affected releases were Air WP Sync – Airtable to WordPress 2.9.1–2.9.4, WP Sync for Notion – Notion to WordPress 1.7.4, Add-on Brevo for Gravity Forms 2.6.3, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Airtable 2.5.4, Add-On for Contact Form 7 to Notion 1.6.4, and Orders Sync to Airtable for WooCommerce 1.0.2. The release immediately preceding each plugin’s affected version or range did not contain the backdoor.

Each tainted release loaded a new PHP file that passed itself off as an analytics and update module. An earlier WordPress plugin backdoor case also hid malicious code behind an update-related feature.

In the WP connect incident, Wordfence found the same module across all six plugins, with a slightly earlier draft in Air WP Sync 2.9.1.

The module ran during normal site requests and used WP-Cron, WordPress’s scheduler, to check in every 30 minutes as a fallback. It sent the site URL, software versions, server account name, and previous command output to a remote server.

The module could execute PHP sent back by that server without a WordPress login. It also disabled verification of the server’s TLS certificate.

The backdoor could run shell commands, read or change files, query database tables, and extract usernames, email addresses, and password hashes.

A hash is not a plaintext password, but a stolen hash can be used to test password guesses offline. The malware could also plant a webshell, a script that provides remote access, or set up an hourly task to run malicious code.

As earlier reporting on self-rebuilding WordPress backdoors showed, removing the original plugin does not necessarily remove everything it installed.

WordPress.org’s release hold kept the versions out of the update channel while Gandalf, its automated reviewer, independently detected the malicious code and stopped the rollout.

The incident shows why automated plugin update reviews matter even when a commit comes from a trusted developer account. Wordfence tracks the backdoor as CVE-2026-135202, with a critical CVSS score of 9.8. No patched versions were available at disclosure.

items.title: Critical Bluetooth Flaw Could Let Hackers Take Control of Trailer Brakes While Driving
items.summary: A critical Bluetooth flaw in Elecbrakes trailer brake controllers could let someone nearby apply, adjust, or release a trailer’s brakes while it is being towed. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-96805, carries a 9.6 severity score. It requires no pairing, PIN, or action from the driver. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency disclosed the issue on November 19, 2026, alongside two related vulnerabilities. Firmware fixes are available for the EB2 and VM1, but owners must start the update themselves in the Elecbrakes app. The older ELBC 2000 also has the flaw and had no fix at disclosure. The distinction matters because a trailer brake controller governs how much braking force the trailer applies, not how the tow vehicle’s own brakes operate. Element Digital researchers Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy identified the vulnerabilities after Forck noticed his in-car remote had connected to someone else’s trailer without a pairing prompt. They tested only equipment they owned, on private property or in a closed setup. Their report describes a product vulnerability, not a malware campaign. Critical Bluetooth Flaw The controller uses Bluetooth Low Energy to communicate with the Elecbrakes app and wireless remote. On vulnerable firmware, the controller did not verify that braking instructions came from an authorized device. Unlike the PerfektBlue automotive Bluetooth flaws , which affected infotainment software, the Elecbrakes flaw directly exposed a function that controls braking force. In controlled driving tests, stronger unauthorized braking produced noticeably greater deceleration than lighter braking at the same speed. On a public road, unexpected trailer braking could upset the balance of the tow vehicle and trailer. Earlier reporting on a wireless train braking flaw describes a separate technology but highlights the same safety principle: a brake controller must verify who is giving it instructions. The second critical vulnerability, CVE-2026-125273, concerns replay: a controller could accept a previously issued instruction again without checking whether it was fresh. The test setup (Source – Element Digital) It also scored 9.6. That differs from the Volkswagen Bluetooth hacking demonstration , where researchers exploited infotainment software to access cabin functions and data rather than directly commanding trailer brakes. The third issue, CVE-2026-124281, scored 6.1 and affects the wireless firmware update channel. CISA warned that inadequate protection could allow unauthorized firmware changes. The researchers did not install modified firmware on a live controller, so the potential for lasting changes should not be confused with the brake activation they demonstrated in controlled testing. Firmware Fixes and What Elecbrakes Owners Should Do Elecbrakes received the report on May 18 and released fixes on July 6. The CISA industrial control advisory directs EB2 owners to install firmware 3.0.4.4.3 or later and VM1 owners to install 1.3.4.2.1 or later. Open the Elecbrakes app, connect to the controller, and check the installed version. If it is older, start the update manually rather than assuming it has already installed. The patched controllers restrict braking and access to update mode to an authenticated connection. Initial pairing requires physical confirmation through the tow vehicle’s brake pedal. The change made older wireless remotes incompatible with the new pairing process, so Elecbrakes offered affected EB2 and VM1 owners free replacement remotes. Owners who use a remote should check whether theirs needs replacing. All versions of the ELBC 2000 were listed as affected, with no firmware fix available at disclosure. As earlier reporting on legacy Renault vehicle software illustrates, equipment can remain in use long after its software ages. ELBC 2000 owners should contact Elecbrakes for model-specific guidance and check the app periodically for a remediation update. The manual update also leaves a gap between releasing a fix and protecting trailers on the road. By late October, Elecbrakes told the researchers that about 60% of daily active EB2 and VM1 users had installed the latest firmware. That figure does not account for owners who rarely open the app. Fleet operators should verify the firmware on each controller rather than using that rollout figure as evidence that their own units are patched. items.title: Hackers Target Check Point Security Management Servers, Putting Corporate Firewall Controls at Risk
items.summary: Hackers are breaking into Check Point Security Management Servers. These servers hold the rules that decide what traffic a company’s firewalls allow or block. A new campaign has already hit at least 22 organizations worldwide, and the attacker still has access to many of them. Check Point management servers are a high-value target because they work like a control room for firewalls. Whoever controls one can read the firewall settings, copy stored credentials, and change the security policy. Confirmed activity ran from October 17 to November 2, 2026. The victims are in financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing. Researchers at GreyNoise identified the activity and are tracking it as GreyNoise Threat 13, or GT13. They have not tied it to any known threat group. They also cannot say whether the attacker is a nation-state or why they chose these targets. The campaign has no clear focus on one region or industry. Victims sit in the United Kingdom, Germany, France, India, Thailand, South Korea, Australia, the United States, and several other countries. Hackers Target Check Point Security Management Servers The attacker used 99 IP addresses. Every one was either an ExpressVPN exit point or a hacked Check Point device. GreyNoise first saw the activity on October 2, when the attacker broke into a Rejetto HFS file server using CVE-2026-61500. HFS creates session cookies from a weak random number function. By logging in several times in a row, the attacker worked out the secret key and forged an admin cookie, so no password was needed. That hacked server became a relay box, which GreyNoise calls a “hop.” The attacker used it to run tools and store stolen data. These tools included Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, and Paramiko. The attacker also ran at least 30 Python scripts. From there, the attacker used CVE-2026-16232, a Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass, to run scripts on management servers. The attacker launched more than 100 management tasks, copied the firewall database and the internal certificate authority, and tried to unload security policies, which would turn off the firewall. Adversary infrastructure (Source – GreyNoise) This is not the first time Check Point products have been in the crosshairs. Earlier this month, researchers saw hackers who chained Check Point firewall flaws to get root access and wipe files on a VMware ESXi host. Other recent reports described how hackers abused critical Check Point VPN flaws to get in without logging in. GreyNoise could not tell how the attacker first got into the Check Point servers. The attacker already had access to them before breaking into the HFS server. The attacker also probed Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS, and domain controllers. Some of the older flaws they tried, such as the actively exploited CitrixBleed 2 bug, have been public for more than a year. This shows that missed patches elsewhere in a network can still give attackers a way in. AI Tools, Stealth, and What Defenders Should Do GreyNoise thinks the attacker used large language models and agentic AI systems to scan for weak systems, run exploits, and write tools. Some odd gaps in the timeline fit this theory. In one case, an automated download failed and the attacker spent a day fixing it. On November 2, the attacker also tested for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug, CVE-2026-98432. The attacker then used the nftables firewall tool to block packets that could trigger it. This kept other hackers from taking over the relay box. GreyNoise’s view stopped around November 2, but it expects the campaign to continue because the attacker still has access to victim devices. The company is sharing details with government partners and national security teams (CERTs) to warn victims. One error message pointed to an odd file, /usr/lib/.libproc.so, listed in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may be a hidden implant. Check Point customers should patch SmartConsole and management servers and limit which IP addresses can reach them. They should also review logs for the indicators below. Security teams should look for unexpected SSH keys, new certificates, and policy changes. CISA has already added two Check Point flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, so patching should be a top priority. Check Point also publishes fixes and guidance on its security advisory blog . GreyNoise has the full technical report on its campaign research page . items.title: SplitSecure Launches New Access Control Architecture for Humans and AI Agents
items.summary: San Francisco, United States, November 23rd, 2026, CyberNewswire SplitSecure , the cybersecurity technology provider, today unveiled a new access control platform based on secret splitting technology. The platform is intended to replace traditional access controls tools such as password managers, PAM, and vaults. On launch, it supports passwords, passkeys, one-time codes, SAML & OIDC federation, SSH, x.509 CA, OpenPGP, code signing (Nitro, Google Chrome Extensions), and general secrets vaulting. The platform is intended for secure organizations of all sizes, including both large enterprise plans and a free plan for teams of up to six. The access control space today contains a wide variety of tools. A secure organization would typically require a password manager, MFA app, vault, certificate manager, and PAM, among other tools. But despite their variety, all these tools use a common architecture where clients’ secrets are stored in a singular “vault”. It is this architecture SplitSecure seeks to disrupt, with a new way of storing and using secrets based on secret-splitting. Secret splitting is the practice of breaking secrets across multiple devices rather than storing them in one location. This has been common practice in classified government environments for over thirty years but has historically been seen as high-effort and has had only limited adoption in industry. SplitSecure’s new platform is a significant advance of the state of the art, offering a ready-to-use implementation of techniques that were previously limited to advanced security teams in elite organizations. Because of this general advancement, SplitSecure is able to replicate the functionality of many common tools. Its new platform provides password management, MFA, vaulting, certificate signing, and more PAM functionality such as shared accounts and resources. Supported resource types include passwords, passkeys, one-time codes, SAML 2.0 sign-ons, secrets, certificates, SSH certificates, signing keys, OpenPGP identities, and crypto wallets. This new technology also offers the particular advantage that it cryptographically guarantees the service provider has no access to client’s secrets. This is in contrast to traditional PAM tools, in which the provider holds the “keys to the kingdom” at all times and a compromised vendor may be able to compromise client information. Tristan Morris, CEO of SplitSecure, commented: “We were very ambitious […] we wanted a tool where people didn’t have to trust us as the provider, whereby design they’re the custodians of their own secrets. But we also wanted it to be so easy to use you could imagine a non-technical person using it instead of a password manager. We’ve done that, and it’s amazing to see it launch.”He also noted that SplitSecure’s new platform integrates with common identity providers for an easier transition. “It should always be easy to set up,” he said. “Migration, first time setup, our goal was for that to take under half an hour.” Details on supported security and privacy frameworks are available in the SplitSecure Trust Center. The free plan of SplitSecure’s new platform, which is available to all customers now, offers access control with the following key differentiators: Modern Privileged Access: Zero trust, just-in-time access, zero standing privilege, on-demand step-up authentication, multi-party approvals, and quantum resistance come as standard. Condenses Multiple Tools: SplitSecure can condense two to five tools in the security stack. No-Vendor-Threat Architecture: Root keys are held exclusively by the customer, so SplitSecure as the vendor has no access to customer secrets. Built-In Audit and Compliance: Every privileged action are logged automatically with full context on every plan. Paid plans can view the logs for security analysis and forensics. About SplitSecure SplitSecure is a cybersecurity technology provider, established to develop and modernize secret splitting technology. After being founded in 2025 by Tristan Morris and Marc Tremblay, it raised $4.7M from Cowboy, Twelve Below, and Cofound Ventures. Its access control platform combines PAM, password and passkey management, secrets vaulting, and auditing in one product, with root keys held exclusively by the customer. SplitSecure’s new access control platform is free for teams of up to six. Learn more at splitsecure.com or read the documentation . Email: contact@splitsecure.com Website: splitsecure.com Contact Chief of Staff Slava Pashchenko SplitSecure slava@splitsecure.com

As organizations respond to a turbulent week in cybersecurity, Cofense is seeing a significant increase in malicious email activity. Across our global Cofense Remediation customer base, polymorphic attacks across voice and email increased by more than 30%. This is not simply a theoretical risk. Our threat analysts continue to identify credential phishing, business email compromise, scams, and other malicious messages reaching organizations that rely on established email security platforms. What Is Getting Through? AI-driven detection is essential, but it takes more than automated detection to stop sophisticated phishing attacks. Recent Cofense analysis identified that malicious emails still reached organizations protected by AI-only email security solutions, including credential phishing, business email compromise, and sophisticated scams. These findings reinforce the importance of a layered, post-perimeter defense that combines AI-driven detection, human-validated intelligence, and automated remediation to identify and remove threats that evade existing controls. Of the customers who have a robust multi-layered defense, which includes a SEG, an ICES tool and Cofense managed remediation through the Phishing Defense Center, we saw a 71% increase in their daily average malicious rate since the start of the recent cyberattack reporting. Why This Matters AI-driven detection remains essential to defending against today’s phishing threats. But the continued presence of malicious emails in protected environments reinforces a critical point: organizations need visibility into what gets through, not just confidence in what gets blocked. As attackers adapt their techniques, organizations need defenses that can adapt just as quickly. Removing that one message protects the person who reported it. Finding the other versions can protect employees who received a similar email and haven’t flagged it. That’s why teams need a way to investigate across inboxes. Why AI alone isn’t enough AI is essential to modern security. It processes volume and speed that no team could match by hand. Employees at one Cofense Phishing Defense Center customer reported the suspicious email, enabling our analysts to use that report to help protect all our customers from the same threat. Human analysts close that gap. They judge intent and context, and they respond to what automation hasn’t learned yet. Reports from employees and customers feed back into protection, so one organization’s report can help protect many others. In one recent case, a brand-new lure got past several automated systems, including AI-based ones. Employees at a Cofense Phishing Defense Center customer reported the lure, in turn giving Cofense analysts the opportunity to protect all of our customers from this threat. Speed and human judgment working together made the difference. Cofense has seen a 22% growth from 2025 to 2026 so far in non-Microsoft related branding being used in phishing attacks as AI allows threat actors to expand upon the types of threats they are able to create. Depending on the industry, between 39% and 49% of phishing subject lines included the recipient’s name or other personal details. It is becoming increasingly easy for threat actors to use AI to harvest employee information and use it in phishing campaigns. Find the campaign and remove it Say one employee reports a fake service alert. Start with that email, then check whether other inboxes received related versions. AI helps group similar messages for analyst review. An analyst confirms which emails are malicious so the team can remove them, including copies nobody reported. That’s the difference between closing one report and removing the campaign. See how Cofense Vision AI connects related messages What organizations can do now Walk through the steps below with the people who own email security, IT, and incident response. items.title: Automation You Can Explain: Why AI-Driven Phishing Defense Needs Human Oversight
items.summary: AI is transforming cybersecurity, enabling organizations to detect, analyze, and respond to threats faster than ever before. But as organizations increasingly rely on AI to make critical security decisions, an important question emerges: Who is ultimately accountable when AI takes action? In its September 2026 report , Reduce AI Risk by Making Human “Guardians” Your Last Line of Defense, Gartner® examines the growing need for meaningful human oversight as AI becomes more deeply embedded in enterprise decision-making. Download the complete report here. Gartner emphasizes that “real human oversight of AI outputs — not just ticking a compliance box or rubber-stamping decisions — is non-negotiable.” This distinction is particularly important in phishing defense, where automated decisions can have immediate consequences for an organization's security and business operations. At Cofense, we believe AI should empower security teams, not replace their judgment. The future of phishing defense isn't about choosing between human expertise and automation. It's about combining both to deliver faster, more accurate, and more accountable security outcomes. Who Is Accountable When AI Acts Inside Your Inbox? Phishing attacks are increasingly sophisticated, with threat actors exploiting trusted platforms, legitimate services, and evolving techniques to bypass traditional security controls. For security teams facing a constant influx of suspicious emails, AI-driven automation is essential to identifying and containing threats at scale. But what happens when an automated system makes the wrong decision? Consider an AI-powered security platform that identifies a suspicious email campaign and automatically quarantines messages across an organization. When the detection is accurate, the platform can prevent a potential compromise in seconds. But an incorrect classification could disrupt legitimate business communications, while a missed threat could expose employees to credential theft, malware, or business email compromise (BEC). These scenarios and more, demonstrate why automation must be accompanied by clear accountability. Gartner warns that “AI-driven workflows increase enterprise productivity but introduce significant risk, including biases, compliance gaps, and accountability voids.” As systems become more autonomous, organizations must be able to trace, explain, and challenge the decisions they make. For phishing defense, we view that to mean knowing who is responsible for automated actions, understanding why a threat was flagged, and maintaining the ability to intervene when necessary. AI can accelerate decision-making, but accountability must remain with the people responsible for protecting the organization. Why Is Rubber-Stamping AI Not Real Oversight? Only including a human in an automated workflow does not necessarily mean meaningful oversight is taking place. If analysts are simply asked to approve AI-generated recommendations without understanding the reasoning behind them, their involvement becomes a formality rather than an effective security control. Gartner addresses this challenge by calling for organizations to move from a traditional “human-in-the-loop” approach toward a “human-in-the-lead” model. Under this model, human “decision stewards” take an active role in governing AI-driven decisions, with the authority to monitor, challenge, and override decisions when necessary. They recommend tailoring this oversight to the level of risk, applying stronger human controls to high-impact decisions while allowing lower-risk processes to operate with lighter supervision. This approach is especially relevant to phishing defense. Security analysts cannot manually investigate every suspicious email at the speed and scale required to combat modern attacks. AI can handle repetitive tasks, identify malicious patterns, and accelerate response times, while human expertise provides essential judgment when decisions become more complex. The goal isn't to introduce unnecessary friction into every automated process. It's to ensure security professionals have the visibility and authority to intervene when it matters most. Effective human oversight isn't about slowing AI down. It's about making automation more trustworthy. What Does Real Human Oversight Look Like in Phishing Defense? For organizations adopting AI-driven phishing defense, meaningful oversight should be embedded directly into the technology and its workflows. Three capabilities are essential: Human Authority Over Automated Actions Experts emphasize that decision stewards must have the authority to stop, pause, or question AI-driven decisions rather than simply approve them. In phishing defense, this means giving security teams control over how automation operates, including the ability to configure workflows, establish approval requirements, and intervene when necessary. Explainable AI Decisions We see that Gartner highlights the importance of forensic accountability, including the ability to trace and explain AI-driven actions. For security teams, explainability means understanding why an email was classified as malicious and what indicators contributed to that detection. This context allows analysts to validate findings, investigate potential errors, and make informed response decisions rather than accepting AI-generated classifications at face value. Complete Audit Trails According to Gartner, “Traceability makes enterprise governance transparent and defensible in the face of increasing regulatory demands.” Comprehensive audit trails document automated decisions, human interventions, and response actions, giving security teams the evidence needed to investigate incidents, evaluate performance, and demonstrate accountability to leadership and auditors. Together, these capabilities create a foundation for AI-driven phishing defense that balances operational efficiency with transparency and human control. Why Does Human Oversight Matter Most in Regulated Industries? For highly regulated industries such as financial services and healthcare, the consequences of poorly governed AI decisions can extend beyond operational disruption to regulatory exposure and reputational damage. Organizations must be able to demonstrate that automated systems operate within established policies, maintain appropriate controls, and provide sufficient documentation for internal and regulatory review. Yet many organizations are still developing the governance practices necessary to meet these expectations. Gartner reports that only one in five organizations have highly effective AI governance practices and rank projects based specifically on an assessed AI risk-to-value ratio. The research also finds that just 49% of AI leaders conduct regular audits or risk assessments of AI systems recognizing that AI outputs cannot be blindly trusted. As AI adoption expands, governance practices must evolve alongside it. This means evaluating more than detection accuracy and response speed. Security leaders must also consider whether their technology supports transparent decision-making, documented response actions, and appropriate human intervention. Data governance is another critical consideration, particularly when security platforms process sensitive email content. Organizations need to understand where their data is stored, how it is processed, and whether automated workflows align with their compliance requirements. Responsible AI adoption requires more than proving that automation works. Organizations must also be able to explain how it works and demonstrate that appropriate safeguards are in place. What Three Questions Should You Ask Your AI Security Vendor? We see that Gartner recommends establishing clear metrics to measure AI trust and performance, including decision quality, reversals, and operational impact. For organizations evaluating AI-driven phishing defense, three questions can help determine whether a platform delivers automation with meaningful accountability: Who has the authority to approve or override automated actions? Can security teams configure approval workflows, establish appropriate levels of oversight, and intervene when AI-driven decisions require additional review? Can we understand why AI flagged a particular threat? Does the platform provide sufficient context to explain its detections, allowing analysts to validate findings and investigate potential errors? Can we demonstrate accountability for every automated decision? Does the platform maintain comprehensive audit trails documenting detections, response actions, and human involvement? These questions help organizations assess not only how much a platform can automate, but how effectively that automation can be governed. How Cofense Combines Human Expertise with AI-Driven Automation At Cofense, we believe the strongest phishing defense comes from combining the speed and scalability of AI with the experience and judgment of human security professionals. Our AI-driven phishing defense platform is designed around this principle, helping organizations detect and respond to threats that bypass traditional security controls while maintaining visibility and control over automated actions. This approach reflects the principles behind the Gartner “human-in-the-lead” model, where AI supports decision-making while people retain the authority to oversee outcomes. Cofense delivers this through three foundational capabilities: Human-Supervised Automation : Configurable, opt-in automation and analyst approval workflows allow security teams to maintain authority over response actions. Explainable Detections : Visibility into why threats are flagged helps analysts evaluate AI-generated findings and make informed decisions. Comprehensive Audit Trails : Detailed records of automated actions provide the transparency organizations need to support security governance and accountability. By combining purpose-built AI, expert-validated threat intelligence, and human oversight, Cofense helps organizations improve operational efficiency without sacrificing control. This approach delivers measurable results. Cofense's human-supervised AI achieves 9 9.998% accuracy with a 66% lower false positive rate , helping reduce unnecessary investigations while maintaining confidence in threat detection. Cofense customers can also achieve 80–95% automation in phishing incident response , compared with an industry average of 20–30%, allowing analysts to focus on more complex threats and higher-value security activities. Gartner recommends measuring the performance of combined human-AI operations against AI-only and human-only approaches. For phishing defense, this reinforces the importance of evaluating not just automation rates, but the accuracy, efficiency, and reliability of the outcomes those systems deliver. The goal isn't simply to automate more. It's to automate effectively, with the right balance of AI-driven speed and human judgment. The Future of Phishing Defense Is Human-Supervised As AI becomes more autonomous, the need for meaningful human oversight will only grow. The Gartner research reinforces an important principle: Organizations must move beyond passive approval of AI-generated decisions and establish governance models that give people genuine authority over automated outcomes. For cybersecurity leaders, this means looking beyond the speed of AI-driven detection and response to consider how confidently security teams can explain, validate, and control those actions. At Cofense, we believe the best automation is automation you can explain. By combining AI-driven detection, real-world threat intelligence, and human expertise, organizations can strengthen phishing defenses without sacrificing the transparency and accountability modern security operations demand. A new Gartner® report can be downloaded here . Gartner Source: Jorg Heizenberg, Reduce AI Risk by Making Human “Guardians” Your Last Line of Defense, September 18, 2026, ID G00858549. For cybersecurity leaders, this means looking beyond the speed of AI-driven detection and response to consider how confidently security teams can explain, validate, and control those actions. 

At Cofense, we believe the best automation is automation you can explain. 

By combining AI-driven detection, real-world threat intelligence, and human expertise, organizations can strengthen phishing defenses without sacrificing the transparency and accountability modern security operations demand.

items.title: Critical Node.js simple-git Library Vulnerability Enables Remote Code Execution Attacks
items.summary: A critical flaw in simple-git, a popular Node.js library for running Git commands, can let attackers run their own commands on a server. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-134815. It affects apps that pass untrusted input into Git arguments. The National Vulnerability Database says simple-git versions before 4.1.0 contain an argument injection weakness, listed as CWE-88. In plain terms, the library does not properly separate user-supplied text from the options it sends to Git. VulnCheck, which assigned the CVE, rated it 9.2 (Critical) on the CVSS 4.0 scale. The library has a safety guard named allowUnsafePack. It is meant to block dangerous options that make Git run an outside program. Before this fix, the guard only blocked the –exec option for push operations. Attackers can bypass it by adding –exec to other Git actions. Node.js simple-git Library Flaw The risk starts when an application lets outside input reach the listRemote() or raw() functions. An attacker who controls those arguments can slip in –exec for ls-remote, archive, fetch-pack or send-pack. Git then treats the value as the name of a remote program and runs it on the host. The result is remote code execution, which means the attacker’s commands run with the same rights as the Node.js process. The CVSS vector shows the attack needs no login and no user interaction. It also lists high attack complexity and an attack requirement, so a vulnerable app must be set up in a specific way. Even so, the impact on data, system integrity, and availability is rated high. A researcher write-up from Upwind describes the same bypass of the allowUnsafePack guard. Two packages from the steveukx/git-js project are affected. These are simple-git below 4.1.0 and @simple-git/argv-parser below 3.0.0. The parser package holds the checks that spot dangerous flags, so both need updating together. The maintainers shipped the fix in the simple-git 4.1.0 release on 16 November. The notes say allowUnsafePack now blocks –exec for every command except rebase. The release also adds allowConfig and strict options. It adds a git.cmd helper too, which treats every inserted value as untrusted data that cannot add options or change settings. The maintainers thanked 18 contributors for submitting CVE proposals that shaped these changes. NVD published the record on 22 November. This is not the first time simple-git has had trouble with argument handling. In 2022, CVE-2022-24433 showed that injecting Git options into fetch() could run commands. Earlier this year, CVE-2026-28292 used a missing case-insensitive regex flag to get around older fixes. The library sees more than 12 million weekly npm downloads. Another advisory, CVE-2026-6951 , covered an incomplete fix that blocked -c but not –config. The pattern is clear. Block lists of bad options are hard to keep complete, because Git accepts many ways to write the same option. Upgrade to simple-git 4.1.0 and @simple-git/argv-parser 3.0.0 or later. Then run npm ls simple-git to find copies pulled in by other packages, since many projects use it indirectly. Developers should also stop passing raw user input into listRemote() or raw(). Checking values against a fixed list of allowed repository URLs and branch names is a safer habit. Running the app as a low-rights user adds another layer of protection. Node.js libraries that run system commands have been a steady source of serious problems. A command injection flaw in the systeminformation package followed the same idea of unchecked input reaching a shell. Teams should also keep strict control of their dependencies, as shown when the Keyv package compromise reached millions of weekly installs. Use lockfiles, run npm ci in build systems, and review updates before they ship. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: Hackers Actively Exploiting Cisco Expressway Vulnerability to Gain Full Root Access
items.summary: Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-76466, a critical vulnerability in Cisco Expressway that lets remote attackers run operating system commands with root privileges. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 20, 2026, after finding evidence of active exploitation. Cisco says there is no workaround and urges customers to upgrade. Cisco first disclosed the vulnerability on October 21 and assigned it a severity score of 9.8 out of 10. As Cyber Security News reported in its original coverage of the Cisco Expressway vulnerability , fixed software was available before CISA confirmed exploitation. The federal patch deadline was November 23. The catalog entry also directs agencies to follow CISA’s requirements for checking affected devices for signs of compromise. Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Grants Root Access The vulnerability affects the database service used by clustered Expressway devices. Cisco’s security advisory points to persistent cookies and a failure to check client certificates even when TLS verification is enabled for clustering. An attacker who has the required cookies and can reach the affected device over the network can run commands without a normal login. Those commands run as root, the highest level of access on the underlying operating system. Both Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) are affected, whether deployed as virtual machines or physical appliances. For this specific vulnerability, the device must run an affected software release and be part of a cluster. That distinction matters when checking an inventory: the product name and software version alone do not establish whether a device is exposed. The risk can extend beyond the first device. In a case covered by Cyber Security News , researchers at F6 reported that attackers compromised two internet-facing Expressway devices at one organization and reached two internal cluster members through one of them. Security teams should therefore check internal members of an affected cluster, even if those devices are not directly reachable from the internet. Cisco Expressway Fixed Versions Cisco lists X15.5.20 as the first fixed release for customers running X15.5.3 and earlier. Customers on X14 or earlier must migrate to a fixed release. The update also includes Cisco’s October Expressway security hardening fixes , which address several other vulnerabilities. Cisco credited Stefan Aleksic of Jane Street with reporting the root access vulnerability. Cisco Expressway release Affected products and configuration First fixed release or required action X14 and earlier Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E, physical or virtual, when configured in a cluster Migrate to a fixed release. Cisco does not list a fix in the X14 release train. X15.5.3 and earlier in the X15 release train Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E, physical or virtual, when configured in a cluster Upgrade to X15.5.20, the first fixed release listed by Cisco. Administrators should verify the installed version on every cluster member after upgrading. If a vulnerable device was reachable from the internet, preserve available logs and review activity on both the exposed device and its internal peers. The update closes the vulnerability, but it cannot tell you whether someone already used it. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!
